people.name: More Adey
people.bio: Translator and editor who published the first English translation of Ibsen's Brand (1891) under the pseudonym William Wilson, later ran the Carfax picture gallery with Robert Ross, and was joint editor of the Burlington Magazine, 1911-19. The editors of the Complete Letters describe him as a 'Close friend of Robert Ross'; the two shared lodgings at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington, and both were Roman Catholics - Wilde in 1897 teased 'you and More, especially More' as a unit for treating him 'as a Dissenter'. It was to Adey that Ross addressed, in installments, his narrative of Wilde's final illness, death and funeral (14 December 1900), and a rosary Adey had given Ross was placed around Wilde's neck at the laying-out.
people.bio_note: Born/died, Brand translation, 'Close friend of Robert Ross' and Carfax partnership from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 577 n. 2 (repo PDF 629; Burlington Magazine editorship also in the elided portion of that note, which cites Siegfried Sassoon, Siegfried's Journey, 1945, for his later years). Shared lodgings from the editorial note at p. 781 n. 2 (PDF 832): 'More Adey and Robert Ross shared lodgings at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington'. 'You and More' and the editors' 'Ross and Adey were both Roman Catholics' from p. 866 and n. 1 (PDF 916). Death-narrative addressee and rosary from the Epilogue, pp. 1219 and 1221 (PDF 1264, 1266). All pages read as page images 2026-08-03; printed folios confirmed. Full passages in dossiers/ADEY-GILBERT-TURNER_dossier.md. No source read asserts a romantic or sexual dimension to the Ross household partnership; see the dossier's null-finding note.

people.name: André
people.bio: One of two people Wilde reported meeting on a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor in January 1899, while Wilde was staying at La Napoule on the Riviera. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'one beautiful person, called André, with wonderful eyes'. No surname, age, occupation, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
bio_sources: letters-2000
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). The record preserves a first name only. Named in the same sentence-pair as Pietro but as a separate person - 'one beautiful person, called André … and a little Italian, Pietro' - so the two are two nodes, not one. The letter states no age for him and none is inferred. He is on the roster under the 2026-08-03 decision to give the exile-years liaison tier nodes rather than a collective footnote; the collective mentions on the same tier (the Riviera fishing population, the Napoule fisher-lads) name no individual and stay in the collective context_engagement on wilde.json. Full passage in dossiers/EXILE-LIAISONS_dossier.md (L1). DATES: NONE RECORDED (2026-08-03). Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel treats the Nice trip at printed p. 245 (repo PDF 259) and names 'two young men named André and Pietro, the former "with wonderful eyes"' without adding anything the letter does not already say. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by. That absence is itself the historical fact worth keeping - these men enter the written record only because Wilde wrote to his friends about them.

people.name: Kit Anstruther-Thomson
people.bio: Scottish artist and writer on aesthetics, born 1857, known as "Kit". She replaced Mary Robinson as Vernon Lee's close companion from 1887 to 1900 and became her collaborator: the two ran experiments on bodily response to art informed by Robert Vischer's theory of Einfuhlung, the term Edward Titchener Englished in 1909 as "empathy". Their article "Beauty and Ugliness" (Contemporary Review, October 1897) drew a plagiarism charge from Bernard Berenson, later retracted, and the work was collected as Beauty and Ugliness (1912), co-written with Lee. Anstruther-Thomson died in 1921; Lee wrote a substantial introduction to her posthumous Art and Man (1924) as a tribute.
people.bio_note: Dates (1857-1921), the companion years (1887-1900) and the collaboration from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. She does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters; her link to this map runs through Lee.
bio_sources: pulham-y90s-lee-bio

people.name: I. D. W. Ashton
people.bio: English companion of Wilde's exile years, otherwise untraced: the editors of the Complete Letters have only a visiting-card enclosed in one of Wilde's letters, inscribed 'Mr I. D. W. Ashton. Piccadilly Club, W', and record that 'Further than that he has not been traced.' He was in Naples for about a month by 11 November 1897, during Wilde's Naples months with Lord Alfred Douglas, and Wilde - who saw 'a great deal' of him there - introduced him by letter to Reginald Turner as 'a most charming and delightful fellow' who 'has been a very good friend to me'. He appears again in Paris in December 1898, travelling from St Malo, and was expected to go to the States by January 1899. Wilde's letters record two attachments of his - to Joseph in Paris and to a youth named Walter - and Wilde's verdict on him as 'capital company, and a very astounding person in his capacity for pleasure, grand in his cups, and with a heart of gold'. Nicknamed 'Sir John', the name under which he appears throughout the correspondence.
bio_sources: Identity and the untraced verdict: 'Enclosed in this letter is a visiting-card inscribed "Mr I. D. W. Ashton. Piccadilly Club, W". Further than that he has not been traced. Meyerfeld says that he was nicknamed Sir John, and this is corroborated by the complementary references to him and St Malo on pp. 1118-9. See also p. 1067.' - Holland & Hart-Davis, editors' footnote, Complete Letters (2000), p. 979n (repo PDF 1027, printed folio confirmed on rendered page image, 2026-08-03).

Naples, 1897: 'This is to introduce to you our friend Ashton, who has been in Naples for a month, and of whom we have seen, I am glad to say, a great deal. He is a most charming and delightful fellow, and has been a very good friend to me, so I am anxious for you to know him.' - Wilde to Reginald Turner, 11 November [1897], Villa Giudice, Posilippo; p. 979 (repo PDF 1027, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

Wilde's summing-up, and the States: 'Poor Sir John! However, I think he may do well in the States. … but Sir John was capital company, and a very astounding person in his capacity for pleasure, grand in his cups, and with a heart of gold.' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [? 12 January 1899], Napoule; p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).
people.bio_note: The 'Sir John' = Ashton identity key is verified in the source twice over: the editors' note at 979n, and the editors' cross-reference footnote at 1107n2, which reads in full 'See note 1, p.979'. The key therefore does not rest on the earlier index read, and 'untraced' is the editors' own word, not an inference. Spelling of the external name in the note is Meyerfeld. Dating: 'who has been in Naples for a month' on 11 November 1897 puts his arrival at roughly October 1897; 'we have seen' is Wilde and Douglas. NULL FINDING - no ashton--wilde relationship file exists. Across the four passages read in the source (979, 979n, 1107, 1118) there is no romantic or sexual content between Wilde and Ashton in either direction. In every substantive mention Wilde's grammatical position is spectator to Ashton's love-life - 'He found his little friend Joseph…'; 'Sir John is getting cured of his infatuation'; 'the only thing I never could forgive him was his absurd love of Walter'. Wilde's own register toward him is friendship, gratitude and comic affection. Not read so far: printed 1023, 1049, 1067, 1109-10, 1121, and the St Malo corroboration the editors cite at 1118-9 - printed 1118 was read and carries no St Malo reference, so the corroborating passage is presumably at 1119. Full passages in dossiers/EXILE-COMPANIONS_dossier.md (A1-A4). DATES: NONE RECORDED, AND THE EDITORS SAY SO IN TERMS (2026-08-03). Their footnote, re-read as a page image so far with the printed folio 979 confirmed, is the whole of the identification: 'Enclosed in this letter is a visiting-card inscribed "Mr I. D. W. Ashton. Piccadilly Club, W". Further than that he has not been traced.' Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel discusses him at printed pp. 142 and 240 (repo PDF 156, 254) purely as the 'homosexual friend named Ashton' of Wilde's letters, adding no particulars. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted; the man is a set of initials and a club address.

context_engagements.note: Off-roster. A young man in Paris described by Wilde as Ashton's 'little friend', living in the same establishment in December 1898 and serving at table when sober. Wilde reports Ashton's infatuation as a third party and treats it as a comedy of failed moral influence; the sentence 'Sir John is getting cured of his infatuation' does not name its object, so the identification with Joseph is contextual, from the paragraph it closes.

sources.quote: He found his little friend Joseph with a black eye and a swollen nose, caused by intoxication and a political discussion. Joseph also left him on Sunday morning, and did not appear till the next day, having had vine-leaves in his hair. He is a little Dionysiac, and the conversation of Sir John, which is chiefly composed of good advice, drives him to drink. Tonight I dine with Sir John at Bosie's flat: Joseph is to serve, if he is sober: if not, he is to dine with us, I suppose. I am glad to say Sir John is getting cured of his infatuation: and I have begged him never again to try to have a good influence: it simply drives happy bright-eyed lads to delirium tremens.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 6 December 1898], Hotel d'Alsace, Paris, reporting Ashton's arrival from St Malo after a journey of about eight hours. 'Delirium tremens' is italicised in the original.
sources.supports: Ashton's attachment in Paris, December 1898, reported by Wilde as an onlooker
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1153, printed folio 1107 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Contiguous run from the passage transcribed in full in the dossier (A3).

context_engagements.note: Off-roster, unidentified beyond the first name. Wilde names Ashton's love for him as the one thing he could not forgive, in the same breath as his affectionate verdict on Ashton as a companion - the second instance of the pattern in which Wilde reports and judges Ashton's attachments rather than being party to one.

sources.quote: The only thing I never could forgive him was his absurd love of Walter – a plain, crooked, ugly, and tedious youth – but Sir John was capital company, and a very astounding person in his capacity for pleasure, grand in his cups, and with a heart of gold.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule; the sentences before it are 'Poor Sir John! However, I think he may do well in the States.'
sources.supports: Ashton's second recorded attachment, and Wilde's position as its commentator
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Contiguous run from the passage transcribed in full in the dossier (A4). The editors bracket the letter's date with a query mark, preserved here in the context line.

people.name: Fred Atkins
people.bio: Billiard-marker, bookmaker's clerk and music-hall comedian — 'I am twenty years old' on oath in April 1895 — introduced to Taylor by Schwabe in November 1892 and taken to Paris by Wilde that month as nominal private secretary. He lived and worked blackmail with the bookmaker James Burton; on the stand he denied any impropriety with Wilde, and on recall was proved to have lied on oath about a Rochester Row arrest (a gentleman found naked in bed with him, money demanded) and was ordered from the box. The judge's summing-up called him 'a most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness' (as quoted by the Letters editors), and the jury found Wilde not guilty on every Atkins count.
bio_sources: Atkins's testimony and recall, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 206-210, 216-218 (p. 207 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72, 74 (perjury; not-guilty verdict; djvu OCR)
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 714 n 1 (the judge's phrase; Wilde acquitted of the Atkins charges; read at rendered PDF p. 765, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far ('aged twenty' at the April 1895 trial, his own sworn statement). Sometimes went by 'Denny' (his cross-examination). Mary Applegate's stained-sheets testimony (Hyde p. 211) is the only circumstantial support for the Paris allegation and is preserved in the dossier. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED (2026-08-03). The age is now verified in the source rather than from OCR: Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, printed p. 206 - 'FREDERICK ATKINS, examined by Mr. AVORY. How old are you? - I am twenty years old. What is your business? - I have been a billiard marker. I have also been a bookmaker's clerk and a comedian.' Read as a page image in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, IA PDF p. 247), printed folio 206 confirmed; Mr Justice Charles repeats it in his summing-up ('Atkins is now twenty years of age', located in the same OCR text at printed p. 266 region, not read in the source). An age sworn in April 1895 is not a birth date and none is computed. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. The Complete Letters editors' note at printed p. 714 gives his occupations and the judge's 'most reckless, unreliable, unscrupulous, and untruthful witness', but no dates. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

context_engagements.note: Off-roster. Bookmaker ('Watson' in the ring) with whom Atkins lived at Osnaburgh Street, Tachbrook Street and elsewhere, 1891-1894, and worked blackmail — the Rochester Row incident of June 1891 (gentleman found in bed with Atkins; charge dropped) was the perjury trap that destroyed Atkins's testimony. Sworn record of cohabitation and joint extortion, not of a stated sexual relationship between the two men.

sources.quote: Have you ever lived with a man named Burton?—Yes, at Osnaburgh Street, Tachbrook Street, and other places.
sources.context: Fred Atkins cross-examined by Sir Edward Clarke, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
sources.supports: cohabitation with Burton across multiple addresses
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 247 (printed p. 207), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03

people.name: Florence Balcombe
people.bio: Florence Anne Lemon Balcombe, daughter of a retired lieutenant-colonel who had fought in the Crimea, living at 1 Marino Crescent, Clontarf, Dublin. Wilde courted her from August 1876 - he drew her that month and called the courtship 'a memory of two sweet years' - until her engagement in 1878; the editors caption her plate 'Wilde's first love'. She married Bram Stoker on 4 December 1878 at St Anne's Church, Dublin, appeared as a Priestess in Tennyson's The Cup at the Lyceum in January 1881, and remained on cordial terms with Wilde, who sent her Salome in 1893.
people.bio_note: Born/died (1858-1937), parentage and Clontarf address from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 47 n. 3 (repo PDF 72, folio confirmed, read as page image 2026-08-03), which also records Wilde's August 1876 drawing of her. 'Wilde's first love' from the List of Illustrations, p. vi (repo PDF 6). 'Two sweet years' from Wilde's letter of [? 30 September 1878], p. 71 (repo PDF 98). Stoker marriage from p. 72 n. 1 (repo PDF 99). The Cup casting from p. 107 n. 1 (repo PDF 132). Salome presentation letter at p. 552 (repo PDF 604). Full passages in dossiers/EARLY-CIRCLE_dossier.md.

context_engagements.note: Married 4 December 1878 at St Anne's Church, Dublin. Stoker (1847-1912) was then a young Irish civil servant, appointed business manager of Irving's Lyceum Theatre in October 1878; Dracula followed in 1897. Wilde's 1893 Salome letter to her closes 'With kind regards to Bram'.

sources.quote: Florence Balcombe was married on 4 December 1878 at St Anne's Church, Dublin, to Bram Stoker (1847–1912), a young Irish civil servant with literary and dramatic interests.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note on Wilde's parting letters to Florence
sources.supports: The Stoker marriage: date, church, husband
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 99, printed folio 72 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

people.name: Natalie Clifford Barney
people.bio: American heiress, poet, and Paris salon hostess who, per McDermott, 'saw herself as a latter day Sappho', and whose Quelques Portraits-Sonnets de Femmes (1900) made her notorious for openly lesbian verse. She opened a correspondence with Olive Custance after Opals (1897), wooed her with love poems, hosted her in Paris, and travelled with her in Italy around 1901; her memoir Souvenirs Indiscrets (1960) recounts the episode, including a plan to gather Custance and Renée Vivien into a Sapphic community at Mytilene. Her later, celebrated Left-Bank circle (Vivien, Romaine Brooks, and others) lies outside this web's scope.
people.bio_note: Dates (1876-1972) and the wooing account from Sarah Parker's Y90s Custance biography (read in full 2026-08-03); pursuit/Italy details from McDermott's Fortnightly Review profile (2020); 'rumoured entanglements' framing from Parker 2011 (AM p. 1), citing Wickes 1977 and Souhami 2004. Only the Custance link is on-roster; all other Barney liaisons stay off this web per the roster boundary rule.
bio_sources: parker-y90s-custance-bio
mcdermott-2020-fortnightly
parker-2011-girls-love

people.name: Mabel Batten
people.bio: Singer, known as "Ladye", 1856-1916. The Harry Ransom Center's biographical sketch of Radclyffe Hall calls her Hall's first lover and a "singer and society beauty" who "introduced her into a circle of artistic and intellectual women, many of them lesbians" - which places her, in the surviving record, as the person who brought Hall into queer society. She was the cousin of Una Troubridge, who met Hall in 1915 and became Hall's partner after Batten's death in 1916. Batten does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters; her link to this map is through Hall.
people.bio_note: Dates (1856-1916) and the characterisation from the Harry Ransom Center finding aid for the Hall and Troubridge papers (eadid 00163), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. No biography of Batten was consulted so far.
bio_sources: hrc-hall-troubridge-fa

people.name: Harold Bloodworth
people.bio: 'Pug' of George Ives's household - a working-class former footballer who joined in 1909, outlived Ives, and inherited the Adelaide Road house jointly with 'Elephant'. Cook records Ives's diary grief when Pug was away, and his paternal framing of the household as his 'children'.
bio_sources: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), pp. 96, 101
Cook, London and the Culture of Homosexuality (2003), p. 148
people.bio_note: Footballer identity, survival of Ives and the joint inheritance from Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed); the diary passage on sleeping beside Pug and Cubby at printed p. 101 (repo PDF 112, folio confirmed); both read as page images 2026-08-03. The 1909 move-in is from Cook 2003 p. 148. Birth and death dates not established in the works read. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED (2026-08-03). Cook names him at printed pp. 96, 109 and 110 (repo PDF 107, 120, 121) - footballer, joined the household, outlived Ives, inherited jointly, executor of the will, 'had lived with Ives at this point for around 30 years' - and attaches no dates to him anywhere. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT: census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames - work so far could not do. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: An actor, Bradfield
people.bio: A performer in the Greek play at Bradfield College in 1898, whom John Fothergill watched from the audience and then wrote to. The record preserves no name and no age. Fothergill's memoir calls him only 'a boy on the stage' and, sixty years later, 'that boy' - and 'boy' in this period was used of grown men as readily as of children, so nothing about his age follows from it. Fothergill bought a photograph of the cast with him in the middle, wrote to him the same night on hotel notepaper, and had two letters back before a firm of solicitors intervened and raised the police. The memoir closes the episode by noting that he much later saw the man mentioned 'in some official capacity; he too had retired.'
bio_sources: Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), pp. 142-143, quoting Fothergill's unpublished memoir
people.bio_note: From Fothergill's memoir as printed in Sox, printed pp. 142-143 (repo PDF 158-159), folios confirmed and read as page images 2026-08-03. **No age is recorded and none is inferred.** He was called 'A schoolboy actor' here until 2026-08-04, which was an inference from the venue rather than anything the source says, and it contradicted this note; corrected to 'An actor' on Lovelle's reading that 'boy' was period usage for a man of any age. Sox's passage describes a Greek play at a school but never identifies him as a pupil. No name, and no birth or death date in any source consulted. The year 1898 is fixed by Sox's next paragraph, 'It was also the same year - 1898 -'.

people.name: Katharine Bradley
people.bio: Poet, born 1846, the elder half of "Michael Field" and the aunt of her collaborator and life partner Edith Cooper (1862-1913), whom she raised. "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. Bradley and Cooper came from a well-off Birmingham family, read classics at University College, Bristol, and lived together first in Reigate and finally in Richmond; on the Y90s account Bradley was the older and the more glamorous and expansive of the two, and was "Michael" (also the Simiorg, or All-Wise-Fowl) in the private mythology of the diary. Wilde corresponded with "Michael Field" between 1890 and 1893 about their verse dramas and about placing A Question of Memory with J. T. Grein's Independent Theatre. Bradley survived Cooper by less than a year and died in 1914.
people.bio_note: Dates (1846-1914) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03 (the editors print the forename "Katherine"; the roster form "Katharine" follows the Y90s biography and her own usage). Life detail from Stefano Evangelista's Y90s biography of Michael Field (2015), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03.
bio_sources: letters-2000
evangelista-y90s-field-bio

people.name: A 'brown faun', Naples
aka: the wanton sylvan boy of Italy
people.bio: One of the Neapolitans Wilde called 'my dear Neapolitans', and the one he singled out. He is known from a single sentence written to Leonard Smithers from Paris on 2 September 1900, three months before Wilde's death, after the group had gone home to Naples: Wilde misses 'that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb', and says that the Egyptian waiter at the Cafe d'Egypte 'does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy'. Both phrases describe this same man. No name, age, occupation or date of meeting is recorded, and nothing else about him survives.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris; Complete Letters printed 1196 (repo PDF 1242), read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. The two epithets are one man, not two: the sentence sets the Egyptian against him - the Egyptian does not console Wilde for the loss of the boy he has just said he misses. He had previously been described inside the note on the Cafe d'Egypte waiter and deliberately not created; added as a person 2026-08-04 on Lovelle's instruction. PROVENANCE CAVEAT, from the editors' own footnote 1 to this letter: 'The text of this incomplete letter is taken from Forty Years in my Bookshop by W. T. Spencer (1923), corrected and supplemented by the American Art Association catalogue of 1 February 1928.' The heading carries no manuscript line, unlike the Ives letter lower on the same page ('MS Texas'), so this text descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than a surviving manuscript, and the letter is incomplete. No age is stated and none is inferred. Where or when Wilde knew him is not stated either - only that the Neapolitans had returned to Naples by September 1900.
bio_sources: letters-2000

people.name: Constance Lloyd
people.bio: Constance Mary Lloyd (1858-1898), daughter of Horace Lloyd QC (1828-74), first met Wilde in London in June 1881 and accepted his proposal in Dublin, announcing the engagement to her brother Otho on 26 November 1883. They married at St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, on 29 May 1884, honeymooned in Paris, and had two sons, Cyril and Vyvyan. After the 1895 catastrophe she, like her brother, took the name Holland; she visited Wilde in Reading Gaol on 19 February 1896 to break the news of his mother's death - their last meeting. She died at Genoa on 7 April 1898, aged forty, and was buried in the Protestant cemetery there; 'Wife of Oscar Wilde' was added to her gravestone only in 1963.
people.bio_note: All facts from Complete Letters (2000) pages read as images 2026-08-03: p. 221 n. 1 (dates, parentage, 1881 meeting, Holland name change 'like his sister'); p. 222 (engagement letter); p. 227 n. 2 (wedding card: church, date, hour); pp. 227-9 (honeymoon letters); p. 555 ('my two boys') and plate captions 80-81 (sons' names); p. 652 n. 4 (Reading visit 19 Feb 1896, last meeting); p. 1054 n. 1 (death at Genoa, aged forty); plate caption 82 (grave, 1963 inscription).

people.name: Alphonse Conway
people.bio: A Worthing boy — son of a widow who let lodgings, keen to go to sea — whom Wilde and Douglas met launching a boat on the beach in August 1894; for six weeks he was, in Wilde's contemporaneous letter, 'my only companion,' sailing to Littlehampton and bathing with Wilde, and receiving an inscribed cigarette case, a photograph, a novel, a walking-stick and a blue serge suit before the twenty-four-hour Brighton trip of about 27 September. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Worthing and the Albion Hotel, Brighton; the allegation, outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction, was never charged, and Conway — seen outside the Court in May 1895 — never testified.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 137-139 (djvu OCR)
Wilde's final-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 318-319 (djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 344 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas [August 1894], Complete Letters (2000), p. 602, with the editors' note 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n 5; read at rendered PDF p. 654, 2026-08-03)

Antony Edmonds, Oscar Wilde's Scandalous Summer (2014), extract at oscarwilde.org.uk - 1891 baptism record giving 10 July 1878; Richard Wood, 'The Later Fate of Alphonse Conway', oscarwilde.org.uk - argued identification with Harold Payne, d. 15 Jan. 1915
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far, and NO AGE appears in the plea as printed by Hyde (verified in the source image): Wilde on oath estimated 'a youth of about eighteen,' the Letters editors call him 'a newspaper boy' (undated), and Wilde denied he sold papers. The ROSTER's 'aged 16 (plea)' note is NOT supported by the sources read so far — the 16 figure presumably derives from the uncensored libel transcript (Holland, Irish Peacock, 2003, not consulted); flagged for verification there. BIRTH YEAR FOUND (added 2026-08-03, web): 1878. Antony Edmonds, Oscar Wilde's Scandalous Summer: The 1894 Worthing Holiday and the Aftermath (Amberley, 2014), in the extract from the book reproduced on the author's own site oscarwilde.org.uk (page 'Further Information about Alphonse Conway's Origins', read so far), states: 'A document has recently become available that gives Alphonse's date of birth. This is the record at St Andrew's Church, Worthing of the boy's baptism on 28 March 1891, which records his date of birth as 10 July 1878. He was thus twelve years old when he was belatedly baptised, and about six weeks past his sixteenth birthday when he met Wilde.' Edmonds corroborates the year from the April 1891 census, where Sarah Conway's son 'Alphus', born at Bognor, is twelve. WHY THE YEAR ONLY, AND NO DAY: three documents give three different days and this record does not choose between them - the 1891 baptism register 10 July 1878; the birth certificate (found by Edmund Marlowe, reported on the same page, registering 'Alfonso Conway White Payne' at Bognor to Julia Sarah Payne) 13 July 1878, which Edmonds thinks is probably the registration date entered in error; and a Royal Navy service record 14 July 1878, which only applies if the identification below holds. Conflict reported, not resolved. DEATH: STILL NULL, WITH A STRONG BUT ARGUED LEAD. Richard Wood, 'The Later Fate of Alphonse Conway' (oscarwilde.org.uk, published there at Edmonds's invitation, read so far), argues that Conway took his mother's registered surname and his own baptismal middle name and lived thereafter as Harold Payne: a Royal Navy Sick Berth Steward, born Bognor 1878, mother Sarah J. Payne, who enlisted 2 July 1900, was invalided out with tuberculosis in November 1914 and 'died in Portsmouth shortly afterwards, on 15 January 1915, aged only 36', buried in Kingston cemetery, Portsmouth. Wood builds this from census, birth, service, death and probate records and calls it 'surely beyond sheer coincidence'; it is nonetheless an argued identification rather than a record naming the trial witness, so no death date is entered here and the call is left open. Two things in the repo record corroborate the name-change premise independently: Queensberry's plea as printed by Hyde names him 'Alfonso Harold Conway' - the middle name Wood's argument turns on - and the Letters editors call him 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n. 5). AGE AT TRIAL, UNCHANGED: Wilde swore he was 'about eighteen'; the baptism date makes him sixteen in August 1894, which is Edmonds's point and is the likely origin of the widely repeated 16. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web.

people.name: Edith Cooper
people.bio: Poet, born 1862, the younger half of "Michael Field" and the niece of her collaborator and life partner Katharine Bradley (1846-1914). "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. On the Y90s account Cooper was the more retiring and fragile of the two and tended to follow her aunt's lead; in the diary's private mythology she was "Field", Henry, or the Persian Puss. Evangelista notes that despite the two women's constant devotion to each other Cooper was prone to heterosexual infatuations, including a period of attachment to their friend Bernhard Berenson. She died of cancer in 1913; Bradley followed within the year.
people.bio_note: Dates (1862-1913) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03, and corroborated in Evangelista's Y90s biography of Michael Field (2015), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03.

context_engagements.note: American art historian and connoisseur, a friend and Richmond-circle neighbour of both women. Evangelista's Y90s biography records that 'Despite the two women's constant devotion to each other, Cooper was prone to heterosexual infatuations, and for a period she developed a crush on their friend Bernhard Berenson.' Recorded because leaving it out would flatten the Michael Field partnership into a tidiness the source does not support. Off-roster; no dates given beyond the period.

people.name: Olive Custance
people.bio: Poet, born 7 February 1874, eldest daughter of Colonel Frederic Hambledon Custance of Weston Old Hall, Norfolk; she published in The Yellow Book from 1894 and issued four collections — Opals (1897), Rainbows (1902), The Blue Bird (1905), and The Inn of Dreams (1911). Courted around 1901 by both Natalie Barney and Lord Alfred Douglas, she jilted her fiancé George Montagu and eloped with Douglas on 4 March 1902; their son Raymond was born that November. The marriage was worn down by Douglas's litigations and the custody fight for Raymond, and the couple separated in 1913 without divorcing; from 1932 she lived near Douglas in Hove, seeing him nearly every day. She died on 12 February 1944.
people.bio_note: Dates and facts from Sarah Parker's Y90s biography (https://1890s.ca/custance_bio/, read in full 2026-08-03), corroborated by Parker's Volupté article (2019, at p. 61) and, for the courtship/marriage, by Douglas's Autobiography (1929) read at IA page images (pp. 188-200; partisan). Parker (Volupté 2.1 (2019), p. 61) describes her 'sexual identity as an aristocrat and a queer woman'; Parker 2011 reads her poetry as expressing 'bisexual desire'.

people.name: Didaco
people.bio: Florentine actor whom Wilde met at Genoa on his journey from the Riviera to Gland in the early months of 1899, and with whom he spent three days. Wilde described him to Reginald Turner as 'a beautiful young actor, a Florentine, whom I wildly loved', bearing 'the strange name of Didaco' and 'the look of Romeo, without Romeo's sadness'. No surname, age, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.

people.name: Lord Alfred Douglas
people.bio: Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, born 1870, third son of John Sholto Douglas, eighth Marquess of Queensberry, and Sybil Montgomery (who divorced the Marquess in 1887); educated at Winchester and Magdalen College, Oxford, which he left without a degree. Lionel Johnson brought him to see Wilde at Tite Street in 1891, and Wilde dated the friendship proper from May 1892, when Douglas appealed to him over a blackmail scrape. A poet, he was the dedicatee and translator of Wilde's Salome and published Poems in 1896; he later said he destroyed 150 of Wilde's letters to him, including those from Holloway. He arrived in Paris the day after Wilde's death and followed the coffin at the funeral on 3 December 1900. He married Olive Custance by special licence at St George's, Hanover Square, on 4 March 1902; their only child, Raymond Wilfrid Sholto Douglas, was born on 17 November 1902 and from 26 August 1927 lived, with brief intervals, at St Andrew's Hospital, Northampton. Douglas was received into the Catholic Church in May 1911, and was made bankrupt on a money-lender's petition on 14 January 1913. He edited the Academy from 1907, and the rest of his middle life ran through the courts: the Ransome libel trial of 1913, which he lost; Robert Ross's criminal prosecution of him in 1914; a series of actions of his own; and finally his conviction for criminal libel of Winston Churchill, for which Mr Justice Avory sentenced him to six months in the second division. He was taken to Wormwood Scrubs on 13 December 1923 and released for good behaviour on 12 May 1924. In prison he wrote In Excelsis, seventeen sonnets - begun 20 February 1924 and finished on Good Friday, 18 April - which the prison authorities confiscated at his release and which he never recovered; it was published from memory, in the London Mercury in October 1924 and in book form that December. His marriage broke down in 1913 and again after a short reconciliation, but he and Olive were reconciled in later life; she died on 12 February 1944. His late books were the Autobiography (1929) and Without Apology (1938), and his last lyric poem was written in 1927. He died at about four in the morning on Tuesday 20 March 1945, in the Colmans' farmhouse at Lancing where he had spent his last months, and was buried, as he had asked, with his mother in the cemetery of the Franciscan Friary at Crawley.

people.name: Ernest Dowson
people.bio: English poet of the Decadence and one of the Rhymers' Club - the loose association of young poets, meeting at the Cheshire Cheese in Fleet Street, whose two Books of the Rhymers' Club (1892, 1894) carried his work alongside Yeats, Lionel Johnson and Arthur Symons. He met Wilde in 1890 and, with Robert Sherard, visited him at Oakley Street 'in the dark days between his trials'. Living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe in the summer of 1897, he was among the first friends to reach Wilde after his release, dining at Berneval on 3 June and seeing him constantly until his own return to London in mid-July; the twelve surviving letters from Wilde to him are the largest cluster of the Berneval/Dieppe months, and travel from 'Cher Monsieur le Poete' to 'Tout a toi'. Frankel calls him at this period 'one of his closest confidantes' and credits the friendship - together with Wilde's reading of A. E. Housman - as a spur to the composition of The Ballad of Reading Gaol. The correspondence resumed from Naples that October, by then largely about a debt of some 18-20 pounds Dowson owed Wilde; he died at Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900, nine months before Wilde, who asked Smithers to put flowers on his grave.
people.bio_note: DATES (established so far, 2026-08-03): born 1867, died 23 February 1900. The year-pair is from the editors' main-particulars footnote at Dowson's first appearance in the text - Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 877 n. 1 (repo PDF 927): 'English poet (1867-1900). He had met Wilde in 1890 and with Robert Sherard visited him at Oakley Street in the dark days between his trials.' The exact death date is from the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter of condolence to Smithers, printed p. 1173 n. 2 (repo PDF 1219): 'Ernest Dowson died in Robert Sherard's house at Catford on 23 February 1900. He was buried in the Roman Catholic part of Lewisham Cemetery on 27 February.' No birth month or day is given by any source read so far, so none is recorded. Both pages were located in the OCR text mirror, then read as rendered page images with the printed folio confirmed at the foot. B. Yeats, Lionel Johnson, Ernest Dowson, Arthur Symons' among the contributors. The 1890 meeting and the Oakley Street visit between the trials from printed p. 877 n. 1 as above (independently asserted, without Sherard, at Sox, Bachelors of Art (1991), printed p. 141). The Berneval/Dieppe period from Wilde's letters at printed pp. 877-926 and from Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), printed p. 113 (repo PDF 127, folio confirmed on the rendered page): Dowson 'now one of his closest confidantes, whom Wilde had known back in London and who resided near Dieppe, at Arques-la-Bataille, until his departure for London in mid-July'; the Ballad claim at Frankel printed p. 121 (repo PDF 135, OCR/text layer). The Naples debt from Wilde to Dowson, printed pp. 957, 965, 969, 971. Frankel's 'just nine months before his own' at printed p. 114 (repo PDF 128, folio confirmed on the rendered page). NOT RECORDED AS A CONTEXT ENGAGEMENT, but on the record: Fothergill, in his unpublished memoir as printed by Sox at p. 141, 'commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Cafe Royal, but was "faithful only after his fashion"'; and the Complete Letters editors, glossing Wilde's otherwise 'inexplicable' 1898 reference to a 'Mrs Dowson' (printed p. 1018 n. 3), note that 'Ernest Dowson never married and his mother had died in 1895' and read the phrase as 'probably a reference to a newly acquired mistress or one of the prostitutes whose company he enjoyed'. Neither person is on the roster and neither is named, so neither gets a marker. Full passages, page-by-page provenance and the pagination table in dossiers/DOWSON_dossier.md.

people.name: Peter Doyle
people.bio: Irish-born American transit worker, and the companion to whom Walt Whitman wrote the letters published in 1897 as Calamus. Born in Limerick on 3 June 1843 and raised in the American South, he enlisted in the Confederate army in 1861 and was discharged after being wounded; he was in the audience at Ford's Theatre on the night Lincoln was shot. After the war he worked in Washington as a conductor on the Pennsylvania Avenue horsecars, which is how he and Whitman met one winter's evening in 1865 - Doyle twenty-one, Whitman forty-five and the car's only passenger. He later worked for the Pennsylvania Railroad, first as a brakeman and then as a baggage master, and in the mid-1880s settled in Philadelphia and visited Whitman weekly across the river in Camden. He kept Whitman's letters, entrusted them to Richard Maurice Bucke in 1880, and allowed him to publish them in 1897 - a decision without which almost nothing of this relationship would survive. He attended Whitman's funeral. He died in Philadelphia on 19 April 1907, aged sixty-three, and is buried in Congressional Cemetery, Washington.
people.bio_note: Dates, birthplace, war service, occupations and burial from Martin G. Murray's entry on Doyle in Walt Whitman: An Encyclopedia, read in full on the Whitman Archive 2026-08-04 (the site 403s to automated fetching; it was read in a browser). Murray is the author of the fullest published biography of Doyle. The meeting year is given as 1865 there; **Doyle himself, interviewed by Bucke, says 'I think the year of this was 1866'** - the hedge is his, and both readings are kept rather than reconciled. No portrait: Doyle has a Wikidata entity (Q105806793) and an article at 'Peter Doyle (transit worker)', but the portrait pipeline takes the article's own lead image and has not been run for him.

people.name: John Fothergill
people.bio: Architect-trained aesthete, art dealer and later celebrated innkeeper; per Sox the one member of E. P. Warren's Lewes House brotherhood to become well known in Britain. Born 27 February 1876, son of George Fothergill of a fairly well-off Westmorland family; met Wilde at 19 through Robbie Ross and Reggie Turner, put in brief stints at the London School of Architecture (a pupil of architecture at 30 Manchester Street, 'to be near Sir Arthur Blomfield') and the Slade School of Art, dabbled in classical archaeology, and managed the Carfax Gallery. Wilde inscribed Fothergill's copy of The Ballad of Reading Gaol 'To Rowland Fothergill, the Architect of the Moon'. Ran the Spreadeagle at Thame near Oxford as innkeeper-author - the innkeeping diaries published in the 1930s and 1940s made his name - and died in a modest terraced house in Rugby on 26 April 1957, aged 81.

people.name: Georges
people.bio: A young Parisian whom Wilde called 'a great friend of mine' and referred to by the nickname 'le petit Georges'. In a letter to Reginald Turner postmarked 3 January 1899 Wilde wrote that Georges was then at Nice and that he had promised to go over and see him, describing him as 'like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth'. Wilde adds that he was visiting Nice 'on speculative business'. No surname, age or dates appear on the page read.

people.name: Maurice Gilbert
people.bio: Member of Wilde's Paris circle of the exile years, on first-name terms ('Maurice') with the whole inner circle. During Wilde's final illness in November 1900 he came to the sickroom almost daily alongside Reggie Turner, though Turner noted he 'does not like being in the room'; at Robert Ross's request he took the (unsuccessful) photograph of Wilde on his deathbed. He was one of the nine named mourners who walked behind the hearse to St Germain des Prés and is listed among the senders of funeral wreaths. The editors' main particulars are sparse: except that his father was English and his mother French, and that he was a young soldier in the marine infantry, nothing is known of him.
bio_sources: Nicholas Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), p. 209 - 'about whom very little is known'
people.bio_note: All facts from the Epilogue of Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000): sickroom attendance from Turner's letters to Ross, pp. 1217-19 (repo PDF 1262-64); photograph, procession roll-call and wreath list from Ross to Adey, 14 Dec. 1900, p. 1222 (PDF 1267). people.name: Sylvie Goddard
people.bio: Wife of James Goddard ('Kit'), and a member of George Ives's household: Cook records that on marrying, Goddard brought her into the house too, and that their daughters were known there as 'the 2 Kit girls'. Her presence makes the household's composition plain - a married couple and their children living inside the domestic circle Ives called 'my little circle in the world'.
bio_sources: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), p. 96
people.bio_note: From Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed), read as a page image 2026-08-03. Cook gives her only as 'his wife Sylvie' - maiden name, dates and marriage date are not stated in the page read. Cook's printed p. 100 reportedly adds that she kept house for Ives and that she and James remained until their deaths, with the daughters staying until the early 1940s (one, Therese, still visiting in 1944); that page is known so far only from the PDF text layer and is flagged as a pointer on the marriage record pending verification at the rendered page. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED (2026-08-03). She is the least documented member of the household in Cook, who says so himself: her domestic labour 'also went largely without comment' (printed p. 102). He gives her no maiden name, no marriage date and no dates of life; the only chronological facts are that she came into the house on marriage, that she predeceased Ives (her legacy is described as reapportioned 'after Sylvie's death'), and that her daughters stayed until the early 1940s. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT: census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames - work so far could not do. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: Walter Grainger
people.bio: A servant at the house in High Street, Oxford, where Lord Alfred Douglas had rooms — 'about sixteen when I knew him,' Wilde swore of 1893 — who waited at table during Wilde's stays and asked Wilde to find him a place; Wilde brought him to 'The Cottage' at Goring as under-butler from June-July 1893 until Wilde left in October. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Oxford and Goring; the allegations, outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction, were never charged and Grainger never testified. Carson's pursuit of Wilde's answer to 'Did you ever kiss him?' — 'Oh, dear no. He was a peculiarly plain boy' — is recorded by Hyde as the turning point of the libel trial.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 150-151 (djvu OCR)
Wilde's final-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 320 (djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 343-344 (IIIF page images 2026-08-03)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 51-52 (the cross-examination climax; djvu OCR)

people.name: John Gray
people.bio: Poet. His Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893) was designed by Ricketts and initially underwritten by Wilde before the two fell out; in the same year The Blackmailers, a play written in collaboration with his close friend Andre Raffalovich, was produced at the Prince of Wales's Theatre. After the publication of The Picture of Dorian Gray he referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so, though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. He became a Roman Catholic, was ordained priest at thirty-five, and spent his later years in Edinburgh, where Raffalovich built St Peter's Church for him; in 1904 he edited and published Last Letters of Aubrey Beardsley, which were written to Raffalovich.
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 520 n. 3 (repo PDF 540, folio confirmed, read as page image 2026-08-03). Born/died 1866-1934 from the same footnote. Full passages in dossiers/EARLY-CIRCLE_dossier.md.

people.name: Radclyffe Hall
people.bio: Novelist and poet, born Marguerite Antonia Radclyffe-Hall on 12 August 1880, best known for The Well of Loneliness (1928), a serious treatment of lesbianism that was prosecuted and banned in England until 1949. The Ransom Center's biographical sketch records that, "[s]elf-identifying as a sexual 'invert,' Hall adopted a masculine appearance and the name John". Her two long partnerships were with the singer Mabel Batten (1856-1916), her first lover, and with Batten's cousin Una Troubridge (1887-1963), from 1915 until Hall's death. Hall belongs to a later generation than Wilde's circle and does not appear anywhere in his Complete Letters; she reaches this map from the Ives side, as a figure of the homophile politics Ives helped begin. Matt Cook records that she and Troubridge "seem to have been considered" for the Order of Chaeronea and that Ives took an interest in the 1928 obscenity case over her novel. She died on 7 October 1943.
people.bio_note: Birth and death dates, the "invert" self-identification, and both partnerships from the Harry Ransom Center's finding aid, "Radclyffe Hall and Una Vincenzo, Lady Troubridge: An Inventory of Their Papers" (eadid 00163), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. The Order-of-Chaeronea and obscenity-case detail from Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), p. 108, transcribed from the source in dossiers/IVES-DOMESTICITIES_dossier.md (Passage 26); Cook's double hedge is preserved and no Order-membership or Ives edge is created on it.

people.name: Charlie Hickey
people.bio: A young man of Lord Alfred Douglas's circle, described by Douglas in his Autobiography (1929) as 'a charming boy about a couple of years younger than myself and well known to Oscar, a son of Colonel Hickey' - which, Douglas having been born in 1870, would place his birth around 1872. He was with Douglas in Paris in May 1895 while Wilde's second trial was proceeding in London, and is the 'Charlie' who 'sends you his best love' in Douglas's letter to Wilde of 15 May 1895, one of only three Douglas-to-Wilde letters recovered. Nearly four years later, in exile at Napoule, Wilde had a presentation copy of The Importance of Being Earnest addressed to him and asked Reggie Turner after him.

people.name: Violet Hunt
people.bio: Violet Hunt, later a novelist, was the daughter of the landscape painter Alfred William Hunt and the novelist Margaret Raine Hunt, of Tor Villas, Campden Hill, where Wilde took tea with the family during his Salisbury Street years. In 1880-81 he paid her marked attention - 'the sweetest Violet in England I think her', he wrote to her mother in March 1880 - promised and sent her a poem, and thanked her directly in July 1881 for admiring his Poems. Her autobiography The Flurried Years (1926), quoted by the editors for her reminiscence of the young Wilde at Tor Villas, is the family memoir of the acquaintance.
bio_sources: letters-2000
sutherland-1989
people.bio_note:
Facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 88 n. 4 (repo PDF 113, folio confirmed, read as page image 2026-08-03) and Wilde's letters at pp. 88-9, 93, 94 (to Mrs Alfred Hunt) and 114 (to Violet Hunt). BORN-YEAR, CROSS-CHECK RESOLVED 2026-08-04. The 1866 above is the Letters editors' figure and was flagged here for checking against a modern reference work. It is confirmed: Sutherland, Stanford Companion to Victorian Fiction (1989), p. 314, read by Lovelle Cardoso, also gives 1866. en.wikipedia and Wikidata (Q1677011) give 1862, and en.wikipedia cites Sutherland - the work that contradicts it. Its own article explains why: the 1862 date is an emendation, adopted so that Hunt would be old enough to be engaged when Oscar Wilde is said to have proposed to her in Dublin in 1879. That is a date reasoned backwards from an anecdote in order to make the anecdote work, which is the inference this reference declines to make (see CONTRIBUTING, 'What gets rejected'). We keep the attested year and record the emendation rather than adopt it.

The tension is real and is not resolved by keeping 1866. Ellmann has them meeting in London 'when she was not yet seventeen' (see the source on hunt--wilde), which fits neither 1866 (she would be about thirteen when the letters begin in March 1880) nor 1862 (about eighteen). Ellmann also puts the meeting in London at the beginning of the 1880s, not Dublin in 1879, and our own verified letters are London from March 1880. So the Dublin story carries a place and a date that the fullest account of the acquaintance does not support, and it is that story the 1862 date exists to accommodate. Anyone revisiting this should run down the Dublin claim to its origin first; the birth year is downstream of it.

people.name: George Cecil Ives
people.bio: Poet, penologist and pioneering campaigner for homosexual law reform; illegitimate son of Colonel Gordon Maynard Gordon-Ives and, by his own account, the Baroness de Molarti of Spain, raised by his paternal grandmother and living on a private income. Kept a diary from 1886 to 1950 - 122 volumes, around three million words - alongside a forty-five-volume press-cuttings casebook, an archive now split between Yale and the University of Texas at Austin. In about 1893 he founded the Order of Chaeronea, the first homosexual support-and-pressure group in Britain, named for the Theban band slaughtered in 338 BC, and structured it deliberately without hierarchy: any two existing members could invite a third. In October 1894 he published an outspoken justification of same-sex love in the Humanitarian. Lived at 56 St James' Street from July 1891, at Flat E4 the Albany, Piccadilly, from 30 June 1894, from 1897 in his late grandmother's Regent's Park house, and from 1905 at Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill, with an unconventional household of younger working-class men he called his 'children' - a family, in Cook's phrase, connected by co-residence rather than by blood. He was treasurer of the British Society for the Study of Sex Psychology (Edward Carpenter was its life president). Though he identified settledly as homosexual, he also had affairs with women, and considered having a child outside marriage with Matilda 'Tilly' Hayes. His will of 1939, eight typed pages with ten later codicils, left the Adelaide Road house and contents to the two men he was then living with, Harold Bloodworth and Stanley Saunders.

This is a firmer Order-membership attestation than Cook's hedged sentence about Radclyffe Hall and Una, Lady Troubridge (printed 108), who 'seem to have been considered'. ROSTER CANDIDATE. people.name: Lillie Langtry
people.bio: Emily Charlotte Le Breton of Jersey, 'considered the most beautiful woman of her generation' in the editors' words; she married Edward Langtry in her teens, was brought by him to London, and became a leading Society figure and, as the editors put it, a friend of the Prince of Wales. Painted by Whistler, Poynter, Watts, Burne-Jones, Leighton and particularly Millais, whose portrait The Jersey Lily gave her the nickname; Wilde's friend Frank Miles made many drawings of her. In 1899 she married Hugo Gerald de Bathe.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 91 n. 2
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at p. 91 n. 2 (repo PDF 116, folio confirmed), read as page image 2026-08-03. The Prince of Wales is characterized there only as 'a friend' - stated here exactly as the source states it.

context_engagements.note: An Irish widower of thirty who brought her to London (p. 91 n. 2).
Married 1899; he succeeded as fifth Baronet in 1907 (p. 91 n. 2).

people.name: Vernon Lee
people.bio: Aesthetician, critic, novelist and writer of supernatural tales, born Violet Paget at Chateau St Leonard near Boulogne-sur-Mer on 14 October 1856 and resident for most of her life in Italy, latterly at Il Palmerino, Maiano. She adopted the androgynous pen name "Vernon Lee" in the late 1870s and came to public notice in 1880 with Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy. Two long attachments to women structure her life as the Y90s biography records it: the poet Mary Robinson (1857-1944), from 1880 until Robinson's marriage in 1887, and Clementina "Kit" Anstruther-Thomson (1857-1921), her companion and co-author from 1887 to 1900. She met Wilde in London in 1881 at the Robinsons', and appears in the Complete Letters only in the editors' apparatus, which quotes her own letters describing him; there is no correspondence between them in the volume. Amy Levy fell in love with her at Florence in 1886. Lee died at Il Palmerino on 13 February 1935.
people.bio_note: Birth and death dates and places, the pen-name adoption, and both attachments from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. Dates corroborated by the editors' footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), p. 229, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03, which identifies "Violet Paget (1856-1935), who lived mostly in Italy and published many books under the name Vernon Lee".
bio_sources: pulham-y90s-lee-bio
letters-2000

people.name: Amy Levy
people.bio: Anglo-Jewish poet and novelist, born Amy Judith Levy in London on 10 November 1861, the second of seven children of a stockbroker; in 1879 she became the second Jewish woman to attend Cambridge and the first at Newnham College. Wilde published her while he edited the Woman's World: her story appeared in the first number, followed by articles on Christina Rossetti's poetry (March 1888) and on women and club life (June 1888), and two poems and a story during 1889. His one surviving letter to her, of October 1887, solicits more of her fiction - "I think your method as admirable as it is unique" - and after her death he printed a tribute to her in the same magazine, judging that she had "ceased to hold the orthodox doctrines of her nation, retaining, however, a strong race feeling"; she is one of the very few women on this map whose tie to Wilde is professional, mutual, and documented in his own hand. At Florence in 1886 she met Vernon Lee and fell in love with her, sending her the sonnet "To Vernon Lee" and the poem "New Love, New Life"; her biographer Linda Hunt Beckman calls these love poems. She took her own life on 10 September 1889, aged twenty-seven.
people.bio_note: Full dates (10 November 1861 - 10 September 1889) from Linda Hunt Beckman, "Amy Levy", Shalvi/Hyman Encyclopedia of Jewish Women (updated 7 July 2021), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03; Beckman is Levy's biographer (Amy Levy: Her Life and Letters, 2000) and states the birth in London, the family, and the Cambridge firsts. Birthplace given as Clapham, south London by Andrzej Diniejko's Victorian Web biography, also read in full 2026-08-03, which agrees on 10 November 1861. NOTE a discrepancy in the Wilde apparatus: the editors' footnote to Wilde's letter to her, Complete Letters (2000), p. 326 (read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03), gives her dates as "(1862-89)" - a year late on the birth. The two independent Levy sources are preferred; the Letters reading is recorded here rather than silently dropped. The Woman's World bibliography and the manner of death ("She committed suicide by inhaling fumes of charcoal") are from that same footnote. The Wilde tribute and the quoted sentence from it are Beckman's, who dates the tribute to an 1890 issue of the Woman's World; Wilde's tribute has NOT been read at source so far and the quotation is Beckman quoting Wilde.
bio_sources: letters-2000
diniejko-victorianweb-levy
beckman-jwa-levy

people.name: Harry Marillier
people.bio: Henry Currie Marillier, a Bluecoat Boy (pupil of Christ's Hospital, then still in London) 1875-84, lodged at 13 Salisbury Street, Strand, while Wilde was living there in 1880-81 and, as a boy, brought Wilde his coffee. Classical scholar of Peterhouse, Cambridge, 1884-87; his autumn-1885 letter to Wilde, inviting him to the Cambridge Eumenides, opened the 1885-86 correspondence. He later became an engineer and partner in W. A. S. Benson's metalworks, then a literary and art journalist, editing The Early Work of Aubrey Beardsley (1899) and writing on tapestry.
people.bio_note: All facts from the main-particulars footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 266 n. 3 (repo PDF 288, folio confirmed, read as page image 2026-08-03), plus the coffee/Salisbury Street recollection in Wilde's letter of [Postmark 5 November 1885] at the same page. Full passages in dossiers/EARLY-CIRCLE_dossier.md.

people.name: John Marshall
people.bio: Liverpool wine-merchant's son who went up to New College, Oxford, on a Classics scholarship intending Holy Orders, met Ned Warren in his third year (1884), and after Warren's five-year wooing gave up church, a Fellowship path and Liverpool to join him in November 1889 - thereafter co-head of the Lewes House collecting operation, whose eye supplied the classical collections of Boston and, from 1906, the Metropolitan Museum as its Rome-based purchasing agent. He and Warren called each other 'Puppy'; Burdett described the pair 'pacing arm-in-arm on the lawn at Lewes House' as 'replicas of each other'. He married Warren's cousin Mary Bliss on 5 November 1907 - 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union' per Sox - and after her death in 1925 shared his old Rome flat with Warren again. He died there in February 1928 with Warren beside him - his last words, in Warren's account, 'good-bye Puppy' - and is buried at Bagni di Lucca with Mary and Warren, under a plain Grecian urn.
bio_sources: Liverpool family, wine-merchant father: Sox (1991) p. 39 (repo PDF 55, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03)

Liverpool College, Classics scholarship to New College, met Warren 1884 ('It was in his third year at New College (1884) that he met Ned.'), Merton Fellowship path abandoned: Sox p. 40 (PDF 56, rendered 2026-08-03)
Joined Warren: 'By November 1889, "the man of his choice" was at Ned's side.' - Sox p. 44 (PDF 60, rendered 2026-08-03)
Met purchasing agent from Robinson's 1905-06 offer; Rome flat 'made possible by Ned's generosity': Sox pp. 77-78, 107 (PDF 93-94, 123, rendered 2026-08-03)

Died: 'She died there in 1925, and Marshall in Rome in February, 1928.' - Sox p. viii (PDF 12, rendered); Portland newspaper: 'passed away in the latter country in February, 1928' - p. 130 (PDF 146, rendered); Warren's account of the night, pp. 126-127 (PDF 142-143, rendered)
Tomb: pp. viii, 130 (PDF 12, 146, rendered 2026-08-03)

British School at Rome, John Marshall Archive catalogue (archive.bsr.ac.uk, resource 65); Guido Petruccioli, 'Introduction', Ancient Art and its Commerce in Early Twentieth-Century Europe (Archaeopress, 2022), p. 1 - birth year
people.bio_note: Sox states no birth date or year for Marshall in the pages read (text search for '1862' returns nothing); the enlarged Bagni di Lucca monument carries the three names 'with their birth and death dates' (p. 130) but Sox does not print them - born stays null. Death not sharpened past the month: Sox's narration gives 'February, 1928'; Warren's first-person account has Marshall dying at 'five minutes past one' in the night after 'the evening of the 15th'. 'Johnny' is Warren's and the circle's regular name for him; 'Puppy' was mutual (Marshall writes 'Puppy dear' to Warren, pp. 64-65; Warren signs 'Your Puppy', p. 107). Full passages in dossiers/LEWES-HOUSE_dossier.md. BIRTH YEAR FOUND (added 2026-08-03, web): 1862, from two sources consulted so far. (1) The British School at Rome's archival catalogue for the John Marshall Archive - the repository that holds his papers (BSR Archive & Special Collections, ArchivesSpace resource 65, fonds 1900-1928, archive.bsr.ac.uk) - whose biographical note reads 'John Marshall (1862-1928) was a connoisseur of Classical art and a cultivated intellectual.' (2) Guido Petruccioli, 'Introduction', in Ancient Art and its Commerce in Early Twentieth-Century Europe (Archaeopress, 2022), p. 1, read in the publisher's own sample PDF: 'John Marshall (1862-1928) - not to be confused with the homonymous (and far more notorious) American statesman John Marshall (1755-1835) or the British archaeologist John Hubert Marshall (1876-1958) - is known only to a few people.' Both give the year alone, so no month or day is recorded. This closes the gap Sox left: Sox reports that the Bagni di Lucca monument carries 'their birth and death dates' (p. 130) without transcribing them. DEATH-DATE CONFLICT, REPORTED NOT RESOLVED - died stays {y:1928, m:2}: Wikipedia's 'John Marshall (died 1928)' opens '15 February 1928' but attaches no citation to that date (its listed references are Streitmatter, Outlaw Marriages, and De Puma, Etruscan Art in the Metropolitan Museum of Art), so by this module's rule it cannot be entered; Sox's repo text has Warren's first-person account of Marshall retiring on 'the evening of the 15th' and dying at 'five minutes past one' in the night, which points to the small hours of 16 February; BSR and Petruccioli give the year only. Three accounts, two candidate days, and no source read so far that settles it.

context_engagements.note: Off-roster. Legal marriage, 5 November 1907: Warren's cousin, to whom Warren had dedicated The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900). Per Fothergill's memoir she 'courted Ned and Marshall, either of which she was well prepared to marry' and 'naively... thought the marriage would unite Johnny more closely to Ned'; Sox: 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union of Mary and John Marshall, but she was an extremely beneficial help-mate in his collecting at the Metropolitan Museum' (p. 76, rendered). She died at Villa Buonvisi, Bagni di Lucca, in 1925 (p. viii); all three share the tomb there.

sources.quote: John Marshall did not marry Ned's cousin until 5 November 1907.
sources.context: Sox, opening the account of the marriage's effect on the Warren-Marshall partnership; 'Ned's cousin' = Mary Bliss (p. viii: 'Mary Bliss (Warren's cousin)').
sources.supports: The marriage date
