people.name: Sidney Mavor
people.bio: 'The only other individual of decent family and upbringing besides Shelley' among the Crown's young men (Hyde): living at 66 St Helen's Gardens, North Kensington, and by 1895 in partnership in a City business. Taylor met him at the Gaiety Theatre in 1892, groomed him for the Kettner's dinner given by Schwabe ('Mr. Wilde likes nice clean boys'), and Wilde sent him a silver cigarette case inscribed 'Sidney from O. W., October, 1892' before an overnight at the Albemarle Hotel. On the stand he repeated his Bow Street denial — no misconduct, no impropriety ever — and the Mavor counts were struck out; Hyde's footnote preserves Douglas's own account of coaching that denial in the Bow Street corridor. Atkins had 'heard him called Jenny Mavor.'
bio_sources: Mavor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 211-212 (p. 212 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction pp. 72-73 with n (counts struck out; the corridor story from Douglas's Autobiography, 2nd edn. p. 119; djvu OCR) and pp. 85-86 (Mavor dropped at the final trial; djvu OCR)
Atkins's testimony ('Jenny Mavor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 207 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Ellen Grant's testimony ('Mavor and Mason stayed there for nights with Taylor'), Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 199 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far; the General Index of Complete Letters (2000) has NO Mavor entry (verified at the rendered index page, printed p. 1255, where it would fall between 'Maurice, Dr Oliver' and 'Max'; read 2026-08-03). Mavor's own sworn 'I have slept there with Taylor' (p. 211) plus Grant's corroboration would support a mavor--taylor edge — NOT created so far (pair not in the assigned edge list); flagged for roster/assignment review. DATES: NOT ENTERED, BUT THERE IS A NAMED LEAD WORTH ONE HUMAN CHECK (2026-08-03). Web searching surfaced a consistent account that Sydney Arthur Mavor died in 1952 at Upton Lovell, near Warminster, Wiltshire, aged eighty-five, after being struck by a car, and that he had taught English at Hurstpierpoint College in Sussex from 1917 to 1925. The account is attributed to Joseph Bristow, Oscar Wilde on Trial: The Criminal Proceedings, from Arrest to Imprisonment (Yale, 2022) - which would be exactly the authoritative source this module wants - but the only full text reachable so far was an unauthorised scan, so the passage was NOT read in a legitimate copy and no page number is known. A Find a Grave memorial for a 'Sydney Arthur Mavor (1866-1952)' buried at St Augustine of Canterbury, Upton Lovell, is consistent with 'aged eighty-five in 1952' but is user-generated and establishes no link to the trial witness. Both are therefore recorded as leads, not sources, and born/died stay null. TO CLOSE: check Bristow 2022 (index entry Mavor) in a library copy; if it gives dates, they can be entered on that authority alone. AGE ON OATH, FOR CONTEXT ONLY: Wilde, cross-examined in April 1895 about Taylor's rooms, put Mavor at 'About twenty-five or twenty-six', which would place his birth about 1869-70 and sits awkwardly with the 1866 of the Find a Grave memorial; McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF p. 328, has him 'twenty' when Taylor picked him up in late September 1892, which would mean about 1872. Three incompatible figures, none of them a date. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web.

people.name: Harold Mellor
people.bio: Wealthy English expatriate, and Wilde's host, patron and travelling companion through the exile years 1898-1900. Per the editors of the Complete Letters, 'the neurotic son of a Bolton cotton spinner', left wealthy by his father's death in 1893, who 'spent most of the rest of his life abroad, finally committing suicide in his villa at Cannes'; his aunt Ursula Mellor married the Liberal MP Jacob Bright. Wilde met him at Napoule at Christmas 1898 and stayed at his villa at Gland, Vaud, in March-April 1899 and again in July-August 1900; Mellor also funded Wilde's journey to Italy in 1900 'to the extent of £50'. Wilde recorded Mellor's own queer life in two letters: that he had been 'sent away from Harrow at the age of fourteen for being loved by the captain of the cricket eleven', and that he 'has Greek loves, and is rather ashamed of them'. The Italian servant Eolo travelled with him from at least 1898 until 1900.
bio_sources: Life-dates, family, wealth, expatriation and manner of death: 'Harold Mellor (1868-1925) was the neurotic son of a Bolton cotton spinner. His father died in 1893, leaving him wealthy, and he spent most of the rest of his life abroad, finally committing suicide in his villa at Cannes. His aunt Ursula Mellor married Jacob Bright (1821-99), brother of John Bright and Liberal MP for Manchester 1867-95 with two short intervals.' - Holland & Hart-Davis, editors' footnote, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1112n (repo PDF 1158, printed folio confirmed on rendered page image, 2026-08-03).

The meeting: 'A nice fellow called Harold Mellor, who is staying at Cannes, comes over constantly to see me. He is a nephew of Mrs Jacob Bright's.' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [27 December 1898], Napoule; p. 1112 (repo PDF 1158, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

Harrow: 'a charming fellow called Harold Mellor (sent away from Harrow at the age of fourteen for being loved by the captain of the cricket eleven) who is staying with his mother near Cannes, and comes over on his bicycle to breakfast every morning' - Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule; p. 1116 (repo PDF 1162, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

'Greek loves' and the patronage frame: 'I don't like Mellor: he is a silent, dull person, cautious, and economical … has Greek loves, and is rather ashamed of them: has heaps of money, and lives in terror of poverty: so I regard it as a sort of Swiss pension, where there is no weekly bill.' - Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland; p. 1132 (repo PDF 1178, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

The 1900 Italy money: 'Mellor, with whom I am now friends (below zero of course) has invited me to go to Italy to the extent of £50!' - Wilde to Robert Ross, [late March 1900], Paris; p. 1177 (repo PDF 1223, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).

The last visit and Mellor's own surviving letter: 'I have been with Harold Mellor at Gland: he is almost as neurasthenic as I am' - Wilde to Ross, [August 1900]; and editors' footnote 1 on the same page: 'A surviving letter from Mellor to Wilde (MS Clark), written from Gland and dated 21 July 1900, runs: "Am much distressed about your illness . . . I hope to be able to receive you on Monday 30 [July]."' - p. 1194 (repo PDF 1240, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03).
people.bio_note: Dates: the editors' footnote gives the death year only inside the life-dates (1868-1925); it does not date the suicide separately, and the place is 'his villa at Cannes'. Wilde's own estimate of Mellor's age - 'He is about twenty-six, but looks younger' (2 January 1899) - is wrong against the editors' 1868 birth-year, which would make him 30; recorded as Wilde's impression, not as a fact. Register: the friendly words are the first-impression ones of December 1898 and January 1899; from printed 1129 onward Wilde's private register toward Mellor is hostile ('very lamentable', 'this loathsome place', 'Gland, which has become intolerable', 'this dreadful place' - three correspondents in one week, March 1899, all p. 1137, repo PDF 1183, folio confirmed). Sensitive-content register (README): Mellor's age at the Harrow expulsion is fourteen, as the letter states it, no gloss. NULL FINDING - no mellor--wilde relationship file exists: the record in the pages read is companionship, hospitality and patronage in both directions, with no romantic or sexual content and no third-party or editorial characterization of the pair as anything but host and guest. Mellor's own documented queerness is a fact about Mellor and is not evidence about the pair. Cross-thread note: p. 1194 carries Wilde's use of 'neurasthenia' as a diagnosis for himself and for Mellor - relevant to the separate sexual-neurasthenia thread, though nothing there ties the term to sexual aetiology. Full passages, the null-finding table and the unread-page pointers in dossiers/EXILE-COMPANIONS_dossier.md (M1-M9).

context_engagements.note: Off-roster, and NOT a partnership: 'partner_name' is the schema's only slot for a named associate on a person record, and this is a servitude relationship, recorded in the correspondence in terms of purchase and ownership. Eolo was an Italian boy in Mellor's household who travelled with him on the Riviera in 1898-99 and was still with him in Paris in September 1900. Wilde's letters state that Eolo's father sold him to Mellor for 200 lire and had named all seventeen of his children out of a mythological dictionary; that Mellor was bored by him; and, at the far end of the arc, describe him as Mellor's 'slave'. Wilde's own framing in the 1900 sentence is a joke, recorded here as Wilde's and not endorsed; Wilde's sympathy in the 1899 sentence runs to Eolo, not to Mellor. Eolo is presumably the unnamed 'pretty Italian boy' of Wilde's first Mellor letter (p. 1112, 27 December 1898), per the editors' index. A third mention is indexed at printed 1128; that page was not read, so it stays a pointer.

sources.quote: Sometimes a very pretty, slim, fair-haired Italian boy bicycles over with him. His name is Eolo; his father, who sold him to Harold for 200 lire, having christened all his children – seventeen in number – out of the Mythological Dictionary. Harold is a nice fellow, but his boy bores him. It is dreadfully sad.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule - immediately after the sentences on Mellor's Harrow expulsion and daily bicycle visits. 'Eolo' and 'Mythological Dictionary' are italicised in the original.
sources.supports: What the correspondence records of Eolo's position in Mellor's household: the purchase from his father for 200 lire, his name, and Mellor's boredom with him
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1162, printed folio 1116 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Contiguous run from a page transcribed in full in the dossier (M3); no elision inside this quote.

sources.quote: He is now in Paris with his slave Eolo, who like all slaves is most tyrannical.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday, 1 September [1900], Paris, reporting on Mellor after the 'Mellor cure' at Gland; the next sentence begins 'He and I, however, are great' and completes on printed 1195 with 'friends.'
sources.supports: The same relation twenty months later, in Wilde's plain word - Eolo still described as Mellor's property
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1240, printed folio 1194 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

people.name: Frank Miles
people.bio: George Francis ('Frank') Miles, portraitist of Society beauties - the editors note he 'did many drawings' of Lillie Langtry - awarded the Royal Academy's Turner silver medal on 10 December 1879 for a painting of an Ocean Coast. He shared rooms with Wilde at Thames House, 13 Salisbury Street, off the Strand, until August 1880, and then at Keats House, 1 Tite Street, Chelsea; the friendship dates from Wilde's Oxford years, with visits together at Bingham and Moytura in the mid-1870s per the General Index.
bio_sources: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial notes, Complete Letters (2000), p. 78 n. 3, p. 86 n. 2, p. 91 n. 2, p. 94 n. 1; General Index entry, p. 1256
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 19 n. 1 (dates)
people.bio_note: DATES (added 2026-08-03): born 1852, died 1891, from the editors' first-mention footnote, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 19 n. 1 (repo PDF 44) - 'George Francis Miles (1852-91), son of the rector, was a popular artist in the early Eighties: his many drawings of Lillie Langtry did much to enhance her popularity. After he had shared two sets of rooms with Wilde in London they quarrelled and separated. Miles spent the last four years of his life in an asylum.' Located in the OCR mirror, then read as a rendered page image and the printed folio 19 confirmed. Years only in the source; no month or day recorded. The same footnote is the source for the asylum years, which the bio does not yet carry. All facts from editorial notes read as page images 2026-08-03: p. 78 n. 3 (Salisbury Street cohabitation to Aug 1880; repo PDF 103), p. 86 n. 2 (Turner medal; PDF 111), p. 91 n. 2 (Langtry drawings; PDF 116), p. 94 n. 1 (Keats House move; PDF 119), General Index p. 1256 (PDF 1301; 'W stays with, 17, 19, 20', Moytura 30-31).

people.name: A fisherman, Napoule
people.bio: A fisherman at La Napoule, on the Riviera, to whom Wilde described himself as 'practically engaged' in a letter to Robert Ross of 2 January 1899. The letter calls him 'a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen'. Nothing else about him - name, family, how they met, what became of it - appears in the pages read.
bio_sources: letters-2000
people.bio_note: THE LABEL IS A DESCRIPTOR, NOT A NAME: the source preserves no name for this man, and 'A fisherman, Napoule' is what the record provides - his trade and where Wilde was living - rendered as a node label. He should never be cited as though 'Fisherman' were a surname. Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1116 (repo PDF 1162, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). AGE: the letter states his age as eighteen. That is the letter's own statement, recorded exactly as it stands per the module's sensitive-content register; nothing is inferred from it and no gloss is added. DO NOT MERGE with the collective mentions on the same tier - 'The fishing population of the Riviera have the same freedom from morals as the Neapolitans have' (Ross, 27 December 1898, printed 1112) and the Napoule fisher-lads (pointer, printed c. 1119, not read) name no individual and stay in the collective context_engagement on wilde.json. He is a node under the 2026-08-03 roster decision because he is a distinct documented person, notwithstanding the missing name. Full passage in dossiers/EXILE-LIAISONS_dossier.md (L2). DATES: NONE RECORDED (2026-08-03). Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel quotes the same sentence at printed p. 245 (repo PDF 259) - 'I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen' - and gives him no name and no dates either. The stated age of eighteen in January 1899 is the letter's own and stays in the bio; it is not converted into a birth year. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by. That absence is itself the historical fact worth keeping - these men enter the written record only because Wilde wrote to his friends about them.

people.name: An Egyptian, Café d'Egypte
people.bio: A waiter at the Café d'Egypte in Paris who, Wilde wrote to Leonard Smithers in September 1900, 'occasionally serves me drinks'. Wilde describes him as 'A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick', and says in the same sentence that he does not console him for the loss of a Neapolitan who had gone home. No name, age, dates or further trace appear on the page read.
bio_sources: letters-2000
people.bio_note: THE LABEL IS A DESCRIPTOR, NOT A NAME: the source preserves no name. 'An Egyptian, Café d'Egypte' is what the record provides - the nationality Wilde ascribes to him and the café where he worked - rendered as a node label; it must never be cited as though it were a name. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE RESEARCH BRIEF, BOTH confirmed in the source: (1) the recipient is LEONARD SMITHERS, not George Ives. The passage stands in Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris; the letter to George Ives, [Postmark 6 September 1900], begins lower on the same printed page and contains nothing of the kind. (2) The café is in PARIS, not Cairo - it is named the Café d'Egypte and Wilde is writing from Paris, so the working label 'the Cairo-café Egyptian' is a misreading of the café's name. The id was therefore set to 'paris-egyptian' rather than the working brief's 'cairo-egyptian', to keep a false place-name out of the corpus; this can of course be reverted. Source: Complete Letters (2000), p. 1196 (repo PDF 1242, printed folio 1196 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image, read 2026-08-03). PROVENANCE CAVEAT, from the editors' own footnote 1 on the same page: 'The text of this incomplete letter is taken from Forty Years in my Bookshop by W. T. Spencer (1923), corrected and supplemented by the American Art Association catalogue of 1 February 1928.' The heading carries no manuscript line - unlike the Ives letter below it, which is 'MS Texas' - so this text descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than from a surviving manuscript, and the letter is incomplete. The letter states no age and none is inferred. A FURTHER DISTINCT PERSON IN THE SAME SENTENCE, NOW HIS OWN ENTRY: 'that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb', also called 'the wanton sylvan boy of Italy' - one man under two epithets, and a different man from this one. people.name: Charles Parker
people.bio: A gentleman's valet, out of employment at the beginning of 1893 when Taylor picked him and his brother up at the St James's Restaurant bar; aged 21 by his own sworn statement at the April 1895 trial. The first and most damaging Crown witness: his testimony describes sodomy at the Savoy and continued relations at Chapel Street, Park Walk, Tite Street and St James's Place, alongside his admitted £30 share of a Wood-Allen blackmail. Arrested and discharged in the Fitzroy Street raid of August 1894, he enlisted on 3 September 1894 and was traced to his regiment by Queensberry's solicitor at the end of March 1895. Wilde was convicted on all four Parker counts; from prison Wilde wrote of 'my connection with Charley Parker of which you may read a full account in my trial.'
bio_sources: Charles Parker's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 191-198 (pp. 191, 193, 197 read as IIIF page images 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Verdict, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 336-337 (djvu OCR)
Wilde to Robert Ross [1896], Complete Letters (2000), p. 670, with the editors' note 'One of the young men who gave evidence at Wilde's trials' (p. 670 n 1; read at rendered PDF p. 721, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far — 'aged 21 at the 1895 trials' per his own testimony. His father was 'a horse dealer' (cross-examination, p. 196). At Taylor's trial he testified again; Grain's cross there opens 'I was previously guilty of this' (djvu OCR, p. 275 region — flagged for verification in the source next session). The age is now verified in the source rather than from OCR: Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde (Notable British Trials), printed p. 191, opening the prosecution evidence at the first criminal trial - 'CHARLES PARKER, examined by Mr. C. F. GILL - I am 21 years of age. I have a brother, William. I have been engaged as a valet and my brother as a groom.' Read as a page image in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, IA PDF p. 230) and the printed folio 191 confirmed. That is an age sworn in April 1895 and nothing more: no birth year is computed from it into the born field. No source consulted gives a date. The obvious next step is not another book: it is the GRO birth index and the 1881/1891 censuses for a Charles Parker, valet, and his brother William, groom - genealogical work outside what so far could do.

people.name: William Parker
people.bio: A groom, brother of Charles Parker, present at the pick-up in the St James's Restaurant bar and at the Rupert Street dinner where Wilde fed Charles from his own fork and spoon and passed him a preserved cherry mouth-to-mouth. He understood from the outset that the brothers 'were to be treated as women, and that you were to have money for it'; he went twice to Little College Street, shared Taylor's bed with his brother one night — his testimony describes an attempted sodomy by Taylor — then took country work as a groom and 'had nothing more to do with Taylor or with Mr. Wilde.' Taylor was convicted of gross indecency with him (count 9) on 21 May 1895.
bio_sources: William Parker's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 198-199 (p. 199 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Verdict at Taylor's trial, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 292 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Taylor's account of the brothers staying a week, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 284 (djvu OCR)

Taylor said he ultimately 'persuaded William Parker to go home to his father' (p. 284, djvu OCR). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED (2026-08-03). Unlike his brother Charles, William gave no age on oath in the Hyde text: his examination-in-chief opens simply 'WILLIAM PARKER, examined by Mr. C. F. GILL - I am brother of Charles Parker. I have been employed as a groom' (located in the IA OCR text of Hyde; the neighbouring page carrying Charles's sworn age was verified at the page image, this passage was not). McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF p. 341, reports only Taylor's guess that the two brothers 'were sixteen or seventeen, or thereabouts' when he met them - a bystander's estimate of two people at once, not an age statement, and nothing is inferred from it. people.name: Harold Woodbury Parsons
people.bio: The last and latest of the Lewes House circle - 'among the latter-day group of Ned's boys and... the most audacious and elusive, and certainly the least likeable' (Sox). Born plain Harold Parsons at Lynn, Massachusetts (he claimed 1883 and a Harvard degree; the birth certificate says 13 July 1882, and he took 'Woodbury' from his brother's name), he was raised by his 'indulgent Woodbury grandfather' on Commonwealth Avenue, Boston. Warren, consulted at a Boston dinner, advised the art-life abroad: from 1906 Parsons studied in Cassel and Dresden, then made Lewes House his English headquarters 'eight months at a time'. Marshall 'came to despise' him. After Warren's and Marshall's deaths he carried the collecting tradition on as European purchasing agent for Cleveland, Kansas City and Omaha, and ended as a celebrated exposer of forgeries - the 'Etruscan' warriors among them - from his base in Rome, where, after a long life 'despite several attempts at suicide', he died in 1968.

Parsons's own gloss of Warren: 'a belated Greek who seemed to live in the age of Pericles and not to belong to the modern world' (p. 221, text layer - pointer).

people.name: Pietro
people.bio: Italian whom Wilde met at Nice in January 1899, on a three-day trip from La Napoule with Harold Mellor. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John', adding 'One would have followed him into the desert'. No surname, age, occupation, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.
bio_sources: letters-2000
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1118 (repo PDF 1164, printed folio confirmed on the rendered page image, 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance reused unchanged). The record preserves a first name only. Named in the same sentence as André but as a separate person, so the two are two nodes. The letter states no age; 'a little Italian' is a description in the letter and is not read here as an age statement, and no number is inferred. The St John comparison is to St John the Baptist - the wilderness saint - which is what makes the desert sentence a compliment rather than a non sequitur; the 'him' of that sentence is Pietro, the immediately preceding name. people.name: H. C. Pollitt
people.bio: Herbert Charles Pollitt, a native of Kendal in Westmorland and an undergraduate at Trinity College, Cambridge, 1889-92, where he made a name as an amateur ballet dancer. He collected Beardsley drawings, which he bought from Wilde's publisher Leonard Smithers. He preferred 'Jerome' to his own Christian names and signed himself so in his letters to Wilde; his Kendal home was called The Green Window. Wilde corresponded with him between November 1898 and January 1899 and appears never to have met him - in January 1899 he was still asking Smithers what Pollitt was like. Wilde sent him inscribed copies of the French translation of The Ballad of Reading Gaol and of The Importance of Being Earnest, and, per the editors, misspelt his surname in all four of the surviving letters.
people.bio_note: All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), read as page images 2026-08-03 with printed folios confirmed. Birth and death years, Kendal, Trinity College 1889-92, the amateur ballet dancing, the Beardsley collecting bought from Smithers, the preference for 'Jerome' and the inscribed presentation copies are from the main-particulars footnote at p. 1103 n. 1 (repo PDF 1149). 'Pollitt's Kendal home was called The Green Window' is p. 1107 n. 1 (PDF 1153, transcribed by the earlier record session). The four surviving letters and the misspelling in all of them are p. 1120 n. 2 (PDF 1166); the misspelt envelope address itself is quoted at p. 1116 n. 1 (PDF 1162). The never-met reading rests on Wilde's own question to Smithers at p. 1117 (PDF 1163). Full passages in dossiers/CORRESPONDENTS_dossier.md. Nothing read so far states how or when Wilde and Pollitt were introduced to each other by correspondence; the earlier index locator at printed 1103 is the first letter, and no Pollitt letter to Wilde is printed in this edition.

people.name: Matthew Stewart Prichard
people.bio: Barrister turned aesthete - 'the keenest and most capable of Ned Warren's assistants' and, per the Introduction, 'once considered the most able of Warren's aesthetes'. Born at Brislington near Bristol; Marlborough College, then New College, Oxford, from January 1884, months after Warren's matriculation; called to the bar in 1892, he abandoned the law to join Lewes House as Warren's secretary with George Harding, imposing order on the household, negotiating the Boston Museum's Bartlett Head in Greece, and speaking of Warren as 'a sort of Buddha at whose feet he used to sit'. Sox: 'Prichard clearly loved Warren who was like a father to him' - and names him the member of the brotherhood 'who was as openly misogynistic as Ned'. Viewed by the jealous Marshall as a rival, he left with Richard Fisher for the Boston Museum of Fine Arts in 1901; later a confidant of Isabella Stewart Gardner (285 letters), of Matisse and the Stein circle in Paris, and an internee-champion at Ruhleben in the First World War. He died in 1936; his ashes were scattered in the back garden of the Buckinghamshire house he shared with his brother.
bio_sources: Born: 'Prichard was born on 4 January 1865 in the little village of Brislington just to the east of Bristol. His parents were Charles Henry Prichard and Mattie Stewart.' - Sox (1991) p. 168 (repo PDF 192, folio confirmed, rendered 2026-08-03)

Died: the Walker draft biography 'was written at the instigation of Dame Una Pope-Hennessy after Prichard's death in 1936' - Sox p. 167 (PDF 191, rendered 2026-08-03); burial/ashes at Parslows Hillock, Bucks., with brother Charles Stewart Prichard - p. viii (PDF 12, rendered 2026-08-03)

Bar 1892, Lincoln's Inn practice; secretaryship with Harding: Sox pp. 170-171 (PDF 194-195, text layer; folio not rendered - finding aid)

Fisher - Marshall's Liverpool College friend, 'Fishlet' at Lewes House - paired off with Prichard per Fothergill's memoir: Prichard 'soon got jealous of me and Marshall: he took little Fisher with him and retired to the North Room at Lewes House... never to be seen again in the upper rooms, nor go riding' (p. 150, rendered). people.name: Marc-André Raffalovich
people.bio: A rich Russian educated in France and England; poet, whose Tuberose and Meadowsweet Wilde reviewed in the Pall Mall Gazette in March 1885, prompting a printed exchange between them over the scansion of 'tuberose'. Wilde is reported to have quipped that he came to London to found a salon and only succeeded in founding a saloon; the editors record the belief that Raffalovich revenged himself by breaking up Wilde's friendship with John Gray, with whom he remained close friends for the rest of his life. He largely supported Beardsley in the artist's last years, and in his own later years built St Peter's Church, Edinburgh, for Gray.
people.bio_note: All facts from the editorial footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 255 n. 2, running onto p. 256 (repo PDF 277-278, folios confirmed, read as page images 2026-08-03); born/died 1864-1934 from the same footnote. people.name: Raphael
people.bio: One of the two young men at La Napoule whom Wilde called his 'two special friends' in a letter to Laurence Housman of about 28 December 1898, singling them out from the local fisher-folk. Wilde wrote that both were 'quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. No surname, age, dates or further trace appear in the letter, and nothing else about him was found in the pages read.

people.name: Charles Ricketts
people.bio: Wood-engraver, book designer, publisher, painter, sculptor and stage designer, born in Geneva in 1866 to a French mother and an English father, and from 1882 a student at the City and Guilds Technical Art School in Lambeth, where he met Charles Shannon (1863-1937) and began the partnership that lasted the rest of his life. The two shared every home they had - Kennington Park Road; Whistler's former house in The Vale, Chelsea, from 1888; Beaufort Street from 1894; three years at Spring Terrace, Richmond; a studio-flat at Lansdowne House, Kensington, from 1902; Townshend House by Regent's Park from 1923; and Chilham Keep in Kent, given them for life in 1918 by their patron Edmund Davis - and ran between them the privately printed magazine the Dial (1889-97) and, from 1896, Ricketts's Vale Press, which issued forty-six books in eight years and was named after their first Chelsea home. For Wilde he designed the title-page and binding of The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), the binding of Intentions and of Lord Arthur Savile's Crime (both 1891), the limited edition of Poems (1892) and the whole of The Sphinx (1894), and with Shannon designed and decorated A House of Pomegranates (1891); he also painted, at Wilde's request, the forged Elizabethan portrait of Willie Hughes for "The Portrait of Mr W. H.", framed in worm-eaten moulding that Shannon pieced together. Wilde met the pair in August 1889 after they sent him the first number of the Dial, called Ricketts "the subtle and fantastic decorator" of his books and nicknamed him "Orchid"; Ricketts destroyed private letters and sections of his journal after Wilde's prosecution, visited him in Reading Gaol, and published recollections of him in 1932. He turned down the directorship of the National Gallery in 1914, was elected RA in 1928, and died of heart failure on 7 October 1931; the collection he and Shannon had built together passed to the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge.
people.bio_note: Dates from two sources read at the rendered page so far: the editors' identifying footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), pp. 410-411 n. 3 ("Charles De Sousy Ricketts (1866-1931)"), and Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 29 ("Charles Ricketts (1866-1931)"). The precise death - heart failure on 7 October 1931 - is Cook's, printed p. 52. "Jean Paul Raymond" was the fictional persona under whose name Ricketts published his 1932 Wilde recollections; the Complete Letters general index enters the book as Recollections of Oscar Wilde (index read in the source, printed p. 1261). people.name: Mary Robinson
people.bio: Poet, born 1857. She met Vernon Lee in 1880 and, on the Y90s account, the two developed a romantic friendship that lasted until Robinson's marriage in 1887 to the orientalist James Darmesteter. Lee first visited her in London in 1881, where Robinson introduced her to the Burne-Joneses, Edmund Gosse, the Morrises, the Rossettis and Oscar Wilde; Robinson's own published recollection of visiting "Casa Paget" in Florence is cited by Pulham for the cosmopolitan range of the Paget circle. She died in 1944.
people.bio_note: Dates (1857-1944) and the relationship account from Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee (2018/2019), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. Robinson does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters; her link to this map runs through Lee. No biography of Robinson was consulted so far, so the record is thin by design.

context_engagements.note: French orientalist. Off-roster; recorded because the marriage is the terminus of the lee--robinson record.

people.name: Edoardo Rolla
people.bio: Young Genoese seaman whom Wilde had written to ahead of his move from Switzerland to Genoa in the first week of April 1899, and hoped to find waiting for him there. Wilde described him to Robert Ross as 'a young lad, by name Edoardo Rolla, one of the sea-farers', with 'fair hair', 'always in dark blue'. No age, dates or other trace appear in the letter, and no record of whether the meeting took place was found in the pages read.

people.name: Robert Ross
people.bio: Canadian-born literary journalist, art critic and gallery-owner, grandson of Robert Baldwin, first Prime Minister of Upper Canada; brought to England aged two, he went up to King's College, Cambridge, in October 1888 and left abruptly in 1889 after a student-magazine libel, a ducking in the college fountain and a nervous breakdown. He met Wilde in 1886 and lodged with the Wildes at 16 Tite Street through part of 1887; he remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. In 1893 he and Lord Alfred Douglas were jointly threatened with prosecution over a schoolboy pupil of the Rev. Biscoe Wortham's at Bruges, and Ross spent the following winter out of reach at Davos. By 1897 he shared lodgings with More Adey at 24 Hornton Street, Kensington - by his biographer's account 'not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends' - and later ran the Carfax picture gallery with him. He kept daily attendance through Wilde's final illness, brought the priest who received Wilde into the Catholic Church, was at the bedside at the death on 30 November 1900, hired the Bagneux grave in his own name and moved the remains to Pere Lachaise in 1909. From early 1903 until the autumn of 1913 his life was shared with Frederick 'Freddie' Smith, a clerk of eighteen when they met, whom he employed as his secretary and with whom he openly set up house at 15 Vicarage Gardens, Kensington, from 1906. He published Wilde's De Profundis in 1905, cleared the estate of bankruptcy, became art critic and then art editor of the Morning Post, and was passed over for the directorship of the Tate. From 1911 Douglas and T. W. H. Crosland ran a campaign of surveillance and criminal accusation against him that produced the 1913 Ransome libel trial, Ross's own eight-day prosecution of Douglas at the Old Bailey, and the 1914 conspiracy proceedings; he was cleared, and afterwards lived quietly in rooms at 40 Half Moon Street, mentoring younger writers including Siegfried Sassoon and, through Sassoon, Wilfred Owen. He died there of heart failure on 5 October 1918, aged forty-nine.
people.bio_note: Born/died, Canadian origin, Baldwin descent, Cambridge dates, 1886 meeting, 'most faithful friend' and executorship from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 360 n. 1 (repo PDF 382; the footnote cites Margery Ross, Robert Ross: Friend of Friends, 1952, and Maureen Borland, Wilde's Devoted Friend, 1990). people.name: Stanley Saunders
people.bio: 'Elephant' of George Ives's household, a later addition who jointly inherited the Adelaide Road house with 'Pug' (Harold Bloodworth). Cook describes him as an apparently lovable but difficult alcoholic; his drinking eventually drove the Goddard daughters out of the house, and Ives - a teetotaller for whom the drinking was itself a source of angst - kept him nonetheless.
bio_sources: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), pp. 96, 100
people.bio_note: From Cook 2014 printed p. 96 (repo PDF 107, folio confirmed), read as a page image 2026-08-03, where the surname is printed 'Stanley Suanders' - evidently a typo for Saunders, the spelling used elsewhere and in this roster; recorded here rather than silently corrected. The account of the daughters leaving and Ives choosing Elephant is from Cook 2014 printed p. 100, known so far only from the PDF text layer - verify at the rendered page before quoting. Dates not established. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED (2026-08-03). Cook names him only at printed pp. 96 and 109 (repo PDF 107, 120), and at 96 the surname is printed 'Stanley Suanders' - the typo already recorded above. No dates are attached to him anywhere in the book. Searched so far, WITHOUT RESULT: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), repo PDF - every occurrence of the surname in the whole book, plus the endnotes and bibliography for the household chapter; the Ives repo transcripts (ives_diaries_burnet.txt, ives_letters_burnet_collated.txt, ives_letters_burnet_transcription.txt, ives_lewis_correspondence_2026-06.md), which contain no occurrence of any of the household surnames; and the open web, which returned only the Palgrave chapter version of Cook's same text ('George Ives, Queer Lives and the Family') and no dates. Cook is the only scholar to have written this household up and he dates their arrivals, their departures and Ives's will, but never a person: he gives no birth or death date for any member of the household. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CLOSE IT: census, GRO index and probate research on common English surnames - work so far could not do. Ives's own proved will (Cook, printed pp. 109-110), which leaves the Adelaide Road house to Bloodworth and Saunders, names Bloodworth an executor and portions the Goddards, is the natural documentary starting point, since a grant of probate fixes addresses and often identifies legatees.

people.name: Ernest Scarfe
people.bio: A valet's son and sometime valet, 'a young man of about twenty' by Wilde's sworn estimate, who went out to the Australian gold-diggings in 1893 — meeting Lord Douglas of Hawick, Bosie's elder brother, on the voyage — and returned to a clerkship in St Paul's Churchyard. He knew Taylor from the Knightsbridge Skating Rink; Taylor introduced him to Wilde at 10 St James's Place, where the waiter counted five or six visits, and he dined alone with Wilde and received the customary £4 cigarette case, last dining with him at the Avondale Hotel in February 1895. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at St James's Place (Oct 1893-Apr 1894); Scarfe was never called and no charge was ever laid; a begging letter from 'Ernesto' that Wilde mentions to Douglas in mid-1894 is tentatively identified with him by the Letters editors.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 148-149, 152 (djvu OCR)
Taylor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 286 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Thomas Price's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 205-206 (djvu OCR)
Hyde, Trials (1948), Introduction p. 47 n (the Hawick voyage acquaintance, 1893; djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 343 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 598 n 2 ('Possibly Ernest Scarfe, a valet'; read at rendered PDF p. 650, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far ('about twenty' is Wilde's estimate, April 1895, of the 1893-94 acquaintance). Taylor's account has Scarfe introducing HIM to Marling at the Skating Rink; Wilde's has Taylor introducing Scarfe to Lord Alfred Douglas at a skating rink — the introductions run in both directions in the record and are left unreconciled. DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED (2026-08-03). Scarfe was never called as a witness, so there is no sworn age for him at all - the 'about twenty' already recorded is Wilde's estimate under cross-examination in April 1895 ('He is a young man of about twenty, of no occupation. He had been in Australia at the gold-diggings'). The Complete Letters editors do not identify him beyond a hesitant footnote: the recipient of an 1894 letter is glossed 'Possibly Ernest Scarfe, a valet (see Trials, pp.148-9)' - located in the OCR mirror at repo PDF 650 (printed folio around 598, NOT confirmed in the source) - and the General Index entry is the cross-reference 'Ernesto see Scarfe, Ernest'. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted.

people.name: Maurice Schwabe
people.bio: The circle's connective figure and its most protected name: nephew by marriage of Sir Frank Lockwood, the Solicitor-General who prosecuted Wilde's final trial. Schwabe introduced Wilde to Taylor (Wilde's and Taylor's concurring sworn testimony), introduced Atkins to Taylor, and gave the Kettner's dinner at which Mavor met Wilde; Atkins placed him, 'a man of about twenty-two years of age,' in Wilde's bed in Paris in November 1892. At the trials his name was written on paper and passed to counsel rather than spoken; Wilde testified in April 1895 that Schwabe had been out of England for about two years, and he was never called.
bio_sources: Atkins's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 206-207 (p. 207 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Hyde's footnote identifying Schwabe, Trials (1948), p. 137 n (djvu OCR)
Wilde's re-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 158 with Hyde's note 'Schwabe' (djvu OCR)
Taylor's cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 283 ('That is the person you say introduced Wilde to you?—Yes.'; djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea of justification, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 342 ('Maurice Salis Schwabe'; IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
State Library of New South Wales, collection-item description for Lord Alfred Douglas, 'My darling pretty boy', letter to Maurice Schwabe, 1893 (Mitchell Library, Safe 1/2c) - birth and death years
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far. The General Index of Complete Letters (2000) contains NO Schwabe entry — verified at the rendered index page (printed p. 1263, where the entry would fall between Schreiner and Schuster; read 2026-08-03) — so no editorial 'main particulars' footnote exists there to cite. The plea's Schwabe clause is the only one of the named-man clauses printed without a 'did then and there commit' averment. DATES FOUND (added 2026-08-03, web): born 1871, died 1915, from the State Library of New South Wales, which holds the 1893 Lord Alfred Douglas letter to Schwabe ('My darling pretty boy', Mitchell Library, call no. Safe 1/2c). The library's collection-item description, read on sl.nsw.gov.au so far, states: 'Maurice Salis Schwabe (1871-1915) was exiled to the antipodes by his family to avoid his involvement in the sex scandal erupting around the celebrated author Oscar Wilde', arriving in Sydney in 1893. Years only, and the catalogue names no underlying record, so nothing finer is entered and these should be read as a library-catalogue statement rather than a document. (The deeper catalogue record at collection.sl.nsw.gov.au returned HTTP 403 and was not read.) SEARCHED WITHOUT RESULT: McKenna, Secret Life (2008), repo PDF pp. 327-333, 547, 568, 586, 604 - the fullest narrative treatment in the repo, and it gives no dates; Laura Lee's blog posts under her 'Maurice Schwabe' category and her book page - no dates, and she notes that Schwabe 'did not leave any autobiographies or a large cache of his correspondence in an archive'; the Complete Letters OCR mirror, which contains no occurrence of the name at all, consistent with the earlier finding that the General Index has no Schwabe entry. TO SHARPEN: Laura Lee, Wilde Nights & Robber Barons: The Story of Maurice Schwabe (2023) is a full-length biography built on police, court and bankruptcy records and is the obvious place to get exact dates; it was not obtainable so far. UNREAD LEAD, NOT EVIDENCE: a Great War Forum thread titled 'Maurice Shaw / Schwabe, HLI - cause of death?' indicates he enlisted under the anglicised name Shaw and died of wounds in France in late September 1915; that page returned HTTP 403 and was NOT read, so it is recorded here only as a place to look.

people.name: A 'Sea-God', Naples
people.bio: A young man Wilde met during a three-day stop at Naples on his Italian journey of April 1900, and with whom, in his own words to Robert Ross, he 'fell in love'. Wilde calls him a Sea-God and says he was at the Regia Marina School - the Italian naval school - 'instead of being with Triton'. No name, age, dates or further trace appear on the page read.
bio_sources: letters-2000
people.bio_note: THE LABEL IS A DESCRIPTOR, NOT A NAME: 'Sea-God' is Wilde's epithet for him, made to fit the joke about the naval school and Triton. The source preserves no name, and the node should never be cited as though 'Sea-God' were one. The only concrete fact the record gives about him is his institution - the Regia Marina School at Naples - which is why the label carries the city. Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, 16 April [1900], c/o Cook & Son, Piazza di Spagna, Rome, Complete Letters (2000), p. 1179 (repo PDF 1225, printed folio 1179 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page image, read 2026-08-03). The letter's heading - recipient, date and address - stands on an earlier printed page that was not read; it was located in the OCR mirror, which is finding-only, so the attribution to Ross and the 16 April date are flagged as mirror-derived rather than verified in the source. What IS verified in the source: the editors' footnote 2 on the same page reads 'Easter Day 1900 was on 15 April', and Wilde places his Vatican appearance 'yesterday', which is consistent with the mirror's 16 April heading. The letter states no age and none is inferred. OTHER DISTINCT PERSONS ON THE SAME PAGE, NOT CREATED AS NODES (roster change control - adding a person is a deliberate ROSTER.md edit, not a research-session side effect): the Palermo Sicilian-horse drivers Manuele, Francesco and Salvatore ('I loved them all, but only remember Manuele'), and the young seminarist Giuseppe Loverde, whose age the letter states as fifteen and whom Wilde says he kissed daily behind the high altar. All four are transcribed in dossiers/EXILE-LIAISONS_dossier.md (L6) and recorded but not added as candidates. Full passage in the same dossier. DATES: NONE RECORDED (2026-08-03). Searched so far: the whole OCR mirror of the Complete Letters (2000) for every occurrence of the name, plus the edition's General Index; Frankel, Oscar Wilde: The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF, the fullest scholarly account of the exile years; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008) and Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDFs. Frankel covers the Naples stop at printed p. 266 (repo PDF 280) and, at printed p. 277 (repo PDF 291), raises the possibility that a 'good-looking young Italian' Wilde entertained later that year was the same man - a suggestion, not an identification, and it supplies no name or dates. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted, and none is likely to be: the record preserves a first name (or a trade) in another man's correspondence and no surname to search by. That absence is itself the historical fact worth keeping - these men enter the written record only because Wilde wrote to his friends about them.

people.name: Charles Shannon
people.bio: Painter and lithographer, born on 20 April 1863, the second son of a Lincolnshire country rector, and from 1881 a student at the City and Guilds Technical Art School in Lambeth, where he met Charles Ricketts (1866-1931); the two began a partnership and a shared household that lasted until Ricketts's death and never once involved living apart. Shannon was the painter of the pair and one of the first British artists after Whistler to take up lithography as an art rather than a trade, teaching himself from a printer's handbook and contributing to L'Estampe Originale in Paris; he co-founded and co-edited the Dial with Ricketts (1889-97), was art editor of the Pageant (1896-97), and became an Associate of the Royal Academy in 1911 and a full Academician in 1920. For Wilde he designed the bindings of Lady Windermere's Fan (1893), A Woman of No Importance (1894), The Importance of Being Earnest (1899) and An Ideal Husband (1899), and with Ricketts designed and decorated A House of Pomegranates (1891); Wilde nicknamed him "Marigold" and called him "the drawer of dreams", and Max Beerbohm later dubbed the two of them "the ladies of the Vale". Shannon had affairs with women, sat more than once on the edge of marrying one of his models, and did neither; his biographers divide over what to make of it, and no statement by him about his life with Ricketts in the language of sexual identity survives. In 1929 he fell while hanging a picture, suffered brain damage from which he never recovered, was nursed by Ricketts and then, after Ricketts's death, by paid nurses in Kew, and died in 1937; the collection the two men had built together passed to the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge.
people.bio_note: Birth date (20 April 1863) and birthplace from Koenraad Claes's Y90s biography of Shannon, fetched and read in full 2026-08-03 - which gives the town as Quarrington "in the East Midlands"; "Lincolnshire" follows McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008 edn), PDF p. 190, read at the rendered page. Death year (1937) from two sources read at the rendered page: the editors' identifying footnote in Wilde's Complete Letters (2000), pp. 410-411 n. 3 ("Charles Hazlewood Shannon (1863-1937)"), and Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 29. Exact death date NOT established so far. CONFLICT to resolve: Claes gives ARA 1911 and RA 1920; the Wilde editors' footnote gives "Shannon in 1921". The forename is spelt Haslewood by Claes (who notes Hazelwood is also common) and Hazlewood by the Wilde editors. Career detail from Claes; the household chronology, the nursing and the Kew arrangement from Cook, printed pp. 31-33 and 52; the Wilde bindings from Complete Letters p. 411 n. 3; "Marigold" and "the ladies of the Vale" from McKenna, PDF p. 190, read in the source.
bio_sources: claes-y90s-shannon-bio
cook-2014
letters-2000
mckenna-2008

people.name: Edward Shelley
people.bio: Clerk at Wilde's publishers Elkin Mathews & John Lane (the Bodley Head) from 1891 — 'of decent family and upbringing' in Hyde's phrase — whom Wilde invited to dine at the Albemarle Hotel in February 1892; his testimony describes kisses, embraces and two nights in Wilde's bed, resisted, with no completed act. Wilde sent him inscribed books ('To one I like well') and theatre tickets, seating Pierre Louÿs beside him at the Lady Windermere's Fan first night; Shelley quarrelled with Wilde at the Savoy in March 1893 and broke off the acquaintance by letter. He testified at both criminal trials; the count concerning him was withdrawn for want of corroboration, and the editors of the Letters record that after the trials he joined the Grenadier Guards and served in the Boer War.
bio_sources: Shelley's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 212-214 and 296-297 (pp. 212-213 read as IIIF page images 2026-08-03)
Withdrawal of the count, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 305-307 (djvu OCR)

Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 529 n 2 ('Edward Shelley (1874-1915). A young employee of Elkin Mathews and John Lane...'; read at rendered PDF p. 549, 2026-08-03) and p. 530 (Grenadier Guards / Boer War; read at rendered PDF p. 550)
Wilde to Pierre Louÿs [mid-June 1892], Complete Letters (2000), p. 529 ('Vous serez à côté d'Edouard Shelley'; read at rendered page)
people.bio_note: Dates 1874-1915 are the Letters editors'. Aged 'twenty-one years of age' by his own sworn statement in April 1895. The djvu OCR of Hyde gives 'In 1893 they were publishing a book' — the page image reads 1892 (verified 2026-08-03).

people.name: Frederick 'Freddie' Smith
people.bio: Robert Ross's companion for a decade. Fryer records that Ross met him early in 1903, when Smith was an eighteen-year-old clerk and Ross almost twice his age; he became Ross's secretary, a position that also served as cover, and in 1906 moved into 15 Vicarage Gardens over his family's objections. He acted on the amateur stage as 'F. Stanley Smith'. The relationship ended in the autumn of 1913, and in 1914 he was named in Lord Alfred Douglas's plea of justification, where witnesses testified to having seen Ross embrace him.
people.bio_note: All facts from Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross (2000), transcribed by the Fryer research pass 2026-08-03 and verified at rendered pages. Birth and death dates are not given by Fryer: he states only that Smith was eighteen early in 1903, which would place his birth about 1884-85 - an inference, deliberately not entered in the born field. NOTE ON HIS ORIGINS: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), printed p. 100, states that Smith left George Ives's household to move in with Ross. Cook cites nothing for it - the sentence carries no note marker, and the nearest endnote (21, printed p. 271) is methodological literature on household and family. Fryer, who documents Smith abundantly, never mentions Ives in connection with him, and the dates sit awkwardly (Cook puts the Adelaide Road household from 1905; Fryer has Smith with Ross from early 1903). The Ives-to-Ross move is therefore recorded as an unsourced claim, not as fact. DATES: NONE RECORDED; CONFIRMED AGAIN so far (2026-08-03). Fryer's first-mention passage, printed p. 177 (repo PDF 199), is as close as the biography comes: 'early in 1903, he met a young man with whom he entered into a relationship quite unlike his other brief encounters with boys. Frederick (Freddie) Smith was an attractive, unpretentious, eighteen-year-old clerk'. Every later mention (printed pp. 192, 193, 198, 200, 207, 214, 230, 237, 238; repo PDF 214, 215, 220, 222, 229, 236, 252, 259, 260 - Fryer's second-half offset is printed = PDF minus 22) is narrative and dateless. Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF, contains no Freddie Smith at all - every 'Freddie' there is Freddie Manners-Sutton, the Crosland prosecutor, a different man entirely, and the two should not be conflated. Also searched: the Complete Letters mirror and Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014). No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted; the age eighteen in early 1903 would put his birth about 1884-85 and is still not entered.

people.name: Evguenia Souline
people.bio: Russian émigrée nurse, born 5 January 1904, and the woman to whom Radclyffe Hall wrote the letters collected as Your John. Almost everything known about her early life comes through Hall's letters rather than from her own papers: her editor records that we do not know where or to whom she was born, that Souline is not a Russian name, that no patronymic and no father's name is ever given, and that the recurring details are White Russian origins and being a general's daughter - which would make her father an officer of the Russian Imperial Army. Uprooted at seventeen by the revolution, she lived among the Russian exiles in Paris "basically without family, without status, and without financial reserves", and worked as a private nurse at the American Hospital at Neuilly. In 1934 Hall, at the spa of Bagnoles-de-l'Orne and unable to nurse Una Troubridge through a bout of gastroenteritis, sent to the American Hospital for a nurse; Souline was the nurse who came. The attachment that followed lasted until Hall's death in 1943. Her own side of the correspondence does not survive: of nine years of letters to Hall, one, from 1939, is extant. She died in 1958, a date her editor gives with a question mark.
people.bio_note: Birth date, the circumstances of the meeting, the nursing post and the evidentiary situation from Joanne Glasgow's introduction to Your John (1997), printed pp. 1-3, read at rendered page images 2026-08-04 (printed folio 2 confirmed in the running head). The death year is from the Library of Congress cataloguing-in-publication data printed in the same volume, which gives "Souline, Evguenia, 1904-1958?" - **the question mark is the cataloguer's and the year should be treated as uncertain**. Souline does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters and has no Wikipedia article; no Wikidata entity was matched, so she has no portrait on the map, which is itself the pattern the README describes - the record thins for people without property or status.
bio_sources: glasgow-1997-your-john

people.name: Alfred Taylor
people.bio: Marlborough-educated son of a cocoa manufacturer who came into a fortune of £45,000 on coming of age in 1883 and thereafter 'lived a life of pleasure' (his own testimony), keeping perfumed, permanently curtained rooms at 13 Little College Street and later 3 Chapel Street where he introduced young men — the Parkers, Wood, Mavor, Atkins, Scarfe — to one another and to Wilde, who was brought to him by Maurice Schwabe in 1892. Arrested in the Fitzroy Street raid of 12 August 1894 and discharged; arrested again in April 1895, he refused to turn Queen's Evidence against Wilde, was convicted on 21 May 1895 of gross indecency with Charles and William Parker, and was sentenced with Wilde on 25 May to two years' hard labour, Mr Justice Wills declaring it impossible to doubt he had 'kept a kind of male brothel.' The Letters editors give his full name as Alfred Waterhouse Somerset Taylor, born circa 1862, and record that after his release he lived in Canada and the USA.
bio_sources: Taylor's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 242 (age 33; Marlborough; £45,000; djvu OCR, folio '2A2' visible) and p. 286 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Mr Justice Wills's sentence, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 339 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)
Verdict, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 292 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, Complete Letters (2000), p. 603 n 2 (born circa 1862; Fitzroy Street raid 12 Aug 1894; refused Queen's Evidence; Canada and the USA; read at rendered PDF p. 655, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: Born date is the Letters editors' 'circa 1862', consistent with Taylor's sworn 'I am thirty-three years of age' (April-May 1895). No death date found in the sources read so far. The trial record has him bankrupt by the Chapel Street period (autumn 1893). DEATH DATE: NOT FOUND, AND POSITIVELY RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED (2026-08-03). Searched so far: the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror (the only 'Alfred Taylor' occurrences are pp. 603 and 679n plus the General Index line 'Taylor, Alfred, 603, 679n' - there is no editorial main-particulars footnote carrying dates); McKenna, Secret Life (2008) repo PDF (extensive on Taylor, silent on his dates and on his later life); Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, read in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238) - the trial record carries his sworn age, not a date; and the open web. The specialist compilations agree the death is unrecorded: Zagria's 'A Gender Variance Who's Who' heads its entry 'Alfred Taylor (1862 - ?) aristocrat, procurer, waiter' and states 'On release Taylor emigrated to the United States where nothing is known of him except that in the 1920s he was working as a waiter in Chicago, for by chance he served Alfred Douglas, Wilde's old lover, who was visiting the city' (zagria.blogspot.com, January 2010, citing Croft-Cooke, Feasting with Panthers (1968), and Ellmann, Oscar Wilde (1988)); a second web page repeats the same Chicago sentence and nothing further. The trail ends in 1920s Chicago, which means a US death or naturalisation record, not a British one, is where this would be closed. NO WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: the en.wikipedia 'Alfred Taylor (British Army officer)' (Q4723503) is Captain Alfred James 'Bulala' Taylor, 1861-1941, an Anglo-Irish officer of the Scramble for Africa and the Second Boer War, tried for war crimes - not Wilde's co-defendant. A link to it was added here in error and removed 2026-08-04. The born-year above is unaffected: it comes from the Letters editors and Taylor's own sworn age, not from that article.

context_engagements.note: Off-roster (parking lot). Charles Parker's sworn testimony has Taylor describing a 'form of marriage' with Mason, Taylor in woman's dress, with a wedding breakfast; Taylor on oath denied any marriage ceremony but admitted sleeping with Mason 'the first night' (Hyde p. 281) and addressing him 'Dear Charlie... With love.' Wilde's own letters to Mason from Worthing (c. 13 Aug 1894) ask after 'poor Alfred' following the Fitzroy Street raid and after Mason's 'married life' (Complete Letters p. 603, read at rendered page; the editors date Mason 1868-1940 and note Croft-Cooke's suggestion that the marriage was genuine).

sources.quote: Taylor told us on that occasion that he had gone through a form of marriage with a youth named Mason. Did he say who acted as the woman?—Yes; he said he did; that he was in woman's dress, and that they had a wedding breakfast.
sources.context: Charles Parker's examination-in-chief, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
sources.supports: the Taylor-Mason 'marriage' evidence at trial
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 231 (printed p. 193, folio 'N 193'), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03

people.name: Una Troubridge
people.bio: Sculptor, translator and diarist, born Margot Elena Gertrude Taylor on 8 March 1887 and generally known as Una Vincenzo. She trained at the Royal College of Art, sculpted a bust of Nijinsky in his role as the faun (1912), and later became the principal English translator of Colette. She married the naval officer Sir Ernest Troubridge in 1908 and had a daughter, Andrea, in 1910; the Ransom Center's sketch records that the Troubridges "were separated by 1919 because of Una's relationship with Radclyffe Hall". She was Mabel Batten's cousin, met Hall in 1915, and was her partner until Hall's death in 1943, afterwards writing The Life and Death of Radclyffe Hall (1961). Her diaries run to 131 volumes at the Ransom Center. She does not appear in Wilde's Complete Letters. She died in Rome on 24 September 1963.
people.bio_note: Birth and death dates, the marriage and separation, the partnership with Hall and the diary extent from the Harry Ransom Center finding aid for the Hall and Troubridge papers (eadid 00163), fetched and read in full 2026-08-03. Cook (2014, p. 108) names her with Hall among women who "seem to have been considered" for the Order of Chaeronea - a hedge too weak to carry an Ives edge.

people.name: Reggie Turner
people.bio: An old friend of Robert Ross who, in Ross's words, 'had been very kind to Mr Wilde since his release', and the constant presence of Wilde's last weeks at the Hôtel d'Alsace: he sent Ross daily bulletins, was with Wilde 'the whole of the last week of his life', slept at the hotel to give the 4 a.m. remedies, restrained him in delirium, held the ice-bag, and told the doctor he would be responsible for any expenses. He and Ross were, per the editors' plate caption, 'the two friends who were with Oscar on the day he died' (30 November 1900); he walked in the funeral procession and sent a wreath. Wilde's register toward him stayed teasing-affectionate to the end - 'You dear little Jew, don't you think that's enough?' during the ice-bag nursing, and the Rome 1900 photograph sent to Turner inscribed 'A young unmitred Bishop in partibus'. The 1898-99 letters show the ordinary setting of the friendship: Wilde's standing sign-off to him was 'Ever affectionately yours' (p. 1118), and Turner is the correspondent to whom Wilde reports other men's boys, other men's infatuations and a blackmail arrest in a shared idiom that assumes no explanation (pp. 1107-08, 1122). Looking back on Berneval in September 1897 Wilde counted what each friend had given him: Ross a week, Fothergill six days, 'Reggie gave me three days' (p. 942).
people.bio_note: DATES (added 2026-08-03): born 1869, died 1938, from the editors' first-mention footnote to 'To Reginald Turner', Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), printed p. 592 n. 1 (repo PDF 644) - '1869-1938. Illegitimate son of Lionel Lawson, who was an uncle of the first Lord Burnham … Journalist and wit. Lived mostly abroad. Published a number of novels. Oxford and lifelong friend of Max Beerbohm.' Located in the OCR mirror, then read as a rendered page image and the printed folio 592 confirmed. The footnote gives years only; no month or day, so none is recorded. All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000): 'an old friend of mine who had been very kind to Mr Wilde since his release' and 'the whole of the last week' from Ross to Adela Schuster, 14 Dec. 1900, pp. 1227-28 (repo PDF 1272-73); night-nursing, delirium restraint, ice-bag, expenses and the 'dear little Jew' remark from Turner's own letters to Ross, [November 1900], pp. 1217-18 (PDF 1262-63); deathbed-presence caption to plate 84 and the Rome inscription caption to plate 89 from the unpaginated plate section (PDF 600-601); procession and wreath from p. 1222 (PDF 1267). Pages read as page images 2026-08-03; printed folios confirmed. Full passages in dossiers/ADEY-GILBERT-TURNER_dossier.md. Every transcribed passage attests care and devotion, not romance; the dossier's hypothesis of a sexual dimension 'only in some secondary accounts' awaits those secondary reads. NULL FINDING, TWICE CONFIRMED (2026-08-03): no turner--wilde edge exists. Two independent passes found devotion, deathbed nursing and sustained affectionate correspondence, but every erotic subject in the whole correspondence is third-party. An 'alleged' class would require naming who asserts a romance, and no source - primary or secondary - has been found to name; the map has no non-romantic class, so no edge is the honest record.

people.name: A boy in grey velvet, Paris
people.bio: A young man Wilde was seen with outside a small café behind the Madeleine in Paris in late March 1900, eight months before his death. He is known from a single sentence of Wilde's own, written to Robert Ross: Ross's brother Aleck walked past and saw them together. Wilde describes him as 'a beautiful boy in grey velvet - half rough, all Hylas' - 'rough' being the period word for a working-class young man, and Hylas the youth Herakles loved and lost. No name, age or occupation is recorded, and nothing else about him survives.
people.bio_note: Sole source: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [Late March 1900], Grand Cafe, 14 boulevard des Capucines, Paris; Complete Letters printed 1177 (repo PDF 1223), read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. The editors' footnote 3 to that page explains Wilde's joke about Aleck's eye: 'Aleck Ross had lost the sight of one eye in early youth.' Admitted to the roster 2026-08-04 on Lovelle's instruction; he had previously been carried inside a collective 'one-scene companions' entry on wilde.json, which was retired the same day. NO age is stated and none should be inferred.
bio_sources: letters-2000

people.name: Renee Vivien
people.bio: Symbolist poet writing in French, 1877-1909, English by birth, a central figure of Natalie Barney's Paris circle and, in Sarah Parker's phrase, "one of Barney's former lovers" by the time Olive Custance visited Paris around 1901. Custance befriended her there. Barney's memoir Souvenirs Indiscrets (1960) records, as reported by Parker, a plan to gather Barney, Vivien and Custance into a recreated Sapphic community at Mytilene, an endeavour "stymied by Vivien's jealousy". Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904) fictionalises Custance as the "little English poetess Dagmar". She does not appear anywhere in Wilde's Complete Letters; her connection to this web runs entirely through Barney and Custance.
people.bio_note: Dates (1877-1909) from Sarah Parker's Y90s biography of Olive Custance, re-fetched and read in full 2026-08-03 for this record. No biography of Vivien was consulted; the record is deliberately thin and rests on the Barney/Custance scholarship already in the corpus.
bio_sources: parker-y90s-custance-bio

people.name: Edward Perry Warren
people.bio: Boston paper-fortune heir turned expatriate collector of classical antiquities - the great supplier of the Boston Museum of Fine Arts - and 'master of Lewes House' in Lewes, East Sussex, where from 1890 he 'collected art and young men' and tried to forge his secretaries into a 'brotherhood of aesthetes'. Born at Waltham, Massachusetts, 'in the year Lincoln was elected President'; at New College, Oxford, he met John Marshall in 1884 - 'the love of his life' per Sox - whom he wooed by letter for five years and whose forty-year partnership anchored the enterprise. Author of A Tale of Pausanian Love, the privately printed fairy tale The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900, dedicated to Mary Bliss), and A Defence of Uranian Love, written and rewritten in his garden office at 'Thebes'. Died in London on 28 December 1928 after an abdominal operation, ten months after Marshall; cremated at Golders Green on 1 January 1929; his ashes were placed in the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca on 5 April 1929, next to 'his beloved "Puppy"'.

Died: 'Ned was dead on 28 December 1928. After an abdominal operation, he entered the Cambridge House Nursing Home at Dorset Square in London where he died.' - Sox p. 129 (PDF 145, rendered 2026-08-03)
Cremation 1 Jan 1929, ashes to Bagni di Lucca 5 Apr 1929, 'collected art and young men', 'brotherhood of aesthetes', 'his beloved Puppy': Sox pp. vii-viii (PDF 11-12, rendered 2026-08-03)

Oxford matriculation 1883 is implied, not stated ('In January 1884, Prichard entered New College only months after Ned Warren's matriculation', p. 169, rendered). Father: Samuel Dennis Warren of S.D. Warren & Co. (Cumberland Mills paper), p. 3. Full passages in dossiers/LEWES-HOUSE_dossier.md.

context_engagements.note: Off-roster. Warren's 'first choice' of life-companion before Marshall: on an 1889 trip to Wiesbaden and Rome he confided his desire to share his life with 'an alter ego'; West declined - 'not happy with the possible implications of such a relationship', and long set on Holy Orders. 'Despite the rebuff, Ned remained devoted to West', becoming godfather to his sons; West's son Charles Murray West later ran Warren's Maine house and inherited it (Sox pp. 38-39, rendered 2026-08-03).

Thomas married Nan Devey the year after Marshall married (p. 78, rendered), and stayed in Warren's service to the end - one of the few at the Golders Green chapel (p. vii).
