people.name: Walt Whitman
people.bio: American poet, author of Leaves of Grass (first published 1855; its 1882 eighth edition was withdrawn by its publishers on a threatened prosecution for indecency). By 1882 he was living in Camden, New Jersey, across the Delaware from Philadelphia, partly paralysed since 1873. During the American lecture tour of 1882 Wilde visited him there twice - on 18 January, taken by the Philadelphia publisher J. M. Stoddart at Whitman's written invitation, and again in early May - and Wilde's one surviving letter to him (postmarked 1 March 1882) relays Swinburne's admiration and declares an intent to visit again before leaving America. Whitman kept that letter until 1888, when he handed it to Horace Traubel, whose Camden conversation records preserve Whitman's side of the acquaintance.
people.bio_note: Dates (1819-92), Camden residence, the 18 January visit with Stoddart, and the Leaves of Grass withdrawal are from the biographical footnote at Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 144 n. 1 (repo PDF 167, printed folio confirmed, read as page image 2026-08-03). Letter postmark and closing from pp. 144-5 (repo PDF 167-168, same session). Invitation card: Whitman Archive yal.00277 (Beinecke), read via Wayback capture. 1873 paralysis: Philadelphia Press interview, 19 Jan. 1882 (Whitman Archive med.00534, read via Wayback capture). Second visit 'early in May' 1882: Ellmann, 'Oscar Meets Walt', NYRB 3 Dec. 1987 (read at article page). 1888 letter handover: Traubel, With Walt Whitman in Camden, vol. 2, pp. 287-8 (IA withwaltwhitmani0002unse_c4l4, IIIF page images). Full passages in dossiers/WHITMAN_dossier.md.

people.name: Oscar Wilde
people.bio: Dublin-born writer; born 16 October 1854 at 21 Westland Row, educated at Trinity College Dublin and Magdalen College, Oxford. Married Constance Lloyd on 29 May 1884; two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Convicted 25 May 1895 and sentenced to two years' hard labour following the three trials of that spring; released 19 May 1897 and lived thereafter in France and Italy. Died 30 November 1900 at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, of cerebral meningitis; buried at Bagneux, moved to Père Lachaise in 1909.
people.bio_note: All facts from the Chronological Table, Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), pp. viii-xii (repo PDF 8-12), read as page images 2026-08-03.
people.roster_note: The collective 'unnamed and one-scene companions' entry was removed 2026-08-04: every named man in it now has his own node and edge (Andre, Pietro, le petit Georges, the Napoule fisherman, the Cafe d'Egypte Egyptian, Raphael, Fortune, the Naples 'Sea-God'), so the entry only duplicated them. TWO THINGS IT CARRIED HAVE NO NODE: (1) the unnamed 'beautiful boy in grey velvet' seen with Wilde outside a cafe behind the Madeleine by Aleck Ross, late March 1900 (Complete Letters printed 1177) - a roster candidate on exactly the same footing as the Sea-God and the Napoule fisherman, who are already nodes; and (2) Wilde's general remark on the Riviera fishing population, 27 December 1898 (printed 1112), which is a remark rather than a person. Full transcriptions remain in dossiers/EXILE-COMPANIONS_dossier.md (T1-T4).

people.name: Louis Wilkinson
people.bio: Louis Umfreville Wilkinson, a Radley schoolboy when he opened a correspondence with Wilde in the winter of 1898. To get into correspondence he invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray; the editors identify a second invention, his claim to have been at the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan, as made for the same purpose. A third claim was not invented but misattributed: it was his father, not he, who had known Edward FitzGerald, the two being neighbours in Suffolk. He and Wilde never met. Wilde, writing to Reggie Turner in January 1899, described him as 'a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen'. He went up to Oxford, published many novels and other books under the name Louis Marlow, and in Seven Friends (1953) printed many of Wilde's letters to him, there confessing the Ipswich fabrication. His first letter to Wilde and some of the subsequent ones are in the Hyde Collection.
people.bio_note: All facts from Holland & Hart-Davis, Complete Letters (2000), read as page images 2026-08-03 with printed folios confirmed. Birth and death years, the Radley schooling, the Ipswich Dramatic Society fabrication, the pen-name Louis Marlow, Seven Friends (1953), the Hyde Collection provenance and the flat statement that the two never met are from the main-particulars footnote at p. 1109 n. 1 (the note begins on 1109 and concludes at the foot of 1110; repo PDF 1155-56, transcribed by the earlier record session). The Lady Windermere's Fan invention is p. 1127 n. 2 (PDF 1173). The FitzGerald correction is p. 1133 n. 1 (PDF 1179). The age is Wilde's own contemporaneous statement to Reginald Turner at p. 1118 (PDF 1164) and is consistent with the 1881 birth year. Full passages and the letter-by-letter salutation log in dossiers/CORRESPONDENTS_dossier.md. NOT read so far (pointers): the correspondence tail at printed 1136, 1159n, 1168, 1170-71 (Paris invitation) and 1171, and the funeral-wreath mention at approximately printed 1224.

people.name: Alfred Wood
people.bio: An out-of-work clerk who lived three weeks in Taylor's one-bed rooms in January 1893 and was sent to Wilde at the Café Royal by Lord Alfred Douglas's telegram from Salisbury; his testimony describes an act of 'the grossest indecency' at 16 Tite Street, and Wilde was convicted on that count. In a suit of clothes Douglas gave him at Oxford he found Wilde's letters to Douglas — the seed of the Allen-Cliburn blackmail affair — and left for America in spring 1893 with £35 from Wilde; back in London by 1894, he took £175 from a £300-£400 extortion worked with Allen on a gentleman caught with Charles Parker. In De Profundis Wilde described blackmail as the 'sole source of income' of 'people like Alfred Wood.'
bio_sources: Wood's testimony, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 201-205 (p. 202 read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; rest djvu OCR)
Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 134-135 (djvu OCR)
Verdict on count 13, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 337 (djvu OCR)
Wilde, De Profundis, Complete Letters (2000), p. 761, with the editors' note 'A blackmailer who gave evidence at Wilde's trials' (p. 761 n 1; read at rendered PDF p. 812, 2026-08-03)
people.bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far; the Letters editors' note gives none. Ages conflict in the record: Wilde on oath called him 'about twenty-three' in January 1893, while Wood testified he 'was not of age when I went to America' later that year. Taylor dated their first meeting earlier than Wood did (May 1892, at Atkins's rooms, vs. Wood's 'about January 1893'). The letter 'To Mr Wood' at Complete Letters p. 483 ([?Summer 1891]) is editorially 'Unidentified' — a literary correspondent, NOT this Alfred Wood (verified at rendered page 2026-08-03). DATES: NOT FOUND; RECORDED AS UNRECOVERED FROM THE SOURCES CONSULTED (2026-08-03). Wood's examination-in-chief in Hyde opens 'ALFRED WOOD, examined by Mr. AVORY - I was formerly a clerk. In January, 1893, I was not in any occupation' - no age is asked or given, which is why the age evidence for him stays the two conflicting second-hand figures already recorded above. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web. Additional checks made so far: the Complete Letters General Index carries only 'Wood, Alfred, 761' and the De Profundis passage at printed p. 761 gives no particulars; McKenna's endnotes cite his 1895 witness statement from a private collection, not a public record. No birth or death date is recorded in any source consulted. He is said in the trial record to have gone to America in 1893, so a US record would be the place to look.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: What survives is one clause of admiration in a letter to Robert Ross - 'I met one beautiful person, called André, with wonderful eyes' - with no approach, no second meeting and no outcome. That is admiration recorded by Wilde and nothing more, so desire-expressed with outcome 'unknown' is the only class the page supports: romantic-nonsexual would assert a mutual connection the letter does not document, and documented-sexual has no first-person statement behind it. Candour about the bar: this is the thinnest item in the exile-liaison tier. The README requires that desire be legible as desire to a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis, and a bare 'one beautiful person … with wonderful eyes' sits at or just under that line; the reading that this is desire rather than aesthetic notice is this project's, not a scholarly source's, and a later check may reasonably prefer to keep André as a bio record with no edge. Note also that the following sentence's stronger declaration - 'One would have followed him into the desert' - attaches to Pietro, not to André, and is not borrowed here. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and André's own view of the meeting is not recorded anywhere.
relationships.date_label: Met on a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor, reported in a letter the editors date Thursday [? 12 January 1899] from Napoule.
relationships.summary: During his Riviera winter of 1898-99, Wilde crossed from Napoule to Nice for three days with Harold Mellor and wrote to Robert Ross that he had met a beautiful person named André, with wonderful eyes. That single clause is the whole of the record: no surname, no age, no occupation, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read, and no indication of what if anything followed.

sources.quote: I have been over again to Nice with Harold Mellor, for three days. It was most pretty and gay, and music everywhere. I met one beautiful person, called André, with wonderful eyes, and a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John. One would have followed him into the desert.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [? 12 January 1899], Napoule - reporting the Nice excursion. The final sentence's 'him' refers to Pietro, the immediately preceding name.
sources.supports: The whole of the record for André: a named person met at Nice, described as beautiful and with wonderful eyes, with no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 confirmed on rendered page, read as a page image 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance carried forward unchanged (dossiers/EXILE-COMPANIONS_dossier.md T1).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: As with lee--robinson, the evidence read is a non-participant's: Pulham states the companionship and its dates. Note that Pulham's wording is cooler here than in the Robinson paragraph - 'close companion', 'co-written', 'departure from Il Palmerino' - and she does not characterise the bond as romantic in the sentences read, so this record deliberately does not either; the pairing is recorded, not its nature. Lee's own 1924 introduction to Anstruther-Thomson's posthumous Art and Man is participant testimony and would likely change the class; it is recorded as a pointer, unread.
relationships.date_label: companion and co-author 1887-1900; Lee wrote a tribute to her in 1924, three years after her death
relationships.summary: Clementina 'Kit' Anstruther-Thomson replaced Mary Robinson as Vernon Lee's close companion in 1887, the year of Robinson's marriage, and remained so until 1900, living with her at Il Palmerino. The two collaborated on Lee's theory of psychological aesthetics, running experiments on bodily response to art informed by Vischer's Einfuhlung; their article 'Beauty and Ugliness' (Contemporary Review, October 1897) provoked a plagiarism charge from Bernard Berenson which he later retracted, and the work was collected as the co-written Beauty and Ugliness (1912). Anstruther-Thomson died in 1921 and Lee wrote a substantial introduction to her posthumous Art and Man (1924) as a tribute.

sources.quote: The former was co-written with Clementina (Kit) Anstruther-Thomson (1857-1921), who replaced Mary Robinson as Lee’s close companion from 1887 to 1900.
sources.context: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography, in the paragraph on Lee's psychological aesthetics; 'the former' is Beauty and Ugliness (1912). The word 'replaced' is Pulham's and is the link back to lee--robinson: the succession is dated to Robinson's marriage year.

sources.quote: The writer of the following unpublished essays and fragments, my late very dear friend and fellow-worker, Miss C. Anstruther-Thomson, held an unusually large place in the life of many and very different persons, either at the same moment or during successive phases of her constantly altering, although always so harmoniously consistent, personality. … Be this as it may, what each one of us may thus have made of Kit Anstruther-Thomson, as well as what she has actually been to us, is a subject I shall attempt neither to penetrate nor to reveal.

sources.supports: Lee's own retrospective account of the relationship.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The sexual allegation (Paris, 20 November 1892) rests on Queensberry's plea and the Crown's indictment, supported only circumstantially at trial (Mary Applegate's stained-sheets testimony). Atkins himself swore that no impropriety ever took place between him and Wilde; he was then exposed on recall as having lied on oath about the Rochester Row blackmail incident and was ordered from the box by Mr Justice Charles; the jury returned not guilty on all Atkins counts (1 May 1895) and the Crown dropped him at the final trial. Discredited-witness territory — the ROSTER's own note ('testimony discredited') and the taxonomy rule both point to 'alleged'.
relationships.date_label: November 1892 (alleged, Paris); acquaintance 1892–1894
relationships.summary: Fred Atkins, a twenty-year-old billiard-marker, bookmaker's clerk and music-hall comedian, was introduced into the circle by Maurice Schwabe in November 1892 and taken to Paris by Wilde as nominal 'private secretary.' The plea alleged sexual acts there; Atkins on oath denied any impropriety with Wilde while describing Schwabe in Wilde's bed. His credibility collapsed on recall when he was proved to have lied about a Rochester Row blackmail arrest, and the jury acquitted Wilde on every Atkins count.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited and committed acts of gross indecency with Frederick Atkins at 29 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris, on 20 November 1892
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895); Crown indictment counts in Regina v. Wilde and Taylor (1895); circumstantially, Mary Applegate's testimony about the sheets at Osnaburgh Street (Hyde p. 211)
disputed.disputed_by: Atkins's own sworn testimony ('Did any impropriety ever take place between you and Mr. Wilde?—Never.'); Wilde's denials on oath at the libel trial; the jury's not-guilty verdict on the Atkins counts, 1 May 1895
disputed.grounds: the witness was exposed as a perjurer mid-trial (Rochester Row charge-sheet produced; 'Leave the box' — Hyde pp. 217-218) and both prosecution and defence positions on Atkins failed; Hyde's introduction records the jury 'found the prisoners not guilty on the charges relating to Atkins' (p. 74)

sources.quote: Examination continued—I got back to the rooms very late. Mr. Wilde was in bed. I went into his room and had something to drink. A man of about twenty-two years of age was in bed with Mr. Wilde. It was Schwabe. I went to bed by myself. Before I got out of bed in the morning Mr. Wilde came into my room. That was about nine o'clock. He talked about the Moulin Rouge and I told him that I had enjoyed myself. Mr. Wilde then said to me, "Shall I come into bed with you?" I replied that it was time to get up. Mr. Wilde did not get into bed with me.

relationships.date_label: Courtship Aug. 1876 - autumn 1878 (Wilde: 'a memory of two sweet years'); parting letters Sept.-Oct. 1878; she married Bram Stoker 4 Dec. 1878; cordial contact to at least 1893.
relationships.summary: Wilde courted Florence Balcombe of Clontarf from August 1876, when he drew her and described taking 'an exquisitely pretty girl' of seventeen to afternoon cathedral service, through two Dublin years he later called 'the sweetest of all the years of my youth'. On learning of her engagement to Bram Stoker in autumn 1878 he asked back the gold cross he had given her one Christmas, returned her letters, and insisted on parting 'under your mother's roof'. In January 1881 he secretly sent her a crown of flowers via Ellen Terry for her Lyceum debut - 'She thinks I never loved her, thinks I forget. My God how could I!' - and in 1893 he sent her Salome 'with kind regards to Bram'. The editors caption her plate 'Wilde's first love'.

Whether the liaison was consummated rests on works not reachable so far — Parker (2011) calls the Barney/Vivien connections 'rumoured entanglements', citing Wickes 1977: 58-60 and Souhami 2004 — so the sexual layer is carried by pointers. Honest fallback if review restricts to read-verified evidence: 'romantic-nonsexual'.
relationships.date_label: correspondence from c. 1897–98 (after Opals); pursuit, Paris visit, and Italian holiday c. 1901; contact sustained after Custance's 1902 marriage
relationships.summary: After Opals (1897) Barney opened the acquaintance with a letter of admiration, wooed Custance with love poems, and invited her to Paris, where Custance also befriended Barney's former lover Renée Vivien; around 1901 Barney and Custance holidayed together in Italy while Custance was simultaneously conducting her courtship with Douglas. Accounts of the Barney–Vivien–Custance ménage are contradictory: Barney's memoir says she tried to persuade Custance to join a Sapphic community at Mytilene (stymied by Vivien's jealousy), and per McDermott she 'supposedly envisaged marrying Douglas as a way of inducing Olive to live with her too'. Custance kept up contact with Barney after returning to London in 1901 and marrying in 1902, and Custance verse survives among Barney's papers.

null_findings.finding: ! CORRECTION TO AN INHERITED FRAMING. The pointer this replaces described Souvenirs indiscrets as carrying 'the plan to bring Custance and Vivien together in a Sapphic community at Mytilene', on the authority of Parker's Y90s biography. Read at page, the book does not say that. Two separate things have been run together. (1) At PDF p. 42 Barney proposes to Vivien a group of poetesses 'comme celles qui entouraient Sapho à Mytilène' - Mytilene is the SIMILE - and they act on it by inviting Custance to join them in PARIS, rue Alphonse-de-Neuville. (2) The actual Mytilene journey, at PDF pp. 64-66, is Barney and Vivien alone, years later, and Custance is not mentioned in it at any point. Further, the Paris plan failed: Vivien refused to socialise with Custance at all (PDF p. 48). Barney also never names Custance in the volume - she is 'Opale' throughout, and a case-sensitive search for 'Custance' across all 205 pages returns zero. Re-anchor any Parker-derived locator before trusting it.

relationships.summary: Mabel Veronica Batten, a singer known as 'Ladye', was Radclyffe Hall's first lover. The Ransom Center's biographical sketch credits her with introducing Hall into a circle of artistic and intellectual women, many of them lesbians - so she is, in the surviving record, the person who brought Hall into queer society. Batten was also the cousin of Una Troubridge, who met Hall in 1915 and became Hall's partner after Batten's death the following year; the three-way relation gave Hall's biographer Michael Baker his title, Our Three Selves.

sources.quote: While we cannot know for certain what grief John writes of here, it seems likely that the reference is to the death of Mabel Veronica Batten (Ladye), which occurred when John was in the first throes of her passion for Una, a passion very similar to that John was now feeling for Souline. The irony, of course, is that Ladye was grieved by that passion, just as Una was now grieved.
sources.context: Joanne Glasgow's editorial footnote to Hall's letter to Evguenia Souline of 27 July 1934, glossing Hall's own sentence on the same page - 'I slept, Soulina, as once before in my life I slept as the result of a fearful grief'. Note the hedge: Glasgow does not claim to know, and says so first. This is the editor writing about Hall, not Hall writing about Batten, and it is recorded as such.
sources.supports: An editor's reading that Hall's worst remembered grief was Batten's death, and that Batten was grieved by Hall's passion for Troubridge - second-hand, hedged, and the only thing in this volume that bears on this pair.

null_findings.finding: The pointer this replaces expected 'Hall's own words about her attachments'. Your John cannot supply them for THIS pair: it is Hall's love letters to Evguenia Souline, 1934-1942, and Batten had been dead since 1916. Across the copy on disk the words 'Ladye', 'Mabel' and 'Batten' occur on one page only - printed 29 - and only in Glasgow's footnote, now recorded. TWO LIMITS ON THIS SEARCH, both honest: the repo copy is a **30-page extract**, not the whole book (printed folios run 32 to 80 plus front matter), so this is not a whole-volume null; and the volume is by its nature a Hall-to-Souline source. relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook documents a forty-one-year household bond - Bloodworth, 'a teenage footballer', moved into Ives's Adelaide Road house in 1909 and stayed until Ives's death in 1950, one of the working-class men Ives called his 'children' in a household Cook twice marks as unconventional - but stops short of any sexual or romantic characterization. Lewis (podcast) likewise speaks only of 'domestic relationships' with 'a succession of younger men'. The lover reading comes from the project's research leads (Lewis interview prep), which are not citable; hence alleged, pending the Ives diaries or Lewis's published work. CORROBORATION (2026-08-03): Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. That sharpens the evidence but does not lift the class: it remains one historian's careful inference, and he does not assert sexual relations outright. EVIDENCE-TIER CORRECTION 2026-08-03 (): reclassified to self-reported. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.
relationships.date_label: Moved into the Adelaide Road household 1909; stayed until Ives's death, 1950 (Cook).
relationships.summary: Harold Bloodworth ('Pug'), described by Cook as 'a teenage footballer', moved into Ives's Adelaide Road, Primrose Hill household in 1909 and remained for the rest of Ives's life - the longest-staying of the working- and lower-middle-class men Ives paternalistically called his 'children'. The sources read document the household, not a sexual bond; the characterization of Bloodworth as a lover awaits first-person evidence from the Ives diaries.

disputed.claim: That Bloodworth was one of Ives's lovers, beyond being a member of his household from 1909 to 1950
disputed.asserted_by: Project research leads (interview prep drawing on Brian Lewis's account of Ives), which gloss Ives's household 'children', including Bloodworth ('Pug'), as his lovers
disputed.grounds: No citable source read so far asserts it. Cook (2003), p. 148, documents membership and duration in an 'unconventional household' without romantic or sexual characterization; Lewis on the podcast describes 'domestic relationships' with 'a succession of younger men' without naming Bloodworth or stating a sexual bond. Resolution requires the Ives diaries (Harry Ransom Center) or Lewis's forthcoming biography.

sources.quote: When Pug and another long term resident Cubby (Charles Gee) were both away he wrote in his diary: 'I feel sad. I love those two, deeply, tenderly [...] Love's quite different from passion [...] to sleep side by side with one's comrade is beyond all worlds beautiful. Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'.
sources.context: Cook quoting Ives's diary (vol. 76, 20 January 1921, p. 25, per Cook's endnote 35) on Pug and Cubby being away; the ellipses are Cook's own
sources.supports: Ives's own diary on sleeping beside Pug (Bloodworth) and Cubby - 'those two' names both men; participant testimony, quoted by Cook from Diary vol. 76. QUOTE EXTENDED by the Q2 quality pass 2026-08-03: the record previously stopped at 'beyond all worlds beautiful', cutting the clause in which Ives actually says what the intimacy gave him - 'Not exciting, but oh such a protection and sympathy, of healing to the heart's many wounds'. That clause is the most explicit first-hand characterization of this bond anywhere in the sources read, and it is the sentence that distinguishes what Ives had with these men from what the word 'lover' would imply: he names love, disclaims passion, and locates the value in comfort.

sources.quote: While a late night for Pug left Ives feeling 'pretty sure he had arranged to stay with a girl', he observed that 'a wise parent does not ask too many questions' (even though usually 'we have no secrets between us').

sources.supports: The clearest first-hand statement of the terms Ives set for this relationship, and the one that bears directly on the disputed block above: Ives knows Bloodworth spends nights with women, casts himself as parent rather than partner, and declines to ask - while still claiming 'we have no secrets between us'. Ives's diary, vol. 76, 2 October 1920, as quoted by Cook. Read against the lead quotation, the two together give the shape of the bond in Ives's own terms: love and a shared bed, without exclusivity and without the vocabulary of coupledom.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: One-sided by the nature of the record: everything known comes from Fothergill's own memoir, and nothing of the boy's view survives beyond Fothergill's report that he sent 'a couple of nice letters in return'. The outcome is recorded as unknown rather than declined, because the approach was stopped by a solicitors' letter threatening police involvement, not by any refusal the record attributes to the boy. The passage carries its own contemporary judgment - the solicitors wrote that no man of the world could form two opinions about Fothergill's intentions - alongside Fothergill's retrospective self-defence that he was 'still full of my broken platonic love affairs at school and probably had no other intentions'. Both are recorded; neither is endorsed.
relationships.summary: Fothergill saw the boy acting in a Greek play at Bradfield College, bought a photograph of the cast, and wrote to him, giving 30 Manchester Street as his address so that the boy might visit. Two letters came back. A firm of solicitors then required an undertaking that he write no more, on threat of putting the matter before the police; he gave it and heard nothing further.

sources.quote: At a Greek play at Bradfield, I gazed longingly at the charming face of a boy on the stage. I bought a photo of the group with the boy in the middle. Quite infatuated, I dined that night at the old fashioned hotel in Manchester Street and wrote to him on their note paper, and got a couple of nice letters in return. Then, in order to have him visit me I gave No. 30 Manchester Street as my address.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir, as printed by Sox, who introduces it as a 'silly indiscretion' Fothergill recalled from the period after his return from Berneval
sources.supports: Fothergill's own account of the approach, in his own words.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The claim rests on the two women's own joint diary. Evangelista's Y90s biography quotes their boast of being 'closer married' than the Brownings and cites it to Works and Days, p. 16 - so a participant's own testimony is underneath the sentence, which is the self-reported test as the README states it (the vehicle is irrelevant; check whose testimony the historian's citation points to). Not a judgement about acts: nothing here characterises their sexual life beyond their own phrase 'poetic/sexual union' as Evangelista renders it. Independently corroborated as a fact of shared life by Wilde's editors, who identify 'Michael Field' as the joint pen-name of an aunt and her niece.
relationships.date_label: lifelong: joint authorship from 1884 (Callirrhoe) until Cooper's death in 1913; Bradley died the following year
relationships.summary: Katharine Bradley and her niece Edith Cooper lived together, wrote together, and published everything as one poet under the single name 'Michael Field' - eight volumes of verse, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days, in which they recorded their life together and boasted of being more thoroughly married than the Brownings, on the grounds that unlike the Brownings they wrote under one name. Their poems were composed separately and merged in revision until the printed voice was single. Wilde corresponded with 'Michael Field' as a single addressee between 1890 and 1893 about their verse dramas. Cooper died of cancer in 1913 and Bradley survived her by less than a year.

sources.quote: They celebrated their poetic/sexual union in several of their poems and plays, and they even boasted of being “closer married” than the more famous Victorian couple – Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning – because, unlike the Brownings, they wrote under one name (Works and Days, 16).
sources.context: Stefano Evangelista's Y90s biography, opening paragraph. 'Works and Days, 16' is Evangelista's citation to the two women's own joint diary, so the boast is theirs, not his. The preceding sentences read: 'Michael Field is the shared pen name of two women: Katharine Bradley (1846-1914) and Edith Cooper (1862-1913). Bradley and Cooper were aunt and niece but also life-long companions and lovers.'
sources.supports: Participant testimony (their diary) that the two understood their union as a marriage, and understood the single authorial name as what made it one.

relationships.date_label: known only from a letter of 2 September 1900, by which time he had returned to Naples; when and where Wilde knew him is not stated
relationships.summary: Wilde called him one of 'my dear Neapolitans' and said he missed him after the group went home. The whole of the record is one sentence in a letter to his publisher, in which he weighs a waiter in Paris against him and finds the waiter no consolation.
relationships.certainty_reasoning: Self-reported: Wilde is one of the two people and the words are his own. Note the distinction from the Cafe d'Egypte waiter, who appears in the very same sentence and is classified desire-expressed: of the Egyptian, Wilde records only that he serves him drinks and what he looks like, which is admiration at a distance; of this man he writes 'my dear Neapolitans' and 'I miss', and calls his going a 'loss' - the language of an association that existed and ended, not of an approach made. No act is described and none is claimed here, and the erotic register is entirely Wilde's own: a faun, deep woodland eyes, sensuous grace of limb, wanton and sylvan. That register is the evidence; there is nothing else.

sources.quote: Is there any chance of your being in Paris? My dear Neapolitans have returned to Naples and I miss that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb. A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick, occasionally serves me drinks at the Cafe d'Egypte, but he does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris - three months before his death. The same sentence introduces the Cafe d'Egypte waiter, who has his own entry; the two are different men, and the sentence turns on the contrast between them.
sources.supports: The association and its ending, in Wilde's own words, and the terms he describes him in.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1242, printed folio 1196 confirmed at the foot of the rendered page, read as a page image 2026-08-04. start.label: engagement announced by Constance, 26 November 1883 (acquaintance from June 1881)

phases.note: Acquaintance and courtship: first met London, June 1881 ('I can't help liking him' - Constance to Otho, 7 June 1881, quoted p. 221 n. 1).
Engagement (Dublin, announced 26 Nov 1883) to wedding (St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, 29 May 1884, 2.30 p.m.).

Marriage: honeymoon Paris (Hotel Wagram, June 1884); two sons; passionate letter of 16 Dec 1884; by 1893 much apart (Constance in Rome/with the boys while Wilde at Babbacombe, p. 555) - but only three letters to her survive, the rest destroyed after her death (p. 241 n. 6).

Trials and separation: hand-delivered notes Feb/April 1895; she visited Reading 19 Feb 1896 to break Lady Wilde's death - their last meeting; changed her and the children's name to Holland and refused Wilde access to the sons (custody/divorce-question pages not yet transcribed - pointer); died Genoa 7 April 1898.

relationships.summary: Wilde's wife. Constance Mary Lloyd (1858–1898), daughter of Horace Lloyd QC, met Wilde in London in June 1881, accepted him in Dublin in November 1883, and married him at St James's Church, Sussex Gardens, on 29 May 1884. Two sons, Cyril (b. 1885) and Vyvyan (b. 1886). Only three of Wilde's letters to her survive - a passionate one of December 1884 and two pencilled notes from the 1895 catastrophe; the rest were destroyed after her death. She visited him in Reading Gaol on 19 February 1896 to tell him of his mother's death - their last meeting - kept his allowance, took the name Holland, withheld the children, and died at Genoa on 7 April 1898; Wilde telegraphed 'Am in great grief' and visited her grave in 1899.

relationships.date_label: August–September 1894, Worthing and Brighton
relationships.summary: Wilde and Douglas met Alphonse Conway launching boats on Worthing beach in August 1894; for six weeks he was Wilde's companion, lunching and dining with the family, and receiving a cigarette case, photograph, book, walking-stick, and a blue serge suit before a twenty-four-hour Brighton trip (~27 September, adjoining rooms). Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Worthing and the Albion Hotel; the charge was never brought to trial and Conway never gave evidence, though he was seen outside the Court in May 1895.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Legal marriage with the exact date (4 March 1902, St George's, Hanover Square, by special licence) is stated independently by Parker's scholarly biography (read in full) and by Douglas's own memoir read at IA page images, so the 'marriage' class is mechanical. The record also carries the documented 1901 courtship-by-correspondence (Prince/Princess/Page personas), the birth of their son Raymond (17 November 1902), the 1913 separation, and the attachment maintained to Custance's death in 1944.
relationships.date_label: correspondence from June 1901; eloped 4 March 1902; separated 1913; attachment maintained until her death, 1944
relationships.summary: The courtship began with Custance's admiring letter to Douglas in June 1901 and ran on role-play correspondence — Fairy Prince for Douglas, Princess and boyish Page for Custance — plus secret meetings, several in the upper room of Robert Ross's Carfax gallery. Douglas abandoned an American heiress-hunt for her; Custance jilted her fiancé George Montagu and eloped with Douglas on 4 March 1902, honeymooning at the Hôtel Rastadt, Paris; their son Raymond was born 17 November 1902. Strained by litigation, money trouble, and the custody fight for Raymond, the couple separated in 1913 but never divorced; from 1932 Custance lived near Douglas in Hove, seeing him nearly every day until she died in 1944.

sources.quote: Custance wrote to Douglas in June 1901, praising the “fairy land” of his poems and signing herself as “Opal” (which, as Patricia Pulham notes, refers not only to her debut volume but also to her changeable, flirtatious personality). The two poets began to correspond, playfully using the personas of Fairy Prince for Douglas, and Princess and boyish Page for Custance; alternating these masculine and feminine identities allowed Custance to negotiate Douglas’s bisexual desires.
sources.context: Parker's scholarly biography of Custance on Yellow Nineties 2.0, paragraph on the Douglas courtship; the same paragraph notes the match was opposed by Custance's parents.
sources.supports: Courtship by correspondence begins June 1901; the Prince/Princess/Page personas; Custance's 'Opal' signature.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Promoted from the context_engagement already on custance.json now that Vivien is on the roster - but promoted at the weakest class, because the evidence is one scholar's reading of one novel. Parker says Vivien's roman a clef 'suggests' an affair; a novel is not testimony, and nothing independent - no letter, diary, or second observer - was found to support it. That is exactly the README's 'uncorroborated': a lone source, never tested. It does not mean anyone challenged it, and the disputed block below says so explicitly rather than manufacturing an opponent. What IS well evidenced, and belongs on the record whatever the affair's status, is the friendship: Parker documents that Custance sustained contact with Vivien after returning to London in 1901. UPDATED 2026-08-04: the novel itself has now been read at page, in Foster's translation of the 1904 first edition, and it weakens rather than supports the affair reading (see disputed, grounds). The class does not move - it was already at the floor - but the basis is no longer an unread pointer.

relationships.summary: Olive Custance met Renee Vivien in Paris around 1901 through Natalie Barney, whose former lover Vivien was, and the two became friends. Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904) fictionalises Custance as the 'little English poetess Dagmar', and Sarah Parker reads the novel as suggesting the two had a brief love affair - the sole basis for that claim in anything read here. Custance kept up contact with Vivien as well as Barney after moving back to London in 1901, the year before she eloped with Lord Alfred Douglas.

Je reculai comme un être que la démence a frappé à demi recule devant le meurtre conçu en une heure insensée. … La vierge aux boucles légères s’éloigna pendant de longs jours.

It confirms the substance - the offered kiss is refused, and Dagmar is 'la vierge' at this point - while showing that Foster's English overstates the possessiveness: Vivien writes 'La vierge aux boucles légères', the virgin with the light curls, where Foster gives 'My little virgin with the short curls', adding a possessive and a diminutive and changing the adjective. Foster likewise renders 'le Prince inconnu' as 'the Unknown Lover'. The narrative facts are Vivien's; some of the colouring is the translator's.

disputed.claim: That Olive Custance and Renee Vivien had a brief love affair in or around 1901.
disputed.asserted_by: Sarah Parker's Y90s biography of Custance, reading Vivien's roman a clef A Woman Appeared to Me (1904), in which Custance appears as 'the little English poetess Dagmar'; Parker's verb is 'suggests'.
disputed.disputed_by: Nobody, in anything read so far - no source contests it. It is recorded as uncorroborated because nothing independent supports it, not because it was challenged.
disputed.grounds: A single scholar's inference from a single work of fiction written by one of the two parties three years after the fact. THE FICTION HAS NOW BEEN READ (2026-08-04), and it does not depict the affair Parker's word points to. The narrator desires Dagmar and declares love, but when Dagmar offers a kiss the narrator draws back from it; Dagmar is called 'my little virgin'; she then announces her 'Prince' and marries. The novel closes with San Giovanni relaying Dagmar's question whether the narrator resents her, 'that she couldn't cure you by loving you with the terrific ardor you demanded of her' (p. 58). So on its own terms the book depicts an unconsummated courtship declined by both parties in turn, not a love affair. Gayle Rubin, introducing the translation, reads it the same way: the narrator 'attempts to console herself with Dagmar'. The French of the first edition has now been read too, and it holds: 'devant le baiser qu’elle m’offrait, je reculai'. Parker's reading is not unreasonable - the erotic charge is real and sustained - but the text does not carry it as far as 'enjoyed a brief love affair', and this remains a novel either way. Parker's own peer-reviewed article (2011, p. 1) puts the Barney and Vivien connections in the register of 'rumoured entanglements'. The friendship and sustained contact are separately documented and not in question.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: First-person primary evidence by a participant - Wilde's own account to Reginald Turner - but what it attests in plain words is love and three days of company: 'a beautiful young actor, a Florentine, whom I wildly loved … We spent three days together.' That is short of the documented-sexual bar, which requires sexual relations attested. A reader holding the coding hypothesis will read 'We spent three days together', in the exile letters to Turner, as reporting a sexual liaison; that is a reading, and it is this project's, not the editors' - no scholarly source was consulted, so consensus is unavailable. desire-expressed is defined as an approach or declaration and not a relationship, which fits badly: three days together is more than an approach and the outcome is not unknown. romantic-nonsexual is therefore proposed, per the README gloss that 'nonsexual' describes the evidence and not a finding of fact. One-sidedness caveat: the recorded affect is Wilde's ('whom I wildly loved'); Didaco's side is nowhere recorded, and the only mutual element in the text is conduct - 'We spent three days together.'
relationships.date_label: Three days at Genoa, on Wilde's journey from the Riviera into Switzerland, recounted in a letter postmarked 20 March 1899 from Gland. The letter dates neither the stop nor the days; the February 1899 placing of that journey is an itinerary inference, not read in the source.
relationships.summary: On his way from the Riviera to Harold Mellor's villa at Gland, Wilde broke his journey at Genoa and met a young Florentine actor named Didaco, with whom he spent three days. He reported it to Reginald Turner in a letter postmarked 20 March 1899 - a named, dated, first-person-attested liaison of the exile years, and one of the few for which Wilde records the other man's name. Nothing further about Didaco survives in the correspondence read: the letter ends on the following printed page with no second mention.

sources.quote: On my way I stopped at Genoa, where I met a beautiful young actor, a Florentine, whom I wildly loved. He has the strange name of Didaco. He had the look of Romeo, without Romeo's sadness: a face chiselled for high romance. We spent three days together.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland, Switzerland - the closing paragraph on the printed page; the letter continues onto printed 1133 and ends there without returning to Didaco.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's account of meeting Didaco at Genoa, of loving him, and of three days spent together
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1178, printed folio 1132 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states flatly that 'Ives slept with Lord Alfred Douglas at the Albany' and, quoting the Ives diary in the source, records the night Ives refused a third man ('thought it wouldn't do in the Albany') and Ives's own words 'I had no objection to the thing itself'. This is a scholarly work resting on participant diary evidence, which the taxonomy accepts for documented-sexual; but the diary passages themselves are paraphrased or quoted only in fragments by Cook, and the fuller text is reportedly printed in Kaplan (not available so far) - flagged for human review with a pointer. CORROBORATION (2026-08-03): Cook returns to this in Queer Domesticities (2014) p. 99, where the sexual relationship is stated in his own voice as settled background - the anecdote turns on his refusing a *third* man, not on the fact of the pair. Note this is the same historian as the 2003 source, so it strengthens the evidence without adding an independent voice.
relationships.date_label: Oct. 1893 (introduced at Wilde's Savoy dinner, 15 Oct.) - mid-1890s; the Albany night(s) undated by Cook, necessarily after 30 June 1894 (E4 move-in). Attachment ended when 'Douglas turned on Wilde' (Ives marked him 'traitor' in the diary; undated).
relationships.summary: A brief liaison within the Wilde circle: Wilde brought Ives and Douglas together at a Savoy dinner on 15 October 1893 (recorded in Ives's diary), and Douglas visited and spent at least one night at Ives's chambers at E4 the Albany, where Ives refused to allow a third man to join them - 'it wouldn't do in the Albany'. Ives's diary records that he repeatedly warned Douglas over his recklessness while having 'no objection to the thing itself', and after Douglas turned on Wilde, Ives wrote 'traitor' against his name.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: MCKENNA read in the source, 2026-08-03 - this record's basis changed. The claim is no longer an unread pointer: McKenna states a Douglas-Ross relationship 'sexual as well as emotional' in his own voice, and supports it with Douglas's Autobiography. Two things follow. (1) The class rises from uncorroborated to second-hand: a named biographer, now consulted, attests the connection. It does not rise further, because the only participant testimony - Douglas's own - says that Ross 'professed devotion and admiration', which is not a statement of a sexual or romantic relationship; that reading is McKenna's. (2) The dating is corrected: McKenna places the meeting in 1893, with Wilde's involvement with Walter Grainger as the time-marker, not before or around Douglas's 1891 introduction to Wilde as this record previously framed it. Against McKenna stand two biographers read in full who never assert it - see the disputed block. What the verified record otherwise documents is co-membership of Wilde's circle from mid-1892, friendly relations through the 1902 wedding, and the bitter feud from 1913.
relationships.date_label: co-present in Wilde's circle by mid-1892; alleged early-1890s intimacy; friendly until c. 1912; open enmity from 1913 until Ross's death (1918)
relationships.summary: Douglas and Ross were fellow intimates of Wilde from 1892 and remained on good terms long after Wilde's death: Custance and Douglas courted in the upper room of Ross's Carfax gallery with his consent, and Ross stood at the back of the church at their 1902 wedding. McKenna and others have alleged a brief affair between the two around Douglas's entry into the circle; no primary evidence for it was reachable so far, and the Letters apparatus records only the Lionel Johnson introduction of 1891. From the Ransome libel trial of 1913 — brought over a book Douglas said was written 'at the instigation of' Ross — the friendship collapsed into open war: Douglas libelled Ross in deliberately actionable terms ('a notorious sodomite', among others) until Ross prosecuted him at the Old Bailey, where an eight-day trial ended without a verdict; the enmity ran until Ross's death in 1918.

disputed.claim: That the Douglas-Ross connection was sexual or romantic, as distinct from a close friendship.
disputed.asserted_by: Neil McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde, PDF p. 378, read in the source 2026-08-03: 'some sort of relationship ensued, sexual as well as emotional'. His own characterization; the Douglas quotation he adduces attests devotion and admiration only.
disputed.disputed_by: Two biographers read in full, by informative silence. Douglas Murray, Bosie (2020 edn): 388 Ross occurrences across 103 pages, every pre-1900 one read in context, never asserts or rejects an affair; at the point where it would belong he writes friendship. Jonathan Fryer, Robbie Ross (2000), Ross's own biographer: asserts nothing romantic, and his index subheadings for Douglas are 'battle against Ross' and 'and the Dansey affair'. Fryer states negatives explicitly when he means them - he writes that Ross and More Adey shared lodgings 'not as lovers, but as two bachelor friends' - which is what makes his silence here carry weight.
disputed.grounds: One asserting biographer against two silent ones, with the single piece of participant testimony falling short of the claim. Fryer does record that Ross named Douglas among the three most important men in his life (p. 198) - importance, in indirect speech, not romance.

For some extraordinary reason Ross always seemed to resent my marriage. All the same, I continued to be on good terms with him for several years after it took place, and he professed to be devoted to Olive, and made every effort to ingratiate himself with her.
sources.context: Douglas on his 4 March 1902 wedding; p. 197 (image-verified) has the pre-wedding meeting 'in the upper room of Robert Ross's little picture shop, "Carfax," in Ryder Street, with his consent.' sources.quote: This is what happened to me in 1913. I had long ceased to have any connection with the Wilde gang or cult. … Yet when I appealed to the courts for protection against a malicious statement made in a book at the instigation of the late Robert Ross (who hated me and had sworn to revenge himself on me because I declined to go on associating with him) to the effect that I was responsible for the ruin of Oscar Wilde, the courts, instead of protecting me as they should have done, allowed me to be flung to the wolves.
sources.context: Douglas on the Ransome libel trial (1913), which he lost; his aftermath campaign is described at pp. 42-43 (image-verified, in the dossier): 'I swore the day after the Ransome trial that I would never rest till I had publicly exposed Ross … I libelled Ross and at last forced him to take criminal proceedings against me', with the libels listed at p. 43 ('a notorious sodomite', etc.) and 'The trial lasted eight days at the Old Bailey.' All of it Douglas's partisan telling.
sources.supports: The break dated to 1913 (Ransome trial) — with Douglas himself placing the estrangement earlier ('because I declined to go on associating with him'); Douglas's belief that Ross instigated the Ransome book.

sources.quote: Friendship with Wilde meant that Douglas began to move in a new circle of people. … Of them, perhaps the most important was Robert Ross. … Whether or not he was 'the first boy Oscar ever had', he was certainly devoted to Wilde, and when he was ousted as Wilde's lover by a series of attractive young men, he grew bitter. When Douglas first got to know him, though, Ross was an amusing and appealing personality. The two quickly became friends, as did More Adey who shared rooms with Ross.
sources.context: Murray's full account of how Douglas came to know Ross, in the chapter on Douglas's entry into Wilde's circle (1891-92). This is the passage where a Douglas-Ross affair would have to appear if Murray held one; it does not. The elisions drop only Murray's characterisation of the circle ('cultured, usually witty and sometimes talented') and Ross's Canadian birth, 1886 meeting with Wilde and King's, Cambridge years. Murray's account of Ross being displaced is about WILDE's affections, not Douglas's.
sources.supports: Non-corroboration of the alleged early-1890s Douglas-Ross affair by a named biographer who can be read in the source: Murray's account of their meeting is friendship formed inside Wilde's circle, with the rivalry running through Wilde rather than between the two men.

sources.quote: Ross had known a pupil there, Philip Danney, since the lad was fourteen. Danney was now sixteen and Ross invited him to 'stay' with him in London. A smitten Ross communicated the boy's presence in London to Douglas, who was still in Goring with Wilde.
sources.context: Autumn 1893, from a letter of Max Beerbohm to Reginald Turner. The school was the Reverend Biscale Hale Wortham's at Bruges. Murray continues on the next PDF page: Douglas's 'response was to rush to London, seduce the boy and take him back to Goring', and quotes Oscar Browning's summary - 'On Saturday the boy slept with Douglas, on Sunday he slept with Oscar.' Danney's father went to the police and then dropped it 'when he realised that although Ross and Douglas would be sentenced to two years each, his own son would spend six months in prison'; Ross hid in Davos and Douglas left for Egypt. Ages are stated exactly as Murray states them (README register rule).
sources.supports: The closest thing in Murray to intimacy between the two men in the alleged period - and it runs through a third person, not between them: Ross passes the boy's whereabouts to Douglas, and the two are jointly exposed to prosecution. Evidence of shared sexual milieu, not of a relationship.

sources.quote: I agree with you that it is better that we should keep apart. I don't consider that you have ever been a real friend of mine, in the sense that More and others have been my friends. And I may tell you frankly that I don't think your character has improved with age.

The paragraph before it, quoted by Murray on the same page, contains the sentence Murray calls 'actionable in itself': 'I do not care to meet those who are engaged in active propaganda of every kind of wickedness from anarchy to sodomy.' Ross's solicitor Sir George Lewis advised him against proceeding. Murray notes the reference to More Adey 'would soon be proved sadly misguided'.

null_findings.finding: COMPLETE SCAN of all 304 pages: eleven sentences contain both a Douglas token (Bosie/Douglas) and an intimacy token (lover/affair/slept with/sexual/seduced/in love with). NONE asserts a Ross-Douglas relationship. All eleven are false positives: 'the two lovers' means Wilde and Bosie (p. idx105); 'affair' means 'matter' (the Dansey affair, the Salome Row); Drumlanrig and Rosebery; Bosie's 'sexual interest in young women'; Crosland's attack ON Ross as a 'seducer of young boys'; and two index pages. The strongest single datum runs the other way: Douglas's own solicitors tried to get a Pentonville prisoner to state he had had sexual relations with Ross. Fryer - the biographer with the best access to Ross's papers and every incentive to know - never makes the claim. This confirms the absence the pointer was raised to test.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Murray quotes in the source, in the Foreword to the 2020 edition, letters written by Douglas to Schwabe in 1893 that surfaced in an Australian archive after the 2000 publication: Douglas addresses Schwabe as his 'darling pretty boy' and calls himself Schwabe's 'loving boy-wife'. That is first-person primary evidence by a participant, quoted in the source by a scholarly work, which is the README's decision rule for 'documented-sexual'. Murray's 2000 text had already read the pair that way by inference ('It is fairly easy to guess what Douglas's relationship with Schwabe had been'), and Murray revisits the inference in 2020 in light of the letters. Downgrade to 'consensus' if the editor reads 'boy-wife' as short of an attestation of sexual relations - the letters are ardent and self-describing but do not narrate an act.
relationships.date_label: friends 'for some years' before 1892; the surviving letters written 1893; Schwabe staying with Douglas several months after Douglas's March 1902 wedding
relationships.summary: Maurice Schwabe was Douglas's friend before he was Wilde's: Murray has Douglas introducing him to Wilde's circle out of his own Oxford set, and reads their relationship as sexual. Letters from Douglas to Schwabe of 1893, unknown when the biography was first published in 2000 and quoted in the Foreword to the 2020 edition, address Schwabe as 'My darling pretty boy' and sign Douglas as his 'loving boy-wife'. Schwabe, returned from Australia, was staying with Douglas several months after Douglas's marriage to Olive Custance in March 1902 - which is what makes Murray, re-reading, 'wonder' whether his own account of Douglas's later life was too clean.

sources.quote: Since the publication of this book some missing letters from Bosie to Maurice Schwabe have surfaced in an Australian archive. Written in 1893, Bosie addresses Schwabe as 'My darling pretty boy', continuing, 'I really love you far more than any other boy in the world and shall always be your loving boy-wife, or your "little bitch" if you prefer it.'
sources.context: Foreword to the 2020 Edition, in the paragraph where Murray revises his 2000 view of Douglas's later sexuality; the preceding sentence is 'it does seem unlikely that there was no gay feeling in Bosie in later life', and the following sentences record that Schwabe, back from Australia, stayed with Douglas several months after Douglas's wedding, and that Murray, re-reading, 'wonder[s]'.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: First-person participant evidence read in the source so far: Wilde's love letters to Douglas 1892-1897 ('madness of kisses', 'with undying love', 'the supreme, the perfect love of my life'), Douglas's own surviving letter of 15 May 1895 ('My darling Oscar... your own loving and devoted boy'), and the prison letter (De Profundis) narrating the relationship. These verbatim sources attest a mutual passionate love relationship beyond dispute; explicit attestation of sexual acts rests additionally on the 1895 trial record and later Douglas admissions, which are being sourced by the trials-edge agent - if that record is not accepted, the floor supported by this file alone is a documented mutual romantic relationship. Editors' note (p. 646 n. 1) records that the Holloway/Courtfield letter texts are retranslations whose wording may be distorted 'but their substance need not be doubted.'

start.label: introduced by Lionel Johnson, 1891 (editors: most likely beginning of July); Wilde dated the friendship proper from May 1892

end.label: contact until Wilde's death; Douglas chief mourner at the funeral, 3 December 1900

phases.note: Acquaintance: four meetings in ~18 months by Wilde's own count (quoted p. 461).

Intimacy: 'I worship him' (to Ross, spring 1892); Babbacombe menage early 1893; Savoy/St James's Place routine 1893 (De Profundis, p. 686); quarrel-reconciliation cycle incl. Egypt separation winter 1893-94 ('our love has passed through... estrangement', pp. 577-8).

Arrest, trials, prison: Douglas visits Holloway daily, leaves for France 25 April 1895 at the lawyers' urging; love letters both directions May 1895; then prison silence and the recriminating prison letter (De Profundis, Jan-Mar 1897).

Post-release: correspondence resumed within a fortnight; reunion at Rouen 28-29 August 1897; Naples together from late September (cohabitation end-date and allowance crisis at pp. 979-996 not yet transcribed - pointer).

Paris years: intermittent contact ('Oscar has only seen Douglas once' - Ross, April 1898, p. 1054 n. 2); Douglas arrived the day after Wilde's death and followed the coffin, 3 December 1900 (p. 1222).

relationships.summary: The central relationship of the circle. Douglas (b. 1870), third son of the Marquess of Queensberry, was brought to Wilde at Tite Street by Lionel Johnson in 1891; Wilde dated the friendship proper from Douglas's blackmail appeal of May 1892. The surviving letters run from 'Dearest Bosie' (Nov 1892) through the Hyacinthus letter (Jan 1893, later used for blackmail and read at the trials), the crisis letters of 1893-95, De Profundis (1897), and the post-prison reunion at Rouen and Naples (Aug-Sep 1897). Queensberry's card of 18 February 1895 and the collapse of Wilde's libel suit led to Wilde's conviction; the relationship survived in attenuated form until Wilde's death in Paris, where Douglas was chief mourner.

sources.quote: Love me always, love me always. You have been the supreme, the perfect love of my life; there can be no other.

sources.quote: It was in the year 1891 that there entered Wilde's life the man who was to be in some sense his inspiration and in every sense his evil genius. Lord Alfred Bruce Douglas, the third son of the eighth Marquess of Queensberry, had been born in 1870, educated at Winchester and was now a second-year undergraduate at Magdalen College, Oxford. Lionel Johnson, a Winchester contemporary and Oxford friend, brought him to see Wilde at Tite Street.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial headnote on the first Wilde–Douglas meeting; the same note quotes Wilde to More Adey, 7 April 1897: "The friendship began in May 1892 by his brother appealing to me in a very pathetic letter to help him in terrible trouble with people who were blackmailing him. I hardly knew him at the time. I had known him eighteen months, but had only seen him four times in that space."
sources.supports: Meeting 1891 (editors: most likely ~beginning of July); introduction by Lionel Johnson; Douglas's parentage and birth year; Wilde's own May-1892 dating of the friendship.

sources.quote: My Own Boy, Your sonnet is quite lovely, and it is a marvel that those red rose-leaf lips of yours should have been made no less for music of song than for madness of kisses. Your slim gilt soul walks between passion and poetry. I know Hyacinthus, whom Apollo loved so madly, was you in Greek days. … Always, with undying love, yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, [? January 1893], [Babbacombe Cliff] — the 'Hyacinthus' letter; editors' n. 1: "This letter … was later stolen, used as material for the attempted blackmail of Wilde, and finally read out in court during the Queensberry and later trials."
sources.supports: Explicit love-letter register in Wilde's own hand; the letter itself became trial evidence.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 564 (printed p. 544, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: Dear Lady Queensberry, You have on more than one occasion consulted me about Bosie. Let me write to you now about him. … I like to think myself his greatest friend – he, at any rate, makes me think so – so I write to you quite frankly to ask you to send him abroad to better surroundings.
sources.context: Wilde to Lady Queensberry (Douglas's mother), [8 November 1893], 16 Tite Street; the letter urges sending Douglas to Egypt. Editors' n. 1: "This letter certainly helped to send him abroad for some months."
sources.supports: Wilde intimate enough with Douglas's mother to be consulted about him; the late-1893 crisis and engineered Egypt separation.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 627 (printed p. 575, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: I am happy in the knowledge that we are friends again, and that our love has passed through the shadow and the night of estrangement and sorrow and come out rose-crowned as of old. Let us always be infinitely dear to each other, as indeed we have been always.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, [Circa 20 December 1893], 10 & 11 St James's Place; Douglas had gone to Cairo on 2 December (editors' n. 3).
sources.supports: "Our love" in Wilde's own words; the quarrel-and-reconciliation pattern across the Egypt separation.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 629 (printed p. 577, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: My dearest boy, This is to assure you of my immortal, my eternal love for you. Tomorrow all will be over. If prison and dishonour be my destiny, think that my love for you and this idea, this still more divine belief, that you love me in return will sustain me in my unhappiness and will make me capable, I hope, of bearing my grief most patiently.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, Monday Evening [29 April 1895], HM Prison, Holloway, on the eve of the first Crown trial. Editors' n. 1 warns the text is a retranslation (via the Mercure de France affair) whose wording may be distorted "but their substance need not be doubted"; the same note records Douglas's statement that he later destroyed 150 of Wilde's letters.
sources.supports: Mutual love asserted at the moment of catastrophe ('that you love me in return').
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 697 (printed p. 646, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: My darling Oscar, Have just arrived here. It seems too dreadful to be here without you, but I hope you will join me next week. … Do keep up your spirits, my dearest darling. I continue to think of you day and night, and send you all my love. I am always your own loving and devoted boy BOSIE
sources.context: Lord Alfred Douglas to Wilde, Wednesday, 15 May 1895, Hôtel des Deux Mondes, Paris — printed by the editors in n. 3, who introduce it as "One of the only three letters from Douglas to Wilde which have been recovered (MS Clark)". Wilde was then on bail between the trials.
sources.supports: Reciprocity in Douglas's own voice during the trials — first-person evidence from the second participant.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 700 (printed p. 649, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03
sources.speaker: Lord Alfred Douglas

sources.quote: Dear Bosie, After long and fruitless waiting I have determined to write to you myself, as much for your sake as for mine … Our ill-fated and most lamentable friendship has ended in ruin and public infamy for me, yet the memory of our ancient affection is often with me, and the thought that loathing, bitterness and contempt should for ever take that place in my heart once held by love is very sad to me …
sources.context: Opening of Wilde's prison letter to Douglas (De Profundis), [January–March 1897], HM Prison, Reading; the letter runs to p. 780. Editors' caution (p. 684 n. 1): "Wilde's indictments of Douglas in this letter need to be approached with caution. While some are undoubtedly valid, others, in the light of later research, seem both unfair to Douglas and inaccurate if taken entirely at face value."
sources.supports: Wilde's own retrospective naming of the relationship ('that place in my heart once held by love'); the prison rupture. Also p. 686 (read): the 1893 daily-inseparability routine ('We did not separate as a rule till after midnight').
sources.provenance: repo PDF pp. 734-7 (printed pp. 683-6, folios checked), read as page images 2026-08-03

sources.quote: Everyone is furious with me for going back to you, but they don't understand us. I feel that it is only with you that I can do anything at all. Do remake my ruined life for me, and then our friendship and love will have a different meaning to the world. I wish that when we met at Rouen we had not parted at all. … But we love each other.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas, Tuesday, 7.30 [? 31 August 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe — after their reunion meeting at Rouen. Editors' n. 1 (p. 933): "This fateful meeting seems to have taken place on 28–9 August. In his Autobiography Douglas wrote: 'Poor Oscar cried when I met him at the station. We walked about all day arm in arm, or hand in hand, and were perfectly happy.'"
sources.supports: The post-prison reunion decision against the circle's opposition; Rouen meeting 28-29 Aug 1897; corroborated to Ross, 4 Sept 1897 (p. 934, read): "Yes: I saw Bosie, and of course I love him as I always did, with a sense of tragedy and ruin."
sources.provenance: repo PDF pp. 982-4 (printed pp. 932-4, folios checked), read as page images 2026-08-03

sources.quote: You tell me that you, and Bobbie, on being asked whether Bosie was 'a disreputable person' felt bound at once to say yes: and that you declared that my wife was acting 'strictly within her legal rights according to the agreement' in depriving me of my allowance, because I have the pleasure of Bosie's companionship, the only companionship in the world open to me.
sources.context: Wilde to More Adey, postmark 21 November 1897, Villa Giudice, Posilippo - written while living with Douglas at Naples, after Constance stopped the allowance.
sources.supports: Cohabitation at Naples from late September 1897 and its end when Constance's allowance and Lady Queensberry's terms cut the money off - pages not yet transcribed.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1037, printed folio 989 read off the rendered page - NOT p. 991; the volume's PDF/printed offset is not constant., read as a page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: On Sunday, the next day, Alfred Douglas arrived, and various people whom I do not know called. … On Monday morning at 9 o'clock, the funeral started from the hotel – we all walked to the Church of St Germain des Prés behind the hearse – Alfred Douglas, Reggie Turner and myself, Dupoirier, the proprietor of the hotel … the second [coach contained] Alfred Douglas, Turner, the proprietor of the hotel, and myself … Wreaths came from, or at the request of, the following: Alfred Douglas, More Adey, Reginald Turner …
sources.context: Robert Ross's account of Wilde's death and funeral (funeral Monday 3 December 1900, per n. 1; Wilde died 30 November 1900). The letter's heading falls on a preceding page not read so far; the narrator is identified as Ross by p. 1222 n. 2.
sources.supports: Contact until death: Douglas came at once, walked behind the hearse and rode in the second coach, and sent a wreath.
sources.provenance: repo PDF p. 1267 (printed p. 1222, folio checked), read as page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: Douglas's candour in days when such acts could still condemn a man to prison is some proof of the truth of his statement, and his coyness is understandable.
sources.context: Murray's own comment on the passage of Douglas's memoir he has just quoted, in which Douglas describes what did and did not take place between him and Wilde on the first night, probably January 1892, at Tite Street. Douglas's account states that sodomy never took place, that Wilde 'treated me as an older boy treats a younger one at school', and names one specific act; Douglas adds that he never liked it, only consented to oblige Wilde, and that Wilde 'very soon cut it out altogether'. Douglas was 21. The full passage is transcribed in dossiers/DOUGLAS-MURRAY_dossier.md; only Murray's framing sentence is carried here.
sources.supports: Douglas's own first-person account of the sexual relationship with Wilde, its specific and limited content, and its brevity - independent corroboration, from Douglas's side, of an edge otherwise carried by Wilde's letters.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 52 of Murray_2020_Bosie (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/douglas/sources/), read as page image 2026-08-03. sources.quote: The sexual relationship between Wilde and Douglas was short-lived, but it was replaced in both by a taste for rent boys.
sources.context: Murray on spring 1893, in the paragraph where the blackmail over the 'Hyacinthus' letter begins; the preceding sentence distinguishes 'the romantic love for Douglas' from 'the sexual encounters with rent boys' as the two sides of Wilde's life.
sources.supports: The biographer's dating of the sexual phase as brief, with the romantic attachment outlasting it - the shape our date fields already carry (1891/92 start, contact to 1900).
