relationships.certainty_reasoning: Murray states in passing that the blackmailers into whose hands Wilde's letters to Douglas fell were men 'with whom they had slept' - 'they' being Wilde and Douglas, the subject of the sentence. That is a single secondary source, asserting in the plural and without a footnote at the point of assertion, and no first-person evidence is offered for the Douglas half of the claim; Wood's own sworn testimony (which carries the wilde--wood edge) concerns Wilde. Single-source and non-itemised, therefore 'alleged'. What is documented independently at the same pages is only the connective fact: Douglas befriended Wood, gave him old suits, and Wood found Wilde's letters to Douglas in the pockets.
relationships.date_label: acquaintance by late 1892 - early 1893; the blackmail from April 1893
relationships.summary: Alfred Wood was an out-of-work clerk from Oxford, who had worked as a valet in Douglas's Oxford rooms; Douglas befriended him and gave him several old suits, and Wilde's letters to Douglas reached the blackmailers from there - Murray thinks by theft from the rooms rather than by the pockets, as Wood claimed. Murray, describing the moment the two halves of Wilde's life converged, calls Wood one of the blackmailers 'with whom they had slept' - the only statement in the book that Douglas's relations with Wood were sexual, and one made in passing and in the plural.

disputed.claim: That Douglas, as well as Wilde, had sexual relations with Alfred Wood.
disputed.asserted_by: Douglas Murray, Bosie (2020 edn), PDF p. 60 - in a subordinate clause, unfootnoted at that point, and phrased as a class statement about 'blackmailers like Wood'.
disputed.disputed_by: Not rebutted in any source read so far. But nothing corroborates it: Wood's sworn testimony at the 1895 trials describes acts with Wilde, not with Douglas; Douglas was never charged; and the Complete Letters apparatus records only that Douglas gave Wood clothes and introduced him to Wilde by telegram.
disputed.grounds: Single secondary source; assertion made in passing and in the plural rather than itemised; no first-person or testimonial evidence for the Douglas half.

sources.quote: Wilde and Douglas were treading a dangerous path. Douglas had befriended a young and unemployed clerk from Oxford called Alfred Wood, who proved to be less than honest, and when letters from Wilde to Douglas turned up in the hands of blackmailers like Wood with whom they had slept, the two sides of Wilde's homosexual life came together: the romantic love for Douglas and the sexual encounters with rent boys.
sources.context: Murray's chapter on 1893, immediately after Wilde's Savoy letter to Douglas ('you must not make scenes with me') and the appearance of the first blackmailer with the stolen 'Hyacinthus' letter on 21 April 1893.
sources.supports: The whole of the claim: that Douglas befriended Wood, and Murray's assertion that Wilde and Douglas had both slept with him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 60 of Murray_2020_Bosie, read as page image 2026-08-03; no printed folio on the page - the file is an ebook conversion with no pagination (see the pagination note in dossiers/DOUGLAS-MURRAY_dossier.md), so the locator is the PDF page.

sources.quote: Douglas had given the unemployed clerk several of his old suits, and Wood claimed that he had found the letters in the pockets. Wood was in league with two other blackmailers, Allen and Clibborn, and it is highly improbable that Douglas would have been so careless. A likely explanation is that Wood simply stole the letters from Douglas's rooms at Oxford, where he had worked as a valet.
sources.context: Murray on the first criminal trial, where the prosecution laid emphasis on Wilde's letters to Douglas, 'which had been "found" by Alfred Wood' - Murray's scare quotes are his own. Later on the same page: the foreman of the jury asked the judge why no warrant had been issued for the arrest of Lord Alfred Douglas, and 'The judge said that something more than intimacy would have to be proved if a charge were to be made.'
sources.supports: The documented, non-sexual connection between the two men - Wood worked as a valet in Douglas's Oxford rooms, and the old suits Douglas gave him carried Wilde's letters to Douglas into a blackmailer's hands.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 95 of Murray_2020_Bosie, read as page image 2026-08-03; no printed folio on the page (ebook conversion).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: PROPOSED, with the alternatives spelled out, because this pair sits exactly on the README's desire-expressed bar. The evidence read so far is Wilde's own twelve letters to Dowson (the primary source for this pair) plus Dowson's own words about Wilde as printed by Frankel from the Flower-Maas edition - so BOTH participants are on record, which is rare here. What Wilde's side carries, in the letter of ? 16 June 1897 alone, is a declaration of inseparability ('Had I stayed at Arques I should have given up all hopes of ever separating from you'), a compliment on Dowson's appearance in the Hyacinthus register Wilde used for Douglas ('the green costume that goes so well with your dark hyacinth locks'), a statement that Dowson's absence is the one flaw in an otherwise perfect state, and the sign-off 'Tout a toi' - joined across the other letters by 'You were wonderful and charming all last night', 'I want to be consoled', and 'you have it, and other things, always'. That clears the README's bar twice over: the ardour is legible as ardour without the coding hypothesis, AND a scholarly source reads it that way (McKenna: 'their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love'). WHY NOT self-reported, i.e. a relationship edge like marillier--wilde: because the counter-evidence is strong and comes from the better sources. Frankel - the specialist monograph for exactly these years, and the most recent scholarship in the corpus - reads it flatly as 'frank and unguarded friendship' and never suggests otherwise; Dowson's own surviving words about Wilde are admiring, wry and entirely non-romantic; Dowson's documented sexual interest was in women, and by both Sox's and Frankel's accounts he tried to steer Wilde toward women; and the ardent lines are a handful within a correspondence that is otherwise practical (poems, absinthe, a translation, a debt). WHY NOT a null finding, i.e. no edge at all as for Turner: because Turner's file failed for want of any source naming a romance and any first-person ardour addressed to Turner himself, and neither is missing here. OUTCOME: 'unreciprocated' rather than 'unknown' because Dowson's own side of the record survives and is not in kind, and because the one recorded rupture is Dowson cutting off the very curls Wilde had praised - Wilde told Fothergill they had quarrelled and Dowson, to spite him, 'had had all his long curls cut' (Sox p. 141). 'Unknown' is the defensible lower-commitment alternative, since no source records an approach being made and answered; 'declined' is not available, as nothing like Fothergill's written withdrawal exists. ON 'FIRST HYACINTH SINCE DOUGLAS': this phrase, which is the only flatly romantic characterization of the pair in the literature, is NOT used as class-deciding evidence, because whose words it is cannot be established. Sox prints it in an agentless passive with an endnote (n. 12) that names no describer and merely cross-refers to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain it; the phrase appears nowhere in the Complete Letters, so it is not Wilde's; and McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it, closing the loop. See DOWSON_dossier.md sec. L. The edge is hidden by default per the README, so the honest reading of a hidden, arrow-marked flirtation edge is what is proposed here; if Lovelle prefers, dropping to no-edge loses nothing that the person record and dossier do not already carry.
relationships.date_label: Acquainted from 1890; Dowson visited Wilde at Oakley Street between the trials, spring 1895. The letters that carry the ardour are Berneval/Dieppe, June-August 1897, concentrated in the fortnight 16-30 June; Dowson returned to England in mid-July 1897. Four further letters from Naples, October 1897, are practical. Wilde's last word on Dowson is his letter of condolence to Smithers, circa 24 February 1900.
relationships.summary: Dowson met Wilde in 1890 through the London literary world and, with Robert Sherard, called on him at Oakley Street between the trials in 1895 - one of very few who did. In the summer of 1897 he was living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe and became the closest daily companion of Wilde's first free months, dining at Berneval on 3 June and thereafter meeting almost constantly at the Cafe Suisse in Dieppe. Wilde's letters over the following fortnight turn markedly warm: he tells Dowson there is 'a fatality about our being together', asks why he is 'so persistently and perversely wonderful', watches for the green costume that suits his 'dark hyacinth locks', calls his absence the one imperfection in an otherwise perfect day, and signs himself 'Tout a toi'. Dowson's own letters of the same weeks are affectionate but unromantic - he found Wilde's 'enormous joy in life' hard to match - and he is reported to have tried to interest Wilde in women; Wilde later told Fothergill they had quarrelled and that Dowson had cut off his long curls to spite him. The friendship survived it in a lower key, and when Dowson died in February 1900 Wilde asked Smithers to lay flowers on his grave.

sources.quote: There is a fatality about our being together that is astounding – or rather quite probable. Had I stayed at Arques I should have given up all hopes of ever separating from you. Why are you so persistently and perversely wonderful? … I suppose I shall see you in ten minutes from this. I am looking out for the green costume that goes so well with your dark hyacinth locks. … Now I am alive, and all is perfect, except your absence. Tout à toi
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 16 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH. Elisions drop the servant anecdote, the paragraph on Thompson and Socrates, the line 'Come with vine-leaves in your hair' (the editors gloss it to Ibsen's Hedda Gabler), and the first half of the Pernod sentence. Full letter in the dossier. 'Hyacinth' is Wilde's Douglas register: cf. Wilde to Douglas, 'Hyacinthus, whom Apollo loved so madly, was you in Greek days' (Complete Letters p. 544, cited at Frankel p. 328 n. 30).
sources.supports: Wilde's own most explicit statement of attachment to Dowson: inseparability, a compliment on Dowson's hair in the mythological register he used for Douglas, absence as the single flaw in the day, and 'Tout à toi'. This is also the letter Sox is quoting for both 'the green costume' and 'dark hyacinth locks'.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 951, printed folio 901 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Three elisions marked with spaced ellipses; nothing omitted alters the sense of what is quoted. The editors reproduce a photograph of Dowson in the unfoliated plate section (repo PDF 600, plate 85) captioned with the first sentence of this passage.

sources.quote: My dear Ernest, Do come here at once: Monsieur Meyer is presiding over a morning meal of absinthe, and we want you. I am a wreck of course, but la belle soeur is like the moon. You were wonderful and charming all last night. Ever yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 24 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire) - the entire letter. Line breaks between the three sentences run together here.
sources.supports: The register at its warmest outside the 16 June letter, and the daily rhythm of the Dieppe weeks
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 957, printed folio 907 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I must see you: so I propose to breakfast at St Martin L'Eglise tomorrow at 11.30 and you must come: take a voiture and be there. I want to have a poet to talk to, as I have had lots of bad news since you left me. Do try, like a good chap, to be there, and wear a blue tie. I want to be consoled.
sources.context: Postcard, Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Monday [postmark 28 June 1897], [postmark Dieppe] (MS Maguire); signed SEBASTIAN MELMOTH. Italics on 'must', 'voiture' and 'blue' in the original. The 'bad news' is his solicitor's resignation and the cancellation of Douglas's visit (Frankel, p. 116).
sources.supports: Summons and dependence: Wilde asking to be consoled, and prescribing what Dowson is to wear - the second such instruction in a week
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 958, printed folio 908 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I write a little line, whose only excuse is its entire illegibility, to tell you how charming you are (at Berneval) and how much I like your friend, and mine, the dear Achille. … You and Achille and Achille's friend and I must all be at Berneval together. I am making arrangements. Give to Achille my sincere friendship: you have it, and other things, always.
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Wednesday 6.30 [? 30 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed S. M. The letter runs over the printed 908/909 page break. 'Achille' is glossed by the editors as presumably Achille Fromentin. The elision drops the paragraph praising Dowson's 'lovely lyrics' and a passage about a costermonger. The closing clause is addressed to Dowson though its sentence is nominally about Achille.
sources.supports: The only line in the twelve letters that gestures at something withheld from the page ('and other things, always'), and the plan to gather the four of them at Berneval
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 958-959, printed folios 908 and 909 both confirmed on the rendered pages, read as page images 2026-08-03. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full letter in the dossier.

sources.quote: Dowson was described as Wilde's 'first hyacinth since Douglas: But this flower was wilting, and had not much longer to live'. Despite the wilting, Wilde looked for 'the green costume' which went well with Dowson's 'dark hyacinth locks'. Fothergill commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Café Royal, but was 'faithful only after his fashion'. Although Dowson was in the house he did not appear. Wilde said they had quarrelled and Dowson, to spite him, 'had had all his long curls cut'.
sources.context: Sox, in the chapter 'Two Loves Have I', on the guests at Wilde's Chalet Bourgeat during Fothergill's own stay - 'Of the other guests at Chalet Bourgeat at this time, Fothergill mentioned seeing only two: Leonard Smithers … [and] the English poet Ernest Dowson' (p. 140). Sox's Part V note-head states that unnoted quotations in the section are from Fothergill's unpublished memoir, so the chain for the quarrel and the cut curls is Wilde -> Fothergill's memoir -> Sox. Endnote markers (nn. 12-13) omitted. CAUTION, and the reason this quote sits fifth rather than first: the 'first hyacinth' phrase is unattributed. Sox's n. 12 (printed p. 271) reads only 'Also see Hart-Davis, Selected Letters, pp. 290-1' - a cross-reference to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain the phrase. It is not Wilde's; McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it. Whose words they are is a live open question. Note too the chronology tension: the Letters editors have Dowson back in England from mid-July (p. 924 n. 1), while Fothergill's undated visit falls in Wilde's last month at Berneval.
sources.supports: The only romantic characterization of the pair in the literature, and its unresolved attribution; Fothergill's counter-observation that Dowson's own attachment lay elsewhere; and the quarrel in which Dowson cut off the curls Wilde had admired - the evidential basis for outcome 'unreciprocated'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 157, printed folio 141 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03; the setting sentence from repo PDF 156, printed folio 140 confirmed. Endnote 12 read on the rendered page at repo PDF 303, printed folio 271 confirmed, and the superscript markers on p. 141 checked in a 4x zoom render. Sox's index (printed p. 282) lists Dowson at p. 141 only, and a full-text search of the file confirms this is his sole treatment.

sources.quote: For his part, Dowson was impressed by Wilde's "enormous joy in life just at this moment" and "had some difficulty in suppressing my own sourness" as a result. His first impression was that Wilde had changed a great deal for the better: "he seems of much broader sympathies, much more human and simple. . . . His delight in the country, in walking, in the simplicities of life is enchanting." … "His gorgeous spirits cheered me mightily," Dowson wrote of Wilde at this time
sources.context: Frankel quoting Dowson's own letters of summer 1897, from Letters of Ernest Dowson, ed. Desmond Flower and Henry Maas (Fairleigh Dickinson UP, 1968), pp. 384 and 387 - his notes 64, 65 and 68 at printed pp. 324-325. The elision drops Frankel's intervening paragraph on the brothel story and the absinthe. Frankel's own reading of the pair, on the same page and the one before, is 'frank and unguarded friendship' and Dowson as 'one of his closest confidantes' (p. 113).
sources.supports: The second participant's own testimony - the counter-weight that keeps this edge below a relationship class. Dowson's register toward Wilde is admiring and wry, never romantic.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 128, printed folio 114 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Frankel's printed-to-PDF offset established so far as a constant PDF - 14, holding across body and notes (see DOWSON_dossier.md). Frankel p. 113 read at repo PDF 127, folio confirmed. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; Frankel's own internal ellipsis inside the Dowson quotation is his.

sources.quote: They met frequently, and their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love. It is unlikely that the relationship was ever sexual, but there may have been drunken embraces and declarations of undying love.
sources.context: McKenna on the June 1897 Dieppe weeks, immediately before he quotes the 'fatality about our being together' letter. This is the one scholarly reading in the corpus that names the connection as love, and it is explicitly speculative ('seemed', 'may have been'); works.json records that McKenna is never a sufficient basis on his own. The file carries no printed folios, so the locator is a PDF page.
sources.supports: The scholarly-reading half of the README's desire-expressed bar - and, by its own hedging, the reason the class stays at desire-expressed rather than rising higher
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 665, read as page image 2026-08-03; no printed folio or running head appears on the rendered page, consistent with the pagination warning on mckenna-2008 in works.json. McKenna's source note for the adjoining 'first hyacinth since Douglas' phrase, at repo PDF 852, reads 'Sox, Bachelors of Art, page 141'.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, I am greatly distressed to hear of Ernest's death: how sudden it must have been! Poor wounded wonderful fellow that he was, a tragic reproduction of all tragic poetry, like a symbol, or a scene. I hope bay-leaves will be laid on his tomb, and rue, and myrtle too, for he knew what love is. He was a sweet singer … If he is not yet laid to rest or unrest, do put some flowers for me on his grave.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [circa 24 February 1900], Paris - written the day after Dowson died, and Wilde's last word on him. Addressed to a third party, so it is Wilde's own testimony but not part of the correspondence between the two men. The elision drops the simile comparing Dowson's note to birdsong in Shakespeare's day. The editors' footnote on the same page gives the death and burial particulars.
sources.supports: The close of the connection in Wilde's own voice; 'he knew what love is' is elegiac and unspecific - Wilde does not say for whom
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1219, printed folio 1173 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full passage in the dossier.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Both participants speak, in one volume. Whitman's side is the eighty-odd letters Bucke printed in 1897, addressed 'Dear Boy', 'Dear Boy and Comrade', 'Dear Pete', and speaking of 'my dear comrade'. Doyle's side is the interview Bucke took from him and printed in the same introduction, in which Doyle narrates the meeting himself and says 'We were familiar at once—I put my hand on his knee—we understood'. That is the README's self-reported test met from both directions, which is rare on this map. What the record does NOT settle is the sexual question, and this entry does not settle it either: the vocabulary available to both men was comradeship, the 1897 volume is discreet by design - Bucke's own subtitle calls Doyle 'a young friend' - and the standard reference entry calls it a 'romantic friendship' embodying the 'love of comrades' while presenting the letters as 'invaluable reference points for the student seeking to understand Whitman's emotional and sexual nature', which is a scholar declining to close the question in the same breath as raising it. The class here records who attests the bond, not what they did.
relationships.date_label: met on a Washington horsecar one stormy winter evening, 1865 by the scholarship and 1866 by Doyle's own reckoning; closest through the Washington years to about 1873, renewed in the mid-1880s when Doyle moved to Philadelphia, and running until Whitman's death on 26 March 1892
relationships.summary: Peter Doyle was twenty-one and conducting a Pennsylvania Avenue horsecar on a stormy night when Walt Whitman, forty-five, boarded as its only passenger with a blanket round his shoulders. By Doyle's account they understood one another before either had spoken much. They spent the Washington years riding the streetcars, eating fruit at Center Market and walking the Potomac by moonlight - Whitman reciting Shakespeare's sonnets, Doyle telling limericks - and Whitman was taken into Doyle's family. Whitman's stroke in 1873 and his move to Camden put a river and a state between them and the intensity cooled; Harry Stafford filled some of the gap in New Jersey. Doyle moved to Philadelphia in the mid-1880s and visited weekly until the nurses of Whitman's last years crowded him out. He came to the funeral. In 1897 he let Bucke print Whitman's letters to him, which is the only reason the relationship is documented at all; his own letters to Whitman largely are not.

sources.quote: You ask where I first met him? It is a curious story. We felt to each other at once. I was a conductor. The night was very stormy,—he had been over to see Burroughs before he came down to take the car—the storm was awful. Walt had his blanket—it was thrown round his shoulders—he seemed like an old sea-captain. He was the only passenger, it was a lonely night, so I thought I would go in and talk with him. Something in me made me do it and something in him drew me that way. He used to say there was something in me had the same effect on him. Anyway, I went into the car. We were familiar at once—I put my hand on his knee—we understood. He did not get out at the end of the trip—in fact went all the way back with me. I think the year of this was 1866. From that time on we were the biggest sort of friends.
sources.context: Doyle, interviewed by Richard Maurice Bucke and printed verbatim in Bucke's introduction under its own running head, 'INTERVIEW WITH PETER DOYLE'. This is the only substantial first-person account Doyle left of the relationship, and the source every later account of the meeting quotes. Note his own hedge on the year: the scholarship dates the meeting to 1865, Doyle says he thinks it was 1866. Henry James, reviewing the book in 1898, called this interview the most charming passage in the volume.
sources.supports: The meeting, in the other participant's own words - and the class, since it puts Doyle's voice beside Whitman's rather than leaving the edge resting on Whitman alone.

sources.quote: New York, Friday, 25 Sept., 1868. Dear Boy. I received your second letter yesterday—it is a real comfort to me to get such letters from you, dear friend. Every word does me good. … I put down off hand and write all about myself and my doings, etc., because I suppose that will be really what my dear comrade wants most to hear while we are separated.
sources.context: The first letter Bucke prints, opening the section headed 'LETTERS OF 1868'. The salutation is the volume's standard: Whitman writes to Doyle as 'Dear Boy', 'Dear Boy and Comrade' and 'Dear Pete' across the run. The elision drops two sentences about a newspaper and the timing of the post. Small capitals in the printed salutation normalised.
sources.supports: Whitman's own register toward Doyle at the start of the correspondence - 'dear friend', 'my dear comrade' - and the fact of a sustained private correspondence.

sources.quote: The romantic friendship that Walt Whitman shared with Peter Doyle embodied the "love of comrades" celebrated in Whitman's "Calamus" poems. Their thirty-year friendship (1865–1892) left a legacy of loving letters from the older man to his younger companion which are invaluable reference points for the student seeking to understand Whitman's emotional and sexual nature.
sources.context: The opening of Martin G. Murray's reference entry on Doyle, the standard short account and by the author of the fullest published biography of him. Recorded as the second-hand layer: it names the relationship 'romantic friendship' and points the reader at the letters for the sexual question without answering it. Murray also supplies the detail that Doyle was twenty-one and Whitman forty-five at the meeting, and that Doyle is buried in Congressional Cemetery.
sources.supports: The scholarly characterisation of the relationship, and its span - corroboration, not the basis of the class.

null_findings.finding: ASYMMETRY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYONE HUNTS FOR MORE. The volume is Whitman's letters TO Doyle plus Bucke's interview OF Doyle; **Doyle's own letters to Whitman are not in it**. Doyle kept Whitman's and gave them to Bucke in 1880; the reverse run largely does not survive, so apart from the interview this relationship is documented in one direction, like hall--souline. A few Doyle-to-Whitman letters are held elsewhere and are transcribed on the Whitman Archive (e.g. item nyp.00304, Doyle to Whitman, 5-6 October 1868) - not consulted here, and the obvious next step if this edge is ever deepened.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Identical evidence to raphael--wilde, and classified the same way for the same reasons: one sentence names him as the second of Wilde's 'two special friends' at Napoule and calls both 'quite perfect, except that they can read and write', directly after Wilde has described the local fisher-folk as having 'beautiful eyes, crisp hair of a hyacinth colour, and no morals: an ideal race'. The erotic register is Wilde's own - 'no morals' is his flag, not the reader's inference - and a reader without the coding hypothesis still reads a man naming his two favourites within a population he has just praised for its amorality. The reading is this project's; no scholarly source was consulted. romantic-nonsexual was weighed and rejected as sharpening - the only mutuality on the page is the word 'friends', and that class displays as 'Romantic' - and documented-sexual has no first-person statement of sexual relations behind it. desire-expressed, direction 'wilde', outcome 'unknown', is proposed: the README's marked and hidden-by-default lead pool is the right weight class for this. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a correspondent. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and Fortuné's own account of the acquaintance does not exist.
relationships.date_label: Stated in a letter the editors date [Circa 28 December 1898] from the Hôtel des Bains, Napoule. The letter does not say when the friendship began and no later letter read returns to it; the single-month span is the date of the evidence, not a claim about duration.
relationships.summary: In the same December 1898 letter to Laurence Housman that names Raphael, Wilde named Fortuné as the second of his two special friends among the Napoule fisher-folk - 'both quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. That sentence is the whole of the record for him: no surname, no age, no occupation stated, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read.

sources.quote: The people here – fisher-folk all – have beautiful eyes, crisp hair of a hyacinth colour, and no morals: an ideal race. I have two special friends, one called Raphael, the other Fortuné – both quite perfect, except that they can read and write.
sources.context: Wilde to Laurence Housman, [Circa 28 December 1898], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule - the third paragraph of a four-paragraph letter that opens on the pinewoods and thanks Housman for a drawing.
sources.supports: The whole of the record for Fortuné: named as the second of Wilde's two special friends among the Napoule fisher-folk, called quite perfect, with no outcome recorded

relationships.certainty_reasoning: This edge was deferred pending Part V ch. 3-4 (printed 145-166); those chapters were read so far and carry strong texture but no explicit statement of romance or sex. What Sox gives: 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142) and 'taken up with Ned and Marshall' (p. 151); his own sentence that Fothergill's longing for 'something like a gentleman protector' 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned' (p. 150); Fothergill's memoir on the arrangement - 'could I ever be worth his keeping me? At once he said he'd give me £300 a year' (p. 151) - and on his feelings ('He became to me... part of my being... I seem to live as one with him', p. 150); Sox's verdict counting Fothergill among the four men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess' (p. 129); and, on Fothergill's marriage soon after Marshall's, that he 'followed his rival to the altar' (p. 155) - 'rival' being the strongest romantic-parallel word applied to the pair. Against that: every explicit sentence describes employment, patronage, nursing and discipleship, and the protective moustache advice (p. 142) is framed as collecting-security. Proposed 'alleged' with a disputed{} block per the mandate for thin characterization; 'romantic-nonsexual' was considered and rejected as overstating what Sox asserts. Single source (Sox), drawing on Fothergill's unpublished 1954 memoir.
relationships.date_label: Taken up with Warren in Rome from 1899 (Caffè Greco, via John Marshall); a Lewes House secretary-collector on Warren's £300 a year; left for Leipzig and the Slade School (enrolled 1905-06) after the 1904-6 'bad years'. The tie persisted: Fothergill's memoir epigraph addresses Warren 'at Lewes House, c.1905', and at Warren's Golders Green cremation in January 1929 Fothergill could recall no mourners in the chapel 'save Harry Thomas and myself'.
relationships.summary: Returning to Rome in 1899, the 23-year-old Fothergill met John Marshall at the Caffè Greco and 'became one of Ned's Lewes House collectors' - fulfilling, Sox writes, his earlier longing for 'something like a gentleman protector... support, direction and place', which 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned'. Warren descended on his typhoid sickbed 'complete with a valet and a German doctor' and, when Fothergill confessed his inheritance half spent - 'could I ever be worth his keeping me?' - settled £300 a year on him; aware of Fothergill's prior 'friendships with one or two boys', Warren also had him grow a moustache so as not to give the police 'an excuse for suppressing us'. Sox stops short of calling the bond romantic, but counts Fothergill among the four men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess', and remarks of Fothergill's 1906 marriage, soon after Marshall's, that he 'followed his rival to the altar'. Fothergill left for the Slade c. 1905; he was one of the two mourners he could remember in the chapel at Warren's cremation.

disputed.claim: that the Warren-Fothergill bond was a romantic or kept-companion attachment, over and above secretarial employment and patronage
disputed.asserted_by: No single sentence of Sox's - the reading is a composite of his framings: 'taken up with Warren in Rome' (p. 142); the 'gentleman protector' longing 'certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned' (p. 150); Fothergill's 'could I ever be worth his keeping me?' with the £300 settlement (p. 151); 'More than loving Marshall, Harry, Matt and Fothergill, he wanted to possess them' (p. 129); Marshall as Fothergill's 'rival' (p. 155); the Introduction's Warren who 'collected art and young men' (p. viii)
disputed.disputed_by: Nothing read contests a close bond; the reservation is evidential - nowhere in the pages read does Sox assert a romance or sexual relationship between them, and every explicit description is of employment, patronage, nursing and discipleship

sources.quote: Fothergill's earlier expressed longing for 'something like a gentleman protector - someone who would give me support, direction and place' certainly appeared to be fulfilled in Ned. His feelings for Ned were strong: 'He became to me, as to the others, part of my being - or at least so far as my tyrannies and unsympathetic impetuousness allowed me to imitate his god-like love and tolerance . . . He has become more than a part of me, for I seem to live as one with him, a would-be memorial to him.'

sources.quote: At last, Fothergill felt he had to 'face the problem that had long been on my mind and after all Ned's generosity and loving care of me, I had to come out with it. I imagined that he must be assuming that I was rich. But my £4000 had now half gone. Was I going to tell him that I couldn't go on with him? Or could I ever be worth his keeping me? At once he said he'd give me £300 a year and my mind was fresh to convalesce with.'
sources.context: During Fothergill's typhoid convalescence in the Orsini palace at Lecce, where Warren had 'suddenly arrived complete with a valet and a German doctor' (p. 150). Later on the same page: 'Romaine Brooks was not the only one to notice a change in Fothergill once he had taken up with Ned and Marshall.' Chain: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 151. Episode undated in the pages read (early Lewes House years).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Sox's account - built on Fothergill's unfinished, previously unpublished 81-page memoir (written 1954; Sox himself flags it as 'highly disorganized' with 'few dates given', p. 133) and corroborated by the 'architect' references in Wilde's letters to Ross - has the 21-year-old Fothergill visiting Wilde alone at Berneval in summer 1897, where Wilde 'liked him and declared to him' the 'Two loves have I' couplet, casting dark-haired Fothergill as the love 'of comfort' against golden-haired Douglas's 'despair'; the book's jacket glosses the episode as Wilde at one time having Fothergill in mind 'to replace Lord Alfred Douglas in his affections'. The decline is Fothergill's own: 'I don't think I could have given much comfort', followed back in England by his written drop of the correspondence as not 'politic'. Divergence from the roster-owner summary, following Sox: Sox never uses a 'kept man' framing and narrates no explicit sexual proposition - the nearest is Fothergill's confessed longing for 'a gentleman protector' and the visit being coordinated through Ross ('send over the architect'); the classification rests on the declaration-plus-decline shape. Two dossier passages promoted into the record at the editor's direction (2026-08-03): the 'gentleman protector' longing and the photograph-primed Dieppe meeting carry the implicit-arrangement texture - Fothergill's stated wish plus Ross-coordinated logistics - without Sox asserting an explicit arrangement; note the memoir does not say who showed Fothergill the photograph of Wilde.
relationships.date_label: Single visit to Wilde at Berneval, summer 1897: anticipated in Wilde's letters to Ross from 1 June ('send over the architect'); Sox: 'We do not know exactly when Fothergill appeared'; Wilde's 21 Sept. 1897 letter places Fothergill's six days ('Rowland a sextette of suns') within his last month there. Fothergill dropped the correspondence after returning to England (undated by Sox).
relationships.summary: After his May 1897 release Wilde settled at Berneval near Dieppe, and the 21-year-old Fothergill - 'the architect' of Wilde's letters to Ross - visited him there alone, for what Wilde's 21 September letter counts as a 'sextette of suns' in his final month there. Wilde met his boat at Dieppe and, troubled over the estranged Douglas, declared Fothergill his love 'of comfort' against Douglas's golden-haired 'despair'. Fothergill reflected that he could not have 'given much comfort'; back in England, where any association with Wilde was toxic, he answered Wilde's 'charming letters' by writing that it was not 'politic' to go on, and later - by then taken up with Warren in Rome - passed Wilde by at Aragno's cafe without approaching him, a decision his sons say he regretted to the end of his life.

sources.quote: Both Smithers and Fothergill knew Wilde was troubled about Bosie Douglas who was either unwilling to see him or prevented by Ross. Fothergill said Wilde liked him and declared to him: 'Two loves have I: the one of comfort; the other of despair. The one has black; the other golden hair.' Fothergill commented: 'I don't think I could have given much comfort. I was too concentrated on myself. I've ever been incapable of sympathy, even with this sad thing.'
sources.context: At Berneval, with Leonard Smithers the only other guest named as present in this stretch; the chapter title 'Two Loves Have I' is this declaration (Wilde reworking Shakespeare's Sonnet 144, dark-haired Fothergill as 'comfort' against Douglas's golden hair). Fothergill's first-person sentences are from his unpublished memoir.
sources.supports: The approach: Wilde's declaration casting Fothergill as the replacement love 'of comfort'; Fothergill's retrospective refusal of the role
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 157, printed folio 141 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Fothergill's quoted sentences: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 141.

sources.quote: He sat so still, looking at nothing, and had that same, sad friendless face … I wondered - should I go over to him or, would it once more be that awful word "politic", and a betrayal of my duty to Ned's work? I had to decide for this. I passed on, and never saw him again, but my tragic picture of it all sickens me still.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir, as printed by Sox: seeing Wilde alone outside Aragno's Café on the Via del Corso in Rome, after Fothergill had taken up with Warren. Sox introduces it as what Fothergill called 'the tragedy', and adds that the feeling stayed with him to the end of his life and that both his sons say he regretted the decision.
sources.supports: Fothergill in his own words on the end of the connection - the decision not to approach Wilde, and the lifelong regret.

sources.quote: Fothergill's visit has gone heretofore unrecorded although Rupert Hart-Davis's edition of selected letters of Oscar Wilde contains veiled references to it: 1 June 1897, Wilde wrote to Ross that he wanted to continue to live at Berneval and 'send over the architect [Fothergill]'. … On 20 July, again to Ross, Wilde said he 'expected Ross on August the First: also, the architect'.
sources.context: The square-bracketed '[Fothergill]' gloss is Sox's own. Elided middle sentence (5 June, Wilde to Ross on visitor expenses at the Hotel de la Plage): 'Architects, on the other hand, are taken at a reduction. I have special terms for architects.' Sox's endnote markers (nn. 7-9) omitted.
sources.supports: The visit is documented in Wilde's letters to Ross; Wilde anticipated 'the architect' at Berneval from 1 June through the summer of 1897

sources.quote: We do not know exactly when Fothergill appeared and from his memoirs it seems he visited Wilde alone. … on 21 September, Wilde wrote to Ross that despite several visits by friends to Berneval he was so lonely that he was on the brink of killing himself: in the last month there, Reggie Turner had given him three days, and 'Rowland a sextette of suns'.

sources.quote: Fothergill – as usual – was looking for something but could not find what it was, or, as we will see, perhaps was afraid to commit himself: 'I had all the time a secret longing for a perfect friend, a thing which I couldn't define – something like a gentleman protector – someone who would give me support, direction and place, for I had no thought of helping myself or how I could, but went on complacently spending my capital.'
sources.context: Sox introducing Fothergill on the eve of the Berneval episode; the inner first-person sentence is Fothergill's unpublished memoir. Promoted from the dossier at the editor's direction: this stated longing is the implicit basis of the 'prospective companion' framing.
sources.supports: Fothergill's own wish for 'a gentleman protector' - the motive side of the arrangement-texture; his wish, not an arrangement Sox attributes to Ross or Wilde.

sources.quote: From the railings of the boat, as she got to Dieppe harbour, I looked down upon what must be a great man standing alone and looking up. I had seen a photograph of this beautiful looking man and here was a huge and fat person in white flannels with a comical little red beret on top of it all. Rather vulgar I thought. My heart sank, but his sweet kindness put me right quickly.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir on his arrival at Dieppe, Wilde waiting at the harbour ('Fothergill described his arrival at Dieppe:'). He had been primed with a photograph beforehand - the memoir does not say by whom.
sources.supports: The meeting first-person: Wilde met his boat; the photograph seen beforehand (the logistics side of the arrangement-texture); the deflation-then-warmth of the first impression.

sources.quote: When Fothergill returned home he received 'some charming letters with his lovely handwriting', but admitted that the feeling against Wilde and any knowledge of him was then so strong in England that he decided 'to drop him': 'I actually wrote that it was not "politic" to go on with it. What an awful expression!' Wilde replied saying he didn't know what Fothergill meant by 'politic'.
sources.context: Immediately following: 'For Fothergill it was finished, but he said he had assimilated Wilde's manner - even his ponderous intonation "so far as my voice allowed".' The inner first-person sentences are Fothergill memoir text; runs over the printed 141/142 page break at 'he | didn't'.
sources.supports: The decline made effective: Fothergill ended the correspondence by letter as not 'politic' after returning to England; Wilde's baffled reply

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The page gives an existing acquaintance ('A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges'), an arranged meeting Wilde has undertaken to keep ('I have promised to run over and see him'), and four clauses of physical praise. That is the same shape as rolla--wilde, which the corpus already classes desire-expressed - a man written to or promised in advance, described, and looked forward to, with nothing recorded of what happened - and it is classed the same way here for consistency as well as on its merits. Against the README bar, a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis reads an older man promising to travel to see a beautiful young man and dwelling on his face; the desire is legible without the hypothesis, though the reading is this project's and no scholarly source was consulted. romantic-nonsexual was weighed: 'a great friend of mine' and the promise do imply contact from Georges's side, which is more mutuality than the rest of this tier offers. It was rejected because every expression of feeling on the page is Wilde's, because 'friend' is not documented courtship, and because the class displays as 'Romantic'. documented-sexual is unavailable - no first-person statement of sexual relations appears. Recorded exactly and without gloss, because it bears on how the connection should be read: Wilde says Georges 'is visiting Nice on speculative business', and the paragraph continues, on the following printed page, with a remark about combining romance with business; that continuation was not read in the source and is carried below as a pointer. Whether Georges was selling sex is not stated on the page read, and no such finding is entered here. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome - here Wilde states an intention to go to Nice, and no letter read says whether he and Georges met.
relationships.date_label: The intended meeting at Nice, announced in a letter postmarked 3 January 1899 from Napoule, for a trip 'tomorrow'. The friendship itself predates the letter - Wilde calls him a great friend and places him as a Paris boy - but no earlier date was verified in the source.
relationships.summary: From Napoule at the start of January 1899, Wilde told Reginald Turner that Harold Mellor was arriving that day and that the two of them were going to Nice the next day, where a great friend of his, a Paris boy he called 'le petit Georges', was then staying and whom he had promised to see. The letter gives four clauses of physical description and says Georges was at Nice on speculative business. Nothing read records whether the meeting took place.

sources.quote: My friend, my new friend, Harold Mellor comes here today to stay at the hotel, and tomorrow we go to Nice, for the day. A great friend of mine, a Paris boy called le petit Georges, is now at Nice, and I have promised to run over and see him. He is like a very handsome Roman boy, dark, and bronze-like, with splendidly chiselled nose and mouth, and the tents of midnight are folded in his eyes; moons hide in their curtains. He is visiting Nice on speculative business.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [Postmark 3 January 1899], Hôtel des Bains, Napoule - the second paragraph of the letter, following the weather. 'le petit Georges' is italicised on the page. The paragraph continues past the last sentence quoted here onto printed 1118.
sources.supports: The whole of the verified record: an existing friendship, a promised meeting at Nice, Wilde's description of him, and the statement that he was at Nice on speculative business; no outcome recorded

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Proposed on the primary record alone, read in the source: a two-week run of Wilde's 1898 letters to Leonard Smithers in which Gilbert is daily company - nightly bezique, cheap restaurant dinners, taking a cheque to the bank, writing out nearly all the signatures for the signed edition - and in which Wilde's register toward him turns amorous: 'his beaux yeux', 'He grows dearer to me daily', 'sweeter than ever', and the joke that he has 'unfortunately lost my heart' on a side-bet at bezique. Read together these document a real and growing attachment, and they carry weight precisely because they are reported TO A THIRD PARTY rather than addressed to Gilbert - Wilde has no flattering purpose to serve in a business letter to his publisher. The editors independently call Gilbert 'one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends during these last years'. The conservative alternative is live and should be weighed by the editor: each amorous line sits inside a comic bezique register and is separately deniable, and the README warns that Wilde's epistolary extravagance is not by itself an edge. No page read makes any sexual claim in either direction - hence romantic-nonsexual, whose 'nonsexual' describes the state of the evidence, not a finding of fact. The secondary tradition that Gilbert was a shared intimate of Wilde, Ross and Douglas remains unread in the source and is NOT the basis of this proposal. If the run reads to Lovelle as devoted companionship plus habitual Wildean extravagance, the correct disposition is no edge; that call is his.
relationships.date_label: First mention in the letters 25 February 1898, already on meeting terms ('We met by chance this morning'); the concentrated run of affectionate references falls 3-9 March 1898; the association lasted to Wilde's death - Gilbert attended the sickroom, took the deathbed photograph at Ross's request, and walked in the funeral procession, 30 November 1900.
relationships.summary: Maurice Gilbert, a young soldier of the marine infantry with an English father and a French mother, was part of Wilde's Paris household of the exile years. Through the spring of 1898 Wilde's letters to his publisher Leonard Smithers report him as a daily fixture - a nightly bezique opponent whose running score Wilde keeps for Smithers, a dinner companion at a two-franc restaurant, the man who takes the cheque to the bank and writes out the signatures Wilde is too tired to write - in a register that keeps sliding from domestic to amorous: Gilbert's 'beaux yeux', a heart 'unfortunately lost' on a side-bet, a friend who 'grows dearer to me daily' and is 'sweeter than ever'. The editors' own note calls him one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends of the last years, and he was present through the final illness, took the deathbed photograph and walked behind the hearse in November 1900.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with James Goddard ('Kit') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. Promoted to a relationship record at the editor's direction, 2026-08-03; the fuller diary basis sits in the Ives papers and in Kaplan (2005), neither yet consulted. CORROBORATION (2026-08-03): Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. That sharpens the evidence but does not lift the class: it remains one historian's careful inference, and he does not assert sexual relations outright. EVIDENCE-TIER CORRECTION 2026-08-03 (): reclassified to self-reported. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The sexual allegation exists only in Queensberry's plea (Oxford, June 1893; 'The Cottage,' Goring, June-Aug 1893). Grainger — whom Wilde on oath aged at 'about sixteen when I knew him' — never testified in any of the three proceedings, and Mr Justice Charles explained the Grainger and Conway offences were outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction and so never charged. Wilde denied indecencies on oath; his 'peculiarly plain boy' answer to 'Did you ever kiss him?' became the recognized turning-point of the libel cross-examination. Plea-only → 'alleged' with disputed block.
relationships.date_label: June–October 1893, Oxford and Goring (Grainger in Wilde's service)
relationships.summary: Walter Grainger, about sixteen by Wilde's sworn estimate, was a servant at the house in High Street, Oxford, where Douglas had rooms; in June-July 1893 Wilde brought him to 'The Cottage' at Goring as under-butler, where he remained until Wilde left in October. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at both places; the allegation was never charged and Grainger never gave evidence. Carson's pressing of Wilde's flippant answer — that he never kissed Grainger because he was 'a peculiarly plain boy' — is recorded by Hyde as the climax of the cross-examination.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited Walter Grainger to commit sodomy and committed acts of gross indecency with him at Oxford (June 1893) and at 'The Cottage,' Goring (June-Aug 1893)
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895)
disputed.disputed_by: Wilde's sworn denials ('No indecencies ever took place between myself and Grainger'; 'I never on any occas[i]on asked him to come into my bedroom')
disputed.grounds: allegation stands in the plea alone: never charged (outside CCC jurisdiction — Hyde p. 256) and no testimony from Grainger is printed in Hyde; the record's age statement (sixteen) is Wilde's own sworn answer at the libel trial

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Proposed per the project hypothesis of a lifelong partnership from c. 1892, with a transparency caveat: so far verified only Holland & Hart-Davis's editorial apparatus, which attests 'his close friend Andre Raffalovich' (by the 1893 Blackmailers collaboration), that Raffalovich 'remained close friends [with Gray] for the rest of his life', and that Raffalovich built St Peter's Church, Edinburgh, for Gray in their later years together - a lifelong bond, not characterized sexually. Both became devout Catholics and Gray a priest at thirty-five; whether the partnership was celibate (and from when) is a standing question the verified sources do not resolve. A second independent secondary attestation (McKenna pointer below) awaits verification in the source; if a later check finds biographers agree only on devoted companionship, romantic-nonsexual may fit better.
relationships.date_label: Close friends by 1892-93 (The Blackmailers, written together, produced June 1893); 'remained close friends for the rest of his life' (both died 1934); later years together in Edinburgh, where Raffalovich built St Peter's Church for Gray.
relationships.summary: Gray and Raffalovich were close by 1892-93, when they wrote The Blackmailers together (Prince of Wales's Theatre, June 1893) - the editors call Raffalovich Gray's 'close friend' and record the belief that he 'revenged himself' on Wilde by breaking up Wilde's friendship with Gray, 'with whom Raffalovich remained close friends for the rest of his life'. The bond ran unbroken to their deaths in the same year, 1934: Gray became a Roman Catholic priest, Raffalovich built St Peter's Church, Edinburgh, for him, and Gray's edition of Beardsley's last letters (1904) was of letters written to Raffalovich. The verified sources attest lifelong devotion without characterizing the bond sexually; the celibacy question is left open.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Nothing read so far attests a sexual or romantic relationship first-person. What the primary and editorial material documents is patronage (Wilde undertook Silverpoints' production costs, June 1892), public association strong enough that the Daily Telegraph called Gray Wilde's 'protege' - which Wilde publicly denied, calling the acquaintance 'extremely recent' - Gray's self-identification as 'Dorian' within the circle, Wilde's retrospective 'my real life, my higher life was with them' in De Profundis, and an editorially noted falling-out. The sexual/romantic characterization common in later biography was not reachable in the source so far (pointer to McKenna below), so the contested-single-source class with a disputed block is the honest mechanical proposal; a later check may raise it to consensus if two independent secondary attestations are verified.
relationships.date_label: Documented span Feb. 1892 (Wilde publicly calls the acquaintance 'extremely recent') through 1893 (Silverpoints published; The Blackmailers June 1893); the editors note Wilde and Gray later 'fell out' (undated). The conventional c. 1889 start rests on secondary tradition not read so far.
relationships.summary: Gray was publicly tied to Wilde by February 1892, when the Daily Telegraph called him Wilde's 'protege' - a label Wilde corrected in print while praising Gray's 'perfected mode of expression'. In June 1892 Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), and after The Picture of Dorian Gray appeared, Gray 'referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so', though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. The two fell out - the editors record the belief that Raffalovich broke the friendship up - but in De Profundis Wilde still ranked the friendship among those where 'my real life, my higher life' had been. Whether the bond was sexual rests on secondary claims not verified so far.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Hall's own letters are the evidence, which is the README's self-reported test in its plainest form: nine years of them, published entire as Your John, in which she names the attachment continuously and without ambiguity. The class rests on the participant's own words and needs no corroborating layer, though it has one - Glasgow's introduction, and Hall's biographers Dickson and Baker, both of whom read these letters before they were published. Note the asymmetry the record cannot fix: **Souline's side does not survive.** Of nine years of her letters to Hall exactly one, from 1939, is extant, so every word here is Hall's about Souline and none is Souline's about Hall. Glasgow is explicit that Souline's responses can only be speculated about, and reads two alternating reactions in them, "flattered interest and terror". The edge is therefore well-evidenced as to Hall's feeling and one-sided as to the record; it is not classed desire-expressed, because the relationship itself is not in doubt - only Souline's voice is missing.
relationships.date_label: met at Bagnoles-de-l'Orne in the summer of 1934, when Souline came from the American Hospital in Paris as Hall's private nurse; the correspondence runs from July 1934 until Hall's death on 7 October 1943
relationships.summary: In 1934 Radclyffe Hall, fifty-four and between books, went to the Normandy spa of Bagnoles-de-l'Orne to treat an old riding injury. Una Troubridge, her partner since 1915, fell ill there, and Hall sent to the American Hospital in Paris for a private nurse. The nurse was Evguenia Souline, a Russian émigrée in her thirtieth year. What began with a few stolen kisses at the spa became a nine-year attachment conducted very largely by post - Hall wrote at first in letter-and-response intervals, then every two days, then daily and sometimes twice - and it did not displace Troubridge, who remained. Hall's editor calls the arrangement that followed "an imperfect, stormy triangle" and lets it stand as one. The letters were published in 1997 as Your John; Souline's replies were not kept, and one survives.

sources.quote: But in 1934 everything changed. … At Una's urging, therefore, they went to Bagnoles-de l'Orne, a spa in Normandy where John had once been treated for the same injury. During the course of treatment, throughout which Una acted as facilitator, correspondent, indeed general manager, Una herself came down with severe gastroenteritis. Still hobbling, unwell, and feeling unhelpful, John sent to the American Hospital in Paris for a private nurse. That nurse was Evguenia Souline. Until the end of John's life nine years later, the three, John, Una, and Souline, were to form an imperfect, stormy triangle.

relationships.summary: Una Troubridge, a sculptor and translator and Mabel Batten's cousin, met Radclyffe Hall in 1915 and the two became lifelong partners. Troubridge's marriage to the naval officer Sir Ernest Troubridge ended in separation by 1919, the Ransom Center's sketch states, because of the relationship with Hall. The partnership lasted until Hall's death in 1943 and survived Hall's long affair with the Russian nurse Evguenia Souline in her last nine years, which the same sketch records Troubridge as tolerating despite the unhappiness it caused her. Troubridge afterwards wrote The Life and Death of Radclyffe Hall (1961) and left 131 volumes of diaries.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Cook states plainly that Ives shared his bed with Harold Holt ('Cubby') at the Albany, which is more explicit than the household-membership evidence behind the Bloodworth record. It stays 'alleged' on the single-source rule: Cook (2003) is the only work read that attests it, and bed-sharing in a shared bachelor household is not by itself a statement of sexual relations. Promoted to a relationship record at the editor's direction, 2026-08-03; the fuller diary basis sits in the Ives papers and in Kaplan (2005), neither yet consulted. CORROBORATION (2026-08-03): Cook returns to this household at much greater length in Queer Domesticities (2014), where he states that the Adelaide Road relationships 'possibly started sexually' before settling into something platonic, with bed-sharing continuing throughout. That sharpens the evidence but does not lift the class: it remains one historian's careful inference, and he does not assert sexual relations outright. EVIDENCE-TIER CORRECTION 2026-08-03 (): reclassified to self-reported. Cook's account of the Ives household is drawn from Ives's own 122-volume diary and his endnotes cite it by volume and date; the tier follows whose testimony underlies the claim, not whether our record happens to carry a direct quotation rather than the historian's summary of the same diary.

sources.supports: The closest this record can come to Ives characterizing Saunders in his own voice, and the limit is worth stating exactly. Cook records that 'Elephant' was a name Ives himself used, and Ives's diary then names the household collectively as 'my children' - so the relationship Ives claimed with the men he lived with is paternal, proprietary and affectionate at once. But the naming is collective: Ives nowhere names Saunders or 'Elephant' in any first-person passage Cook prints, and Cook never dates Elephant's arrival, so whether Saunders was among the 'six or eight people' of the 1923 entry is not established. Ives's testimony reaching us through Cook, from Diary vol. 85. See the documented-absence note in the pointer entry below.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: One documented passionate kiss - Wilde kissed Ives 'passionately' goodbye at the New Travellers' Club, the word being Cook's in the source quotation from the Ives diary - inside a close, teasing friendship that ran from the early 1890s to Wilde's last months (surviving letters to Ives from Oct. 1893 to Sept. 1900, plus prison messages via Sherard). No source read asserts sexual relations; the editorial note that Ives's anonymous A Book of Chains (1897) held 'poems bearing directly on his feelings for Wilde in prison' supports a romantic charge on Ives's side. Whether there was ever more is unknown - matches the README's own exemplar for this class.
relationships.date_label: Met early 1890s (Cook: 'shortly after' Ives's July 1891 move to St James'; Lewis podcast: 'in about 1893'); kiss undated (New Travellers' Club period); friendship to Wilde's death, Nov. 1900.
relationships.summary: Ives met Wilde in early-1890s London and was drawn into his club and cafe circle; at the New Travellers' Club Wilde once kissed him 'passionately' goodbye (Ives's diary, via Cook). The friendship survived Wilde's imprisonment - Wilde sent word from Reading that he was 'greatly touched' by Ives's wish to visit, and Ives's anonymous 1897 A Book of Chains carried poems on his feelings for Wilde in prison - and continued through the Paris exile, where Wilde teased Ives's 'silly mania for secrecy' and called him 'a great baby', writing to him warmly until three months before his death.

sources.quote: It is a pleasure to me to see you. … I like to talk to you about literature, life, the progress of thought, its power to touch the world, its practical energy - subjects of no interest to others than ourselves.
sources.context: Wilde to Ives, 12 February [Postmark 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris - the same letter as the 'silly mania for secrecy' passage below, five paragraphs further on, where Wilde answers Ives's request that they meet somewhere out of sight
sources.supports: Wilde in his own hand, writing to Ives, saying plainly what the friendship was: a pleasure, and a private subject-matter shared by the two of them and nobody else. Wilde is refusing Ives's insistence on hidden meeting-places, so the sentence doubles as his statement that this bond needs no concealment - the sharpest first-hand characterization of the Ives-Wilde relationship in the record, and unmediated, unlike the diary-quoting passages below.

sources.quote: Yes: I have no doubt we shall win, but the road is long, and red with monstrous martyrdoms. Nothing but the repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act would do any good.

The first-person plural is the point - 'we shall win' puts Wilde inside Ives's cause, and the specific target he names is Ives's own, the repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885. This is the passage most often cited as evidence that the friendship was political as well as personal, and it was missing from this record.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Documented public devotion and close, teasing intimacy: the 1879 poem 'The New Helen', the inscription 'To Helen, formerly of Troy, now of London' in her copy of Poems, Wilde acting as her tutor-amanuensis (her own note calls him 'my kind tutor'), and the warm 'My dear Lil' correspondence continuing after his marriage. Nothing read makes a sexual claim; whether the public devotion was courtship or performance is a real interpretive question, but the documented register is romantic-devotional, so this class fits the read evidence. The 1899 remark about marrying her 'with pleasure' reaches us via Vincent O'Sullivan as printed by the editors - chain noted.

relationships.summary: Wilde's public poetic devotion to the great Society beauty of the age - 'The New Helen', the Troy/London inscription - alongside a working intimacy as her tutor and amanuensis and a durable friendship: she is among the first he tells of his engagement, and he sends her theatre stalls in 1885 with news of Constance's confinement.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: One-sided and documented as such. Levy's own poems addressed to Lee are the vehicle of the desire - her biographer Linda Hunt Beckman, writing the Shalvi/Hyman encyclopedia entry, calls them 'love poems' and adds that 'in letters Levy expressed her admiration' - so the desire clears the README's bar twice over: it is legible as desire to a reader without the coding hypothesis, and a scholarly source reads it that way. Direction is Levy's. Outcome 'unreciprocated' rather than 'declined' because no refusal by Lee is on record: Diniejko states that Levy 'never experienced a requited love attachment with any of the women to whom she was attracted', which is an absence of reciprocation, not a documented rebuff. Diniejko also flags that Levy's sexuality 'remains a point of contention among scholars', and that caveat is part of the record here. This is not classified as self-reported because the class is desire-expressed, which the README treats as its own category rather than a certainty tier.
relationships.date_label: met at Florence, 1886; the poems and letters follow; Levy died in 1889
relationships.summary: Amy Levy met Vernon Lee at Florence in 1886 and fell in love with her. She sent Lee love poems - the sonnet 'To Vernon Lee', set on Bellosguardo, and 'New Love, New Life' - and expressed her admiration in letters; the friendship also brought her into Lee's circle, notably the poet Dorothy Blomfield. Nothing in the sources read records reciprocation by Lee, and Levy's biographer describes a woman who never had a requited attachment to any of the women she loved. Levy died by suicide in 1889, three years after the Florence meeting. The two women's other point of contact is Wilde himself, who was publishing Levy in the Woman's World across exactly these years.

sources.quote: Levy’s visit to Florence in 1886 was pivotal because she met Violet Paget (Vernon Lee), an important figure in the aesthetic movement of the fin de siècle. The love poems Levy sent to Lee (e.g., “To Vernon Lee” and “New Love, New Life”) are revealing, and in letters Levy expressed her admiration. The friendship enabled Levy to become intimate with Lee’s circle of friends, particularly the poet Dorothy Blomfield.
sources.context: Linda Hunt Beckman - Levy's biographer (Amy Levy: Her Life and Letters, 2000) - in the Shalvi/Hyman Encyclopedia of Jewish Women. 'The love poems Levy sent to Lee' is a biographer's characterisation resting on Levy's own poems and letters, which Beckman edited.
sources.supports: That Levy sent Lee love poems and expressed admiration in letters: the desire, and its direction.

sources.quote: Levy’s sexual orientation remains a point of contention among scholars. She was, it seems, a platonic lesbian, who never experienced a requited love attachment with any of the women to whom she was attracted. In 1886, while Levy stayed in Florence, she met and became infatuated with Vernon Lee (Violet Piaget), a novelist and essayist, to whom she dedicated one of her best sonnets.
sources.context: Andrzej Diniejko's Victorian Web biography. The page then prints 'To Vernon Lee' in full. 'Violet Piaget' is Diniejko's misspelling of Paget. Note the scholarly caveat in the first sentence, which is why it is quoted rather than elided.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Only a non-participant speaks in the evidence read. Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography states the attachment and its span; no letter, diary or statement by Lee or Robinson about the relationship was read so far, and Pulham's one citation to Robinson's own writing ('Robinson, 935') is about the visitors to Casa Paget, not about the relationship. Second-hand is a statement about who is talking, not a mark of doubt: Pulham is the standard scholarly account and calls it a romantic friendship without hedging. Vernon Lee's letters are published (Gagel's edition) and would likely move this to self-reported; pointer recorded.
relationships.date_label: met 1880; attachment lasting until Robinson's marriage in 1887
relationships.summary: Vernon Lee met the poet Mary Robinson in 1880, the year Lee came to public notice with Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy, and the two formed what Pulham calls a romantic friendship. Robinson visited Lee's home in Florence and Lee returned the visit in London in 1881, where Robinson introduced her to the Burne-Joneses, Gosse, the Morrises, the Rossettis and Oscar Wilde - which is how Lee entered the London circle this map charts. The attachment ended with Robinson's marriage in 1887 to the orientalist James Darmesteter; Kit Anstruther-Thomson replaced her as Lee's companion that same year.

sources.quote: It is also in 1880 that Lee first met the poet Mary Robinson (1857-1944) with whom she developed a romantic friendship that lasted until Mary married in 1887.
sources.context: Patricia Pulham's Y90s biography of Vernon Lee, in the paragraph on Lee's emergence in 1880. The following sentences record Robinson's account of the visitors to 'Casa Paget' and Lee's return visit to London in 1881, at which she met Wilde.
sources.supports: The relationship, its character as Pulham states it, and both its start and end dates.

sources.quote: The dear sprigs of olive and ilex and spicewood came this morning. They stand in my bedroom in a blue bracken jar and remind me of the January posies you used to bring me from your drives in the Cascine, when you came, all keen outer air & crisp green things, into the salon where I would be reading German Mystics over the fire … A great packet of my poor foolish sad little old letters, so young, so senties, poor little unhappy things, was left at the door one day by a nameless young woman. I have only just now dared to glance at them – for one must not glance at Eurydice in Hades. When you know of some very discreet, honourable & yet good natured person who could take charge of your packet, let me know and she shall have it. … Ever your loving old friend Molly
sources.context: Mary Robinson - by then Mme Darmesteter - to Vernon Lee, Christmas Eve 1893, five years after the marriage. Two things at once: the tenderness of the memory, and the two women arranging the return of each other's old love letters through discreet intermediaries. 'Senties' is Robinson's French, glossed by the editors as 'emotional'; 'the Mouse' elsewhere on the page is Lee's name for her when they were young. The elisions drop a passage on Lee's book and the Revue de Paris, and Robinson's remark about her letters to Symonds. The original is at the Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Anglais 243.
sources.supports: Robinson's own voice on the relationship and on its aftermath - the surviving affection, and the mutual retrieval of the love letters that documented it.

null_findings.finding: WRONG VOLUME FOR THE ORIGINAL ASK, and the pointer has been re-pointed accordingly. The pointer named `gagel-vernon-lee-letters` (the 2016 Pickering Masters entry, which has no repo path) and wanted 'Lee's own account of the relationship and of its ending'. The volume actually on disk is **Volume III, 1890-1896** - the attachment ran 1880-1888, so Lee's own account of it is in Vols. I and II, which this project does not hold; the edition itself points there. What Vol. III does carry, and what is now recorded, is the editors' biographical note and one letter from Robinson's side in 1893. A whole-volume search finds no letter addressed to Robinson in it: 'Robinson' appears on 70 of 815 pages, almost all editorial apparatus, bibliography and archive listings.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The evidence read so far is Wilde's own side of the 1885-86 correspondence, which runs in a sustained romantic register - 'keen curiosity, wonder, delight' at their reunion, 'I wish you were here, Harry', a requested photograph, 'You have the power of making others love you', the 'l'amour de l'impossible' letter addressed to Marillier as a fellow-feeler, reciprocal visits (Cambridge, Tite Street, Hampton), and the insistence 'You are certainly not to call me Mr Wilde.' No first-person sexual claim appears in any letter read, and no secondary attestation was consulted so far, so the documented-courtship class fits the evidence before me; whether biographer consensus reads it as more is left open for a later check.
relationships.date_label: Correspondence postmarked 5 Nov. 1885 - 11 June 1886; acquaintance dates from 13 Salisbury Street, 1880-81, when the schoolboy Marillier brought Wilde his coffee.
relationships.summary: Marillier, the 'blue-coat boy' who had lodged in Wilde's Salisbury Street building in 1880-81, wrote to Wilde from Peterhouse, Cambridge, in autumn 1885; Wilde's replies over the following eight months are the most romantically charged letters he is known to have written to a young man before Ross - a missed train mourned, a photograph requested, a Cambridge visit remembered as 'a dream', and the December 1885 Glasgow letter naming what they shared as 'the love of things impossible... l'amour de l'impossible'. The letters record visits in both directions through the winter; the last surviving letter (June 1886) still insists 'You are certainly not to call me Mr Wilde.'

sources.quote: But your letter has reached me, like a strain of music wind-blown from a far land. You too have the love of things impossible – ἔρως τῶν ἀδυνάτων – l'amour de l'impossible (how do men name it?). Some day you will find, even as I have found, that there is no such thing as a romantic experience; there are romantic memories, and there is the desire of romance – that is all.
