relationships.certainty_reasoning: Sox's own wording is unambiguous and repeated: Marshall is 'the love of his life' (p. 37), 'his future lover' (p. 42), 'his great love' (p. 128), 'his beloved (Puppy)' (p. viii), and after the 1889 capitulation letter Sox writes flatly 'John Marshall admitted he was in love' (p. 44). The evidence Sox prints is participant correspondence in the source (drawn, per his pp. ix-x, from the Warren-Marshall letters printed by Burdett & Goddard 1941 and the originals at the Ashmolean): Warren's 1887-89 wooing letters ('take lodgings with me?', 'dine alone with me'), Marshall's 1889 'my love to you' letter, Marshall's 1893 'Puppy dear... I am sick of being alone' letter, Warren's 1914 letter signed 'Your Puppy', and Warren's first-person account of Marshall's death ('I went to his bed and kissed him good-night... said "good-bye Puppy" several times to me'). Not proposed as documented-sexual: no passage read attests sexual relations in first person - the letters attest love, cohabitation and lifelong partnership; the nearest sexual framings are Warren's authorship of A Defence of Uranian Love (pp. 153-154) and his 'the Museum was truly a paederastic evangel. It must be counted as a result of love' (pp. 128-129), plus Fothergill's 'Ned never touched a woman in his life, nor, perhaps had Marshall' (p. 76), which cuts both ways. Caveat for the owner on the consensus criterion: Sox is the only secondary source read so far; Burdett & Goddard 1941 corroborates the pair-bond in passages Sox quotes ('replicas of each other' p. 39; Ned telling Burdett he had wanted Marshall 'to be buried with me' p. 130) but was not independently read - if two independently-read secondaries are required, this technically sits at single-source until Burdett-Goddard or Martin Green is read; 'alleged' would however misfit a bond that no source read contests. Addendum (p. 21, rendered): analysing Warren's A Tale of Pausanian Love, Sox writes that before they met 'Warren and Marshall were equally inexperienced, and both were very confused regarding their sexuality', and that while Marshall 'was not adverse to the idea of marriage', for Ned 'that course was utterly unthinkable and a betrayal of homosexual idealism' - Sox's most direct statement of the partnership's homosexual-idealist frame.
relationships.date_label: Met at New College, Oxford, 1884 (Marshall's third year); Warren's 'protracted wooing' by letter 1887-89; 'Marshall gave in (1889)' and by November 1889 'the man of his choice' was at Ned's side; Lewes House from 1890. Strained from 1906-07: Marshall married Warren's cousin Mary Bliss 5 Nov. 1907 and moved to Rome, still collecting on Warren's subsidy. Sharing their old Rome flat again at the end, Marshall died in Warren's presence, February 1928 ('five minutes past one', night of the 15th, per Warren's account); Warren died 28 December 1928; his ashes joined the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca, 5 April 1929.
relationships.summary: The forty-year partnership at the centre of the Lewes House 'brotherhood of aesthetes'. Warren met Marshall at New College in 1884 and wooed him by letter for years - 'I had hoped that usually you would consent to dine alone with me' - until Marshall 'gave in' in 1889 with a letter ending 'everything you say and do seems inseparable from you and my love to you'; Sox adds 'John Marshall admitted he was in love'. They called each other 'Puppy', ran the antiquities-collecting enterprise for Boston from Lewes House, and Sox names Marshall 'the love of his life' and 'his future lover'. Marshall's 1907 marriage to Warren's cousin Mary Bliss - a 'betrayal of their common ideal' to Warren; 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union' per Sox - moved the Marshalls to Rome on Warren's subsidy. Warren was living with Marshall again at his death in February 1928: he kissed him good-night and heard 'good-bye Puppy' several times as Marshall died; ten months later Warren was dead, his ashes placed in the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca under a Grecian urn.

sources.quote: Marshall was at last hooked and wrote to Ned: 'You were to me at first a quality, then a collection of qualities, and at last . . . well! you were Warren: and now everything you say and do seems inseparable from you and my love to you. That makes my judgement in the matter infallible.' John Marshall admitted he was in love.
sources.context: September 1889: Marshall had presented his conditions for becoming Ned's secretary; Ned answered 'Dear Marechal, your plan of the secretaryship comes near to what I have been wanting for a long time' and, on Marshall's dining-with-the-servants condition, 'I had hoped that usually you would consent to dine alone with me' (p. 43). Two paragraphs after the quote: 'By November 1889, "the man of his choice" was at Ned's side.' The letter runs over the printed 43/44 page break.
sources.supports: PROMOTED TO LEAD by the Q2 quality pass 2026-08-03, displacing Sox's phrase 'the love of his life'. This is the passage in which a participant says most plainly what the bond was: Marshall's own letter ending the two-year courtship, tracing how Warren stopped being a set of qualities and became simply 'Warren', and closing on 'my love to you'. Marshall's letter to Warren, September 1889, as printed by Sox; Sox's flat sentence after it - 'John Marshall admitted he was in love' - is the historian reading the same letter, and is kept inside the quotation so the reader can weigh the two. Partnership begun November 1889.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 59-60, printed folios 43-44 confirmed on rendered pages, read as page images 2026-08-03. Inner '... ' ellipses are as printed.

sources.quote: With Ned Warren love and collecting were inexorably entwined and the extent and direction of that collecting took shape in the context of the love of his life, John Marshall, his 'Puppy'.
sources.context: Closing sentence of Part II ch. 1 ('Why Do Men Collect?'); the preceding sentence quotes Kenneth Clark on collecting being as irrational as falling in love. The Introduction carries the same framing: 'his beloved "Puppy" (as he called John Marshall)' (p. viii).

sources.quote: In the letter to Curtius, Ned had also commented on how he viewed his future lover: 'I used to think that he took his tragedy in daily life, and his comedy in literature . . . He was a man very much preoccupied with his own subjects, and with his own ideas. Sometimes inappreciative of others who did not strike his own fancy, a better judge of art than of people, but unpretentious and very touching in his affections.'

The same page prints the wooing letters: 27 Feb. 1887, 'What will become of our project for travel?... I wonder whether it would amuse you to take lodgings with me?'; and from Bad-Ems, 'Unless I hear from you at once... I shall cast out my lines for other fish whom I see drifting down stream.'

sources.quote: From Rome he complained to Ned: 'I feel so weak here; I am rather down - I can do nothing. I go round and round seeing worthless things. I suspect everybody . . . I am sick of being alone and Puppy dear, it is bad for me. I would sooner do anything than live alone. Do, therefore, if you can, hurry up the business here. I am a bit unhappy.' This is one of the most personal outpourings we have from John Marshall.
sources.context: Marshall alone at the Rome end of the collecting operation. 'Puppy dear' is Marshall addressing Warren - the nickname ran both directions (Warren signs 'Your Puppy' in the 4 May 1914 letter printed at p. 107; the jacket: 'they called each other "Puppy"'). Sox retro-dates the letter at p. 76 as 'this threat of 1893'. Inner '... ' is as printed; the passage crosses the printed 64/65 break.

sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 80-81, printed folios 64-65 confirmed on rendered pages, read as page images 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: 'a middle-aged cousin of Ned's who came to stay with us: she didn't like me, and courted Ned and Marshall, either of which she was well prepared to marry. But Ned never touched a woman in his life, nor, perhaps had Marshall . . . Naively Mary thought the marriage would unite Johnny more closely to Ned.' … Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union of Mary and John Marshall, but she was an extremely beneficial help-mate in his collecting at the Metropolitan Museum.

' is as printed); the sentence after the elision is Sox's own narration. Same page: 'John Marshall did not marry Ned's cousin until 5 November 1907.' Mary Bliss was Warren's cousin (p. viii); Warren had dedicated The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900) to her (p. 75).
sources.supports: The marriage as the record frames it: Mary's own hope that it 'would unite Johnny more closely to Ned'; Sox: 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union'; Fothergill on the men's celibacy toward women

sources.quote: Ned sensed what was transpiring but, fatalistically, did nothing about it. By the spring of 1907 it became clear that Marshall would marry. Though he told Marshall this was a 'betrayal of their common ideal', Ned said he would stand by his friend 'married or unmarried'.
sources.context: Marshall, often left alone at Lewes while Warren fought his family lawsuit in America, had called Edward Robinson (the Met) and Mary Bliss his 'only loopholes of escape'. Same page: 'Ned seemed so consumed by his new interest in Harry Thomas... that he submerged his feelings for Marshall'; 'After the marriage, however, Ned was as good as his word' - the Rome flat and subsidized income; 'Of the forty years during which Warren knew Marshall, half were after his marriage.' Fothergill's account adds that Ned was reduced to 'frenzied and unreasonable agitation' over the thought of Marshall's marrying (p. 154).
sources.supports: The marriage strain: Warren's 'betrayal of their common ideal' and his standing by Marshall 'married or unmarried'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 94, printed folio 78 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Ned gave a vivid account of his friend's last hours to John Fothergill: 'On the evening of the 15th Johnny went to bed early, say towards nine. … I went to his bed and kissed him good-night; he said that he was going to sleep; usually he read a little in bed. Our rooms were connected by an open door. … he looked wild and said good-bye to the servants and said "good-bye Puppy" several times to me. … In ten minutes he was dead.'
sources.context: February 1928, Rome: 'Marshall returned to Rome, and Ned was there... the two shared a flat they had lived in during their collecting days' (p. 126). The account is a set-off block extract in the original (outer quotation marks added here; 'good-bye Puppy' is in single quotes in the original). It continues: 'I lay on the other side of him propping up his head... I got up and looked at my watch; it was five minutes past one.' Full extract in dossiers/LEWES-HOUSE_dossier.md (W16).
sources.supports: Warren's first-person account of Marshall's death: cohabiting again, the good-night kiss, 'good-bye Puppy' as Marshall's last words to him. Read with the burial passage below (p. 130), this is Warren's own answer to what Marshall was to him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 142-143, printed folios 126-127 confirmed on rendered pages, read as page images 2026-08-03. Chain: Warren letter to Fothergill, as printed in Sox 1991, pp. 126-127.

sources.quote: Ned told Osbert Burdett that he had wanted Marshall 'to be buried with me, but he had made his will just after his wife's death and before he had begun to understand me again.'
sources.context: Sox, in the closing pages on Warren's own death (28 December 1928, ten months after Marshall's); the inner words are Warren's, spoken to his biographer Osbert Burdett. The same page records that Warren's ashes went instead to the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca in spring 1929, under a plain Grecian urn bearing the names of Mary and John Marshall and Edward Perry Warren.
sources.supports: Warren's own most explicit claim on the relationship, and the counterpart to Marshall's 1889 avowal at the head of this record: he had wanted to be buried with Marshall. It is a spousal claim made in the one register the law left open to him, and the clause that follows is Warren's account of why it failed - Marshall's will was made in the estrangement after his wife's death, 'before he had begun to understand me again'. Warren to Osbert Burdett, as quoted by Sox.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 146 (printed folio 130 confirmed on the rendered page), read as page image 2026-08-03.

relationships.date_label: October 1892 (alleged); acquaintance from autumn 1892
relationships.summary: Taylor groomed Sidney Mavor for an introduction to Wilde ('Mr. Wilde likes nice clean boys') at a Kettner's dinner given by Schwabe — the dinner Mavor understood to be Wilde and Taylor's own first meeting. Wilde sent Mavor a silver cigarette case inscribed 'Sidney from O. W., October, 1892' and had him to stay the night at the Albemarle Hotel. On the stand Mavor repeated his Bow Street denial that anything improper ever occurred; the counts were struck out, and Hyde prints Douglas's account of having coached the denial.

disputed.claim: that Wilde solicited and committed acts of gross indecency with Sidney Mavor at the Albemarle Hotel in October 1892
disputed.asserted_by: Queensberry's plea of justification (filed 30 March 1895); the two Mavor counts of the Crown indictment in Regina v. Wilde and Taylor (1895); a note from Taylor to Mavor read by the Crown asking Mavor to 'come at once and see Oscar at Tite Street' (Gill's opening, Hyde p. 191)
disputed.disputed_by: Mavor's sworn evidence ('No misconduct occurred when I stayed in the hotel'; 'No impropriety has ever taken place between me and Mr. Wilde'); the judge's direction striking out the Mavor counts (Hyde pp. 72-73)

Mr. Wilde likes nice clean boys." … Wilde took my address, and soon afterwards I received a silver cigarette case with my Christian name scratched inside it. It was inscribed "Sidney from O. W., October, 1892."

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The documentary record read attests a close friendship from the Oxford years and a documented cohabitation (Salisbury Street to August 1880, then Keats House, Tite Street) - first-person in Wilde's letters and confirmed by the editors - but makes no romantic or sexual claim anywhere. The romantic reading belongs to later secondary tradition. That tradition has now been consulted rather than merely pointed at: McKenna asserts it outright and footnotes nothing for it (see disputed, grounds). The edge therefore stays uncorroborated, with the friendship, the Irish visits and the cohabitation all fully documented in Wilde's own letters.

start.label: friendship from the mid-1870s; cohabitation from 1879

relationships.date_label: c. 1876 - c. 1881 (cohabitation 1879-81)
relationships.summary: Wilde and the portraitist Frank Miles shared rooms for roughly two years - Thames House, 13 Salisbury Street until August 1880, then Keats House, 1 Tite Street - at the center of the 'Tea and Beauties' social world of Wilde's first London years. Whether the bond had a romantic dimension is asserted by McKenna, who states it without citing anything for it; the primary record read makes no such claim.

disputed.claim: That the Wilde-Miles friendship and cohabitation had a romantic or sexual dimension.
disputed.asserted_by: Both works in this tradition have now been consulted at page (2026-08-04). Neil McKenna, Secret Life (2008 edn), PDF p. 34: Oscar and Frank 'were almost certainly already lovers' by the early summer of 1876, and Wilde later confessed to Douglas that 'he and Frank first had sex' at Oxford. Rupert Croft-Cooke, The Unrecorded Life (1972), pp. 40 and 45: 'the first of Wilde's passionate friendships with another man', and 'the chattering love that was between Oscar and him'.
disputed.grounds: Nothing in the primary record makes the claim, and neither asserting work supports it with a source. McKenna's chapter notes for 'Tea and beauties' (PDF p. 723) carry a citation for every quotation in the chapter and none for either 'almost certainly already lovers' or the 1892 confession; both are unfootnoted assertion. Croft-Cooke has no apparatus at all - no notes, no bibliography - but he does something McKenna does not, which is show his reasoning and mark it as reasoning: the 'alien note' he hears in Wilde's letters whenever Miles is mentioned, and the stay at Illaunroe that 'must have been an affectionate adventure'. That is argument from register and circumstance, offered as such. The two also claim different things - Croft-Cooke claims love and passionate friendship, McKenna claims sex - and only the weaker claim is argued. Per this repository's note on McKenna he is never the sole basis for a class above uncorroborated, and Croft-Cooke adds inference rather than evidence, so consulting both settles the class where it is rather than moving it. The friendship, the Irish visits and the cohabitation are documented throughout in Wilde's own letters and are not what is in question.

sources.quote: And now I am trying to settle a new house, where Mr Miles and I are going to live. The address is horrid but the house very pretty. It is much nearer you than my old house, so I hope we shall often, if you let me, have 'dishes of tea' at one another's houses.

sources.quote: Frank Miles and I came down here last week, and have had a very royal time of it sailing. We are at the top of Lough Corrib, which if you refer to your geography you will find to be a lake thirty miles long, ten broad and situated in the most romantic scenery in Ireland. … But on Friday we go into Connemara to a charming little fishing lodge we have in the mountains where I hope to make him land a salmon and kill a brace of grouse.

sources.quote: The only occasions on which one detects an alien note in his letters both to Bouncer and Kitten is when he mentions Frank Miles, and this brings us to the first of Wilde's passionate friendships with another man; one which lasted five years and survived the two men's living together in two London homes.

sources.supports: The second of the two assertions of a romantic dimension, and the one that states its own basis: a change of register Croft-Cooke hears in the letters, not a document.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Unlike the rest of this tier, the sentence states a relationship rather than a notice: 'I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen.' Wilde is asserting a bond, not recording that he saw someone beautiful, so romantic-nonsexual is proposed - the README gloss being that 'nonsexual' describes the evidence and not a finding of fact. No first-person statement of sexual relations appears, so documented-sexual is unavailable. Two things must be weighed against the class and are recorded here rather than buried: first, the register is comic. The sentence answers Wilde's own riff about Ross wanting him to marry 'some sensible, practical, plain, middle-aged boy', and it closes 'So you see there are difficulties' - the joke is on Wilde and on the idea of his remarrying. Second, 'practically engaged' is hedged in its own words, and everything in the sentence is Wilde's assertion: the fisherman's side of it is not recorded, so a mutual connection is documented only in the sense that Wilde claims one. A later check may reasonably prefer desire-expressed on those grounds; this project proposes romantic-nonsexual because the letter's plain sense is a connection already in being, and downgrading it on register alone would let a joke frame delete the content of the claim. AGE: the letter states eighteen, recorded exactly as stated per the module's sensitive-content register; no inference is drawn. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome.
relationships.date_label: Stated in a letter of 2 January 1899 from La Napoule, during Wilde's Riviera winter of 1898-99. The letter does not say when the connection began, and no later letter read returns to it.
relationships.summary: Writing to Robert Ross from La Napoule on 2 January 1899, Wilde deflected the idea of a second marriage by announcing that he was 'practically engaged' to a local fisherman, whom he called of extraordinary beauty and whose age he gave as eighteen. The man is unnamed and appears nowhere else in the correspondence read; the sentence is at once the only evidence for the connection and a joke at the expense of Wilde's own marriageability.

sources.quote: As regards my marrying again, I am quite sure that you will want me to marry this time some sensible, practical, plain, middle-aged boy, and I don't like the idea at all. Besides I am practically engaged to a fisherman of extraordinary beauty, age eighteen. So you see there are difficulties.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 2 January 1899, Napoule - the closing run of a long letter whose earlier paragraphs cover Harold Mellor's daily bicycle visits and the Nice theatre trip.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's statement that he is practically engaged to an unnamed Napoule fisherman, with the age the letter gives, in its own comic frame
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1162, printed folio 1116 confirmed at foot of the rendered page, read as a page image 2026-08-03; transcription and provenance carried forward unchanged (dossiers/EXILE-COMPANIONS_dossier.md M3/T2).

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The record is one sentence of physical description of a man who served Wilde drinks, and the sentence's own point is that he is not a substitute for someone else: 'A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick, occasionally serves me drinks at the Café d'Egypte, but he does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy.' No approach, no meeting outside the café, no outcome. desire-expressed with outcome 'unknown' is proposed because admiration is what the page records and that class is the README's marked, hidden-by-default lead pool; romantic-nonsexual would assert a connection the sentence actively denies, and documented-sexual has nothing behind it. Candour about the bar: with André, this is the thinnest item in the tier, and it is thin in a particular way - the noticing is real and physical, but the man is present in the sentence as a comparison, not as an object of pursuit. A later check may reasonably prefer to keep him as a bio record with no edge; that would not be an unreasonable read of this page. The reading offered here is this project's, not a scholarly source's. EVIDENTIARY CAVEAT, from the editors' footnote on the same page: this letter survives only as text printed in W. T. Spencer's Forty Years in my Bookshop (1923), corrected and supplemented from a 1928 auction catalogue, and it is incomplete - so unlike the rest of this tier the words are not carried by a manuscript. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a correspondent. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and this man's own view of the encounter does not exist anywhere.
relationships.date_label: Stated in a letter postmarked 2 September 1900 from Paris, in Wilde's last months. The letter gives no date for when the café acquaintance began; the single-month span is the date of the evidence, not a claim about duration.
relationships.summary: Writing to Leonard Smithers from Paris in September 1900, Wilde said he missed the Neapolitans who had gone home, and noted that a slim brown Egyptian who occasionally served him drinks at the Café d'Egypte was no consolation for the loss. That sentence is the whole of the record: no name, no age, no meeting outside the café, and no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read.

sources.quote: Is there any chance of your being in Paris? My dear Neapolitans have returned to Naples and I miss that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb. A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick, occasionally serves me drinks at the Café d'Egypte, but he does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris - the third paragraph, between a note on Smithers's creditors and a paragraph on the publication of Salomé. The 'brown faun' and 'wanton sylvan boy of Italy' are one of the departed Neapolitans, a different man from the Egyptian.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's description of the Café d'Egypte waiter and his statement that the man is no consolation for the departed Neapolitan; no outcome recorded

relationships.certainty_reasoning: At Taylor's trial (21 May 1895) the jury convicted him of committing an act of gross indecency — counts 8 and 9, the first concerning Charles Parker, the second William (the Solicitor-General named the counts; the clerk's first question as printed does not repeat Charles's name). Charles Parker's own testimony includes sleeping at Taylor's with his brother and, per Hyde's editorial bracket, 'positive evidence as to the commission of acts of gross indecency at Taylor's rooms in Chapel Street,' though the bracket does not name the partner and Grain's cross elicited Parker's Bow Street statement that at Chapel Street Taylor 'did nothing to me, and I did nothing to him.' The conviction anchors documented-sexual; the internal contradiction is preserved here for the human reviewer.
relationships.date_label: 1893 – August 1894 (association ended at the Fitzroy Street raid)
relationships.summary: Taylor picked the Parker brothers up at the St James's Restaurant bar early in 1893 and brokered them to Wilde; Charles slept at Taylor's Little College Street rooms, stayed a fortnight at his Chapel Street rooms, and remained in Taylor's orbit until both were arrested (and discharged) in the Fitzroy Street raid of August 1894, after which Parker enlisted. Taylor was convicted of gross indecency on the count concerning Charles at his May 1895 trial.

sources.quote: In what way?—He called attention to the prostitutes who frequent Piccadilly Circus and remarked, "I can't understand sensible men wasting their money on painted trash like that. Many do, though. But there are a few who know better. Now, you could get money in a certain way easily enough if you cared to." I understood to what Taylor alluded and made a coarse reply. I am obliged to ask you what it was you actually said?—I do not like to say. You were less squeamish at the time, I dare say. I ask you for the words?—I said that if any old gentleman with money took a fancy to me, I was agreeable. I was agreeable. I was terribly hard up. What did Taylor say?—He laughed and said that men far cleverer, richer and better than I preferred things of that kind. After giving Taylor our address we parted. Did Taylor mention the prisoner Wilde?—Not at that time. Where did you first meet Wilde?—Taylor asked us to visit him (Taylor) next day at Little College Street. We went the next morning. He said he could introduce us to a man who was good for plenty of money, and that we were to meet him (Taylor) at the St. James's bar.
sources.context: Charles Parker's examination-in-chief by Mr. C. F. Gill, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895, continuing directly from the previous page, which ends 'He spoke about men.' Parker had just testified that Taylor 'came up and spoke to us' at the St James's Restaurant bar and 'was an entire stranger'.
sources.supports: How the two men met and what was proposed, in the participant's own sworn words: Taylor's approach at the bar, his proposition quoted verbatim by Parker, Parker's answer that 'if any old gentleman with money took a fancy to me, I was agreeable', and Taylor's invitation to Little College Street with the offer to introduce 'a man who was good for plenty of money'. The plainest first-hand characterization of the connection.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Charles Parker's sworn first-person testimony at the April 1895 trial describes Wilde committing sodomy at the Savoy on their first and second meetings and continued relations at Chapel Street, Park Walk, Tite Street and St James's Place. At the final trial (25 May 1895) the jury convicted Wilde on the four Charles Parker counts (1, 4, 5, 6). Parker was an admitted participant in a separate blackmail affair (£30 from Wood and Allen's extortion), which bears on credibility and is recorded in the dossier; the conviction and the repeated sworn testimony nonetheless make this the evidence class the taxonomy defines as documented-sexual.
relationships.date_label: March 1893 – mid-1894
relationships.summary: Taylor picked up the unemployed valet Charles Parker (21 at trial) and his brother at the St James's Restaurant bar early in 1893 and introduced them to Wilde over a private dinner in Rupert Street; Wilde took Charles to the Savoy that night. Parker's testimony describes sexual relations there and afterwards at Taylor's Chapel Street rooms, Parker's Park Walk lodging, Tite Street and St James's Place, with money and presents (silver cigarette case, gold ring). Wilde was convicted on all four Parker counts at the final trial.

sources.quote: Where did you first meet Wilde?—Taylor asked us to visit him (Taylor) next day at Little College Street. We went the next morning. He said he could introduce us to a man who was good for plenty of money, and that we were to meet him (Taylor) at the St. James's bar. We went the next evening to the St. James's and saw Taylor there. He took us to a restaurant in Rupert Street. I think it was the Solferino. We were shown upstairs to a private room, in which there was a dinner table laid for four. After a while Wilde came in and I was formally introduced. I had never seen him before, but I had heard of him. We dined about eight o'clock. We all four sat down to dinner, Wilde sitting on my left. Who made the fourth?—My brother, William Parker. I had promised Taylor that he should accompany me. Was the dinner a good dinner?—Yes. The table was lighted with red-shaded candles. We had plenty of champagne with our dinner and brandy and coffee afterwards. We all partook of it. Wilde paid for the dinner. Of what nature was the conversation?—General, at first. Nothing was then said as to the purposes for which we had come together. And then?—Subsequently Wilde said to me. "This is the boy for me! Will you go to the Savoy Hotel with me?" I consented, and Wilde drove me in a cab to the hotel. Only he and I went, leaving my brother and Taylor behind.
sources.context: Charles Parker's examination-in-chief by Mr. C. F. Gill, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895 - the whole account of the first meeting, from Taylor's brokering to the cab to the Savoy. The full stop after 'Wilde said to me.' is as Hyde prints it.
sources.supports: How the two men met, in the participant's own sworn words: Taylor's promise of 'a man who was good for plenty of money', the private room at the Solferino, the formal introduction, the dinner for four that Wilde paid for, and Wilde's own words as Parker reports them - 'This is the boy for me! Will you go to the Savoy Hotel with me?' The plainest first-hand characterization of the connection, chosen in preference to the act evidence on the following page.
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 230 (printed p. 192, folio in the source foot), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03; the 'said to me.' full stop and the 'boy for me!' exclamation confirmed at 2.4x zoom on the page image. No elisions.

sources.quote: Charles Parker, examined by Mr. C. F. Gill—I am 21 years of age. I have a brother, William. I have been engaged as a valet and my brother as a groom. He was an entire stranger. He passed the compliments of the day, and asked us to have a drink. We got into conversation with him. He spoke about men.

sources.quote: I had for a fortnight or three weeks a room at 50 Park Walk, Chelsea. At the time I was living at Park Walk, Wilde visited me there. I was asked by Wilde to imagine that I was a woman and that he was my lover. I had to keep up this illusion. I used to sit on his knees and he used to . . . as a man might amuse himself with a girl. Wilde insisted on this filthy make-believe being kept up. … Apart from money, did Wilde give you any presents?—Yes, he gave me a silver cigarette case and a gold ring. I don't suppose boys are different to girls in acquiring presents from them who are fond of them. You pawned the cigarette case and the ring?—Yes.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: William Parker's sworn testimony: the brothers slept with Taylor in the same bed at Little College Street, and Hyde's editorial bracket records that the witness 'described an attempt made by Taylor to commit sodomy.' At Taylor's trial the jury convicted him of 'an act of gross indecency with William Parker' (count 9). The printed testimony describes an attempt while the conviction is for a committed act of gross indecency — the reviewer should note the gap; the conviction plus first-person testimony carries the class.
relationships.date_label: 1893 (brief: two visits to Little College Street, then William left for country work)
relationships.summary: William Parker, a groom, attended the Kettner's-side dinner at which Taylor presented his brother to Wilde ('Your brother is lucky. Oscar does not care what he pays if he fancies a chap'), went twice to Little College Street, and on one night shared Taylor's bed with his brother, where his testimony describes an attempted sodomy by Taylor. He understood from the outset that the brothers 'were to be treated as women, and that [they] were to have money for it.' Taylor was convicted of gross indecency with him in May 1895.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Wilde records admiration and nothing further: a description ('a little Italian, Pietro, like a young St John') followed by a declaration in the impersonal conditional ('One would have followed him into the desert'). No approach, no second meeting and no outcome are recorded, which is exactly the desire-expressed shape - direction 'wilde', outcome 'unknown'. This clears the README bar more comfortably than the André clause beside it: a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis still reads a man saying he would have followed a beautiful young man anywhere, which is a statement about wanting to be near him and not merely a note that he was good-looking. The reading is nonetheless this project's; no scholarly source was consulted. Against a stronger class: romantic-nonsexual would assert a mutual connection the letter does not document - the affect on the page is entirely Wilde's, and Pietro is grammatically the object throughout - and there is no first-person statement of sexual relations for documented-sexual. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and Pietro's own view of the meeting is not recorded anywhere.
relationships.date_label: Met on a three-day trip to Nice with Harold Mellor, reported in a letter the editors date Thursday [? 12 January 1899] from Napoule.
relationships.summary: On a three-day excursion from Napoule to Nice with Harold Mellor in January 1899, Wilde met a young Italian named Pietro and wrote to Robert Ross that he was 'like a young St John' and that 'One would have followed him into the desert'. It is the stronger of the two Nice notices - a declaration rather than a description - but it is still only a notice: no surname, no age, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read, and nothing recorded of what followed.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Proposed on the primary record read in the source. FACTS FIRST: the editors state that four Wilde-to-Pollitt letters survive and that Wilde misspelt his name in all four (p. 1120 n. 2); no letter from Pollitt to Wilde is printed in this edition, so only one side of the exchange exists in the record. The two men appear never to have met during the correspondence: on 3 December 1898 Wilde takes the colour of Pollitt's hair on Ada Leverson's authority and says of a photograph 'not a bit like you, I am sure' (pp. 1106-07), and on 3 January 1899, having received two dissimilar photographs, he is still asking their mutual publisher Leonard Smithers 'What is he like?' (p. 1117). DIRECTION: Wilde's, and the anchor is his first letter - the request for a photograph is made by Wilde, unprompted, on 26 November 1898 (p. 1103), before any photograph is sent. This CORRECTS the earlier record dossier's reading of the 3 December letter as evidence that the photograph traffic was Pollitt-initiated. Across the four letters Wilde requests a photograph, thanks Pollitt for further ones and comments on his appearance in them, invites him to Paris while steering him away from his own hotel, and asks him to write. OUTCOME: unknown - Pollitt answered, sent at least four photographs, signed himself 'Jerome', kept the letters (now MS Princeton) and accepted inscribed presentation copies of the French Ballad of Reading Gaol and The Importance of Being Earnest, which is real reciprocity of a kind; but with no Pollitt text in evidence nothing shows what he understood himself to be answering, and no meeting is recorded. THE COUNTERVAILING READ, which the editor should weigh: the README warns that Wilde's epistolary extravagance is not by itself an edge, and the ANNOTATIONS-TRIAGE pass judged Pollitt 'context-engagement-worthy' rather than edge-worthy on exactly that ground. What lifts this above the ordinary Wilde flourish is narrow and should be named as such: a sustained request-and-comment pattern about a stranger's body, carried across the whole of a four-letter correspondence with a man he had never seen. If that reads to Lovelle as connoisseurship rather than desire, the correct disposition is no edge and a context engagement on wilde instead. desire-expressed edges are hidden by default on the map, so this sits in the lead pool, not the documented web.
relationships.date_label: Four surviving letters, 26 November 1898 to 19 January 1899, all from Wilde in exile (Hotel d'Alsace, Paris, then Hotel des Bains, Napoule): [postmark 26 November 1898] p. 1103; 3 December 1898 pp. 1106-07; [postmark of receipt 31 December 1898] pp. 1115-16; [postmark 19 January 1899] p. 1120. The General Index also lists an unannotated mention at printed 1103. No meeting is recorded at any point.
relationships.summary: Between November 1898 and January 1899 Wilde wrote four surviving letters to Herbert Charles Pollitt - 'Jerome' to his friends, a Kendal-born Cambridge man who had danced ballet as an amateur undergraduate and collected Beardsley drawings from Wilde's own publisher. Wilde opened the correspondence by asking outright for a photograph of him; Pollitt sent two, then more, and Wilde spent much of the remaining three letters comparing them, preferring the one in the Norfolk suit, dismissing a Hollyer portrait as unlike him, and pronouncing a later one in a Coan robe - the editors gloss the word as transparent - most becoming. He carried the Norfolk-suit photograph with him to the Riviera and told Pollitt he looked for him daily. The two never met: as late as January 1899, holding two photographs that did not resemble each other, Wilde was reduced to asking Leonard Smithers what Pollitt was actually like. In the last of the letters Wilde teased him about the spelling of his own name; the editors note drily that it was Wilde who had it wrong, in all four.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Pollitt, Thank you so much for the two photographs you have so kindly sent me. I like the little one, in the Norfolk suit, best: it looks young and nice: the other, the one by Hollyer, looks to me like the portrait of an Oxford Dean – troubled and affected and ineffectual: not a bit like you, I am sure. Mrs Leverson, a recognised authority for the colour of young men's hair, assured me you were quite golden, and I have always thought of you as a sort of gilt sunbeam masquerading in clothes, but, no doubt, you are Protean, and have many forms. When you come to Paris pray be golden entirely, and leave your more serious aspect in charge of Smithers, who needs, indeed, some stern monitor for his manner of living.
sources.context: Wilde to H. C. Pollitt, 3 December 1898, Paris - the opening of the letter, answering two photographs Pollitt had sent.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Created at the editor's direction (2026-08-03), overruling the research pass's null finding, which is preserved in full in LEWES-HOUSE_dossier.md. The romantic reading rests on counter-texture rather than on any romantic statement: Marshall regarded Prichard and Harding as 'rivals for Ned's affection'; Warren's own autobiographical fragment reads disappointment in Prichard at not being able to take 'Johnny's place'; Sox lists Prichard among the men Warren loved and 'wanted to possess' (p. 129, transcription pending); and Warren's surviving salutation to him is the pet-name 'Dear Ducky' (p. 174, text-layer, unrendered). Against it stands Sox's own class-deciding sentence, which is filial and discipular, and his gloss of the rivalry as positional competition over the secretaryship. Hence alleged, with the dispute stated.

relationships.summary: Matthew Stewart Prichard joined Lewes House as Warren's second secretary in the early 1890s and became, in Sox's judgement, the member of the brotherhood closest to Warren's own aestheticism. Whether the bond was romantic or filial-discipular is exactly what the sources leave contested: Warren's household read the two as rivals for his affection, while Sox describes Warren as a father-figure to him.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The evidence is one sentence naming him as one of Wilde's 'two special friends' at Napoule, and calling both 'quite perfect, except that they can read and write', immediately after Wilde has characterised the local fisher-folk as having 'beautiful eyes, crisp hair of a hyacinth colour, and no morals: an ideal race'. Against the README bar: the erotic register is supplied by Wilde himself in the preceding clause - 'no morals' is his own flag of sexual availability - and a reader who does not hold the coding hypothesis still reads a man praising the amorality of a population and then naming his two favourites within it, with literacy as their only flaw. That reading is this project's; no scholarly source was consulted. romantic-nonsexual was weighed and rejected as sharpening: the only mutuality on the page is the word 'friends', which is not documented courtship, and that class displays on the map as 'Romantic' - a claim the sentence does not carry. documented-sexual is unavailable: there is no first-person statement of sexual relations. desire-expressed with outcome 'unknown' is therefore proposed, which is also the class the README designs as a marked, hidden-by-default lead pool - the right home for an item of exactly this weight. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a correspondent. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and Raphael's own account of the acquaintance does not exist.
relationships.date_label: Stated in a letter the editors date [Circa 28 December 1898] from the Hôtel des Bains, Napoule. The letter does not say when the friendship began and no later letter read returns to it; the single-month span is the date of the evidence, not a claim about duration.
relationships.summary: Writing to Laurence Housman from the Riviera at the end of December 1898, Wilde praised the Napoule fisher-folk as an ideal race with no morals and named two of them as his special friends: Raphael and Fortuné, 'both quite perfect, except that they can read and write'. That sentence is the whole of the record for him - no surname, no age, no occupation stated, no second mention anywhere in the correspondence read.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Both men's own testimony underlies the claim, which is the README's self-reported test. The single most explicit surviving characterisation of the partnership by either participant is Ricketts's, written to John Gray in late 1929 and read at the page in Delaney p. 389: the trial of Shannon's injury "is small compared to the forty years of perfect companionship I have enjoyed". Around it sits a body of participant material: Ricketts writing to Shannon from abroad, Shannon's 1898 diary entry with Ricketts's note added to it, and Ricketts's own letters from inside the sickroom of 1929. Matt Cook's chapter on their households is built on the same letters, journals and diary, and Cook states the point outright - the bond "was articulated by the men themselves and by their circle of friends". Note what this class does NOT assert. Cook records that neither man described himself as homosexual, Uranian or inverted, that neither alluded to sex between them, and that Ricketts's biographer J. G. P. Delaney reads Shannon as basically heterosexual on the strength of his affairs with women and his more-than-once contemplated marriage; Cook's own position is that "Even if this couple did not have a sexual relationship (which is possible), that should not detract from the strength of their connection and intimacy". The record here follows the README and declines to adjudicate sexual acts in either direction: what is evidenced, in the participants' own words, is a shared life of some forty-five years in which they never lived apart. Corroborated independently by Wilde's editors, who in 2000 print flatly that Ricketts "lived for many years with Charles Hazlewood Shannon". A candidate for uncorroborated it is not; a candidate for second-hand it would be only if the participants' papers were set aside.
relationships.date_label: met 1882 at the City and Guilds Technical Art School, Lambeth; shared every home from 1886 until Ricketts's death on 7 October 1931; Shannon, left incapacitated by a fall in 1929, survived him until 1937
relationships.summary: Charles Ricketts and Charles Shannon met as students in Lambeth in 1882, when Ricketts was sixteen and Shannon nineteen, and from 1886 shared every house they lived in: Kennington Park Road, Whistler's old house in The Vale in Chelsea, Beaufort Street, Spring Terrace in Richmond, a studio-flat at Lansdowne House in Kensington, Townshend House by Regent's Park, and Chilham Keep in Kent. They ran the Dial together from 1889 to 1897, ran the Vale Press, built one art collection between them, and were treated by their friends - Wilde, who nicknamed them Orchid and Marigold, and "Michael Field", who asked them to furnish a home for their marriage - as a pair. Shannon had affairs with women and more than once considered marrying; Ricketts had relationships with men. Neither man ever wrote down what the two of them were to each other in the vocabulary of sexual identity, and the surviving record of the partnership is domestic, financial and epistolary rather than confessional. After Shannon's crippling fall in 1929 Ricketts nursed him and wrote that the trial was "small compared to the forty years of perfect companionship I have enjoyed". Ricketts died in 1931; their collection went to the Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge.

sources.quote: I realise that, viewed as a whole, this trial is small compared to the forty years of perfect companionship I have enjoyed.
sources.context: Ricketts to John Gray - by then Father John Gray, the priest in Edinburgh, who is on this map in his own right - written in late 1929, in the months after Shannon's fall. Delaney carries it inside his own sentence ("Earlier, to John Gray, Ricketts had written"); the words recorded here are Ricketts's alone, and the enclosing single quotation marks are Delaney's. His endnote 55 is composite and reads "CR to M. Davis, Sun., 30 [?Sept. 1930]; CR to Fr. J. Gray [late 1929]" - the second is this letter. **The letter is unpublished**: it is not in Ricketts's Self-Portrait (1939) and survives only through Delaney. Delaney corrects the arithmetic in the next sentence - "Those forty-six years had in fact, though, been bought at a price". Cook 2014 p. 52 quotes the same line, citing Delaney 389, and prints "I realize"; the page reads "realise".
sources.supports: Ricketts, in his own words, naming the relationship as forty years of companionship - the class-deciding participant testimony, now read at the page of the book that carries it rather than through a historian's quotation of it.

sources.quote: As I grow older, doubtless this will increase. I now view old Vale work with a sort of affection, and the past seems flooded with sunlight, though I was then poor and talentless but young, and youth is a great virtue!

Its subject is the Vale and Dial days: the sentence before reads "I grow warm and excited in talk about the Vale and Dial days, and Shannon's visits to Madox Brown, Watts, and Whistler". ! Cook 2014 p. 52 pairs this fragment with the 'forty years of perfect companionship' line as though both were written after the accident; they are seven years and two correspondents apart.

sources.quote: Ricketts was nostalgic ('I now view old Vale work with a sort of affection, and the past seems flooded with sunlight') but also resigned: 'I realize that, viewed as a whole, this trial is small compared to the forty years of perfect companionship I have enjoyed.'
sources.context: Matt Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 1, in his account of the period after Shannon's 1929 fall left him brain-damaged. Both phrases inside the single quotation marks are Ricketts's own; Cook's endnotes 150 and 151 carry the citations. **! The pairing compresses seven years and two correspondents.** "Flooded with sunlight" is from a letter to Gordon Bottomley of 16 September 1922, about the Vale and Dial days, printed in Ricketts's Self-Portrait at p. 342. "Forty years of perfect companionship" is from a letter to John Gray of late 1929, unpublished, surviving only in Delaney p. 389 - where the page reads "realise", not Cook's "realize". Both letters are now recorded here from their own sources. This entry is kept because Cook's framing is itself the reason the two were read as one moment, and because the reading is a historian's and should be visible as one.
sources.supports: A historian's reading of the partnership's last years - retained alongside the two underlying letters so that the compression is visible in the record rather than inherited from it.

sources.quote: Ricketts wrote romantically from Florence: 'Dear Old Chap [...] At each meal time they plonk down a plate of strawberries which make me think of you – no, this is not quite accurate. I really think of the strawberries. Only when they are done, "I think of thee."'
sources.context: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 1, in a run of quotations from the two men's letters and diaries. The bracketed ellipsis is Cook's, not ours. "I think of thee" is a quotation-within-the-quotation in Ricketts's letter. The addressee is Shannon. **! Cook's transcription diverges from the printed letter.** Self-Portrait p. 96 (Ricketts to Shannon, 1903, from Vienna) reads "At each meal they plank down a plate of strawberries which makes me think of you" - "plank", not "plonk"; "makes", not "make"; and no "meal time". "Old Chap" stands in the sign-off ("Yours, Old Chap, C. R."), not the salutation, so Cook's bracketed ellipsis is carrying a move from the foot of the letter to its head. Confirmed against HathiTrust uc1.$b73973 on 2026-08-04: "plank down a plate" returns scan #126 = printed p. 96; "plonk down a plate" returns no results.

sources.quote: Both men talk in the plural: 'Captain Brinkley's sale. One of the greatest hauls of our lives', wrote Shannon in his diary in 1898; Ricketts added a note – an intimate act in itself – that 'both our banking accounts vanished in this sale'.
sources.context: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 1. The rare instance of Shannon's own voice on the partnership: his diary, and Ricketts writing into it. The same page carries Shannon writing to Ricketts in 1900 ('Remember my instructions about Calais … and mind you arm yourself with port'). **! Cook's transcription diverges**, and the underlying volume corroborates his attribution. Self-Portrait p. 22 reads "Nov. 18, 1898. Captain Brinkley Sale. One of the great hauls of our lives" - not "Brinkley's sale", not "greatest" - and Ricketts's addition is headed "Later note". The volume's own editorial footnote on that page independently confirms whose diary it is: "This entry (actually in Shannon's diary) is the first relating to the Ricketts and Shannon collection." The same footnote gives the income figure Cook quotes at p. 33 - their combined incomes "had rarely exceeded a thousand a year, and were seldom half this" - and adds that the collection was valued for probate at £36,203 and went to the National Gallery, the British Museum and the Fitzwilliam.
sources.supports: Both participants, in their own hands, treating money, purchases and life as jointly held.

sources.quote: Overall, this meant that in more than 40 years together – and between the housemates and the servants – the pair never lived alone. … Neither Shannon nor Ricketts described himself as homosexual, Uranian or inverted, nor did they allude to the sex they might have had together. Ricketts playfully refused to answer the questions of classicist John Addington Symonds on the subject, though in relaying the anecdote down the years he indicated an ease and a certain mischievousness about it. Instead, Shannon and Ricketts' bond and relationship was articulated by the men themselves and by their circle of friends in terms of their co-residence, their emotional, practical and aesthetic investment in their homes, their vast collection of art and antiques, and the artistic and design work that was closely identified with the places where they lived
sources.context: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 1, running from printed p. 33 across the page break to p. 34. The elision drops one sentence about middle-class privacy after World War II. Two things at once: the record of the partnership is the participants' own ("articulated by the men themselves"), and it is not a record of sexual identity or sexual acts, because neither man produced one.
sources.supports: The classification warrant - the men themselves are the source - together with the explicit limit of what survives.

sources.quote: Shannon had affairs with women and contemplated marriage on more than one occasion, giving Rickett's biographer J.G.P. Delaney cause to suggest that he was basically heterosexual. He makes sense of Shannon's (apparent) 'sacrifice' of the 'ordinary joys that his life with Ricketts denied him' through their joint and home-based passion for art and collecting. This does indeed help in understanding some of what energised and underpinned Shannon and Ricketts' relationship, but Delaney's fixing of Shannon and Ricketts' sexuality (as heterosexual and homosexual respectively) does scant justice to the intensity of their bond, or to how they and others perceived it. Even if this couple did not have a sexual relationship (which is possible), that should not detract from the strength of their connection and intimacy.
sources.context: Cook, Queer Domesticities (2014), ch. 1, engaging Ricketts's biographer J. G. P. Delaney (Charles Ricketts: A Biography, 1990). "Rickett's" is the printed spelling. This is the scholarship's own refusal to settle the sexual question, and the reason this record does not either.
sources.supports: That the sexual character of the partnership is disputed among specialists and unsettled - and that the connection itself is not.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 47 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-03; printed folio 34 confirmed on the image. Superscript endnote markers 30, 31 omitted as typography.

sources.quote: Charles De Sousy Ricketts (1866–1931), artist, writer, book and stage designer, lived for many years with Charles Hazlewood Shannon (1863–1937), first in a house (which had belonged to Whistler) in a Chelsea cul-de-sac called The Vale. … Together they ran a privately printed magazine called the Dial from 1889 to 1897. They sent a copy of the first issue (the British Library copy is stamped 21 August 1889) to Wilde, and this brought about their first meeting with him.
sources.context: Holland and Hart-Davis's identifying footnote (note 3) to Wilde's letter to W. Graham Robertson, [? August 1889], the letter in which Wilde reports that Ricketts "seems very cultivated and interesting". The note runs from printed p. 410 onto p. 411. The elision drops the two men's Royal Academy elections and the list of their designs for Wilde's books. This is the main-particulars note for both men in the Wilde apparatus, and it is independent of the Ricketts scholarship.
sources.supports: Both men's dates and the shared household, stated as plain fact by Wilde's editors; and the date the pair entered Wilde's circle.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pp. 432-433 read as rendered page images 2026-08-03; printed folios 410 and 411 confirmed on the images (early offset +22). En-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: They had met at the City and Guilds Technical Art School in Lambeth when Ricketts was just sixteen and Shannon nineteen. They fell in love, and their relationship was to last the best part of half a century.
sources.context: Neil McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008 edn), on Wilde's first acquaintance with the pair in late August 1889. McKenna states the romance flatly and without a source note attached to the sentence; he is a non-participant, so this passage is second-hand corroboration, not the basis of the class. The same page records that "Max Beerbohm was later to dub them 'the ladies of the Vale'".
sources.supports: A biographer's plain assertion that the two fell in love - the strongest such statement located so far, and the weakest kind of evidence in this record.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 190 read as a rendered page image 2026-08-03; no printed folio or running head on the page (ebook conversion), so the locator is the PDF page per the works.json instruction. The conversion renders opening single quotes as backticks; normalised to typographic quotation marks.

sources.quote: Also, they never lived apart. The unconventional relationship was speculated about, but even during the homophobic panic surrounding the Wilde trial, the discretion of their private lives and a lack of interest in sexually controversial themes in their art saved them from notoriety. It seems significant that the Uranian poet and activist John Addington Symonds (1840–1893) in the mid-Nineties was convinced of the fact that they were an item (Delaney 25). Diaries and letters have revealed that Ricketts was certainly homosexual, and that Shannon had affairs with female sitters. Recent scholarship on their shared involvement with the queer culture of their time may confirm the rumours of their being a romantic couple, if not an exclusive one (Cook passim).
sources.context: Koenraad Claes's Y90s biography of Shannon (2021), body paragraph 12. Claes names the evidence base - "Diaries and letters" - and hedges the romantic reading ("may confirm the rumours"), which is why the class here rests on the participants' papers rather than on the characterisation. Note the internal problem in Claes's own sentence: Symonds died in 1893, so "the mid-Nineties" cannot be right; the underlying citation is Delaney p. 25, unconsulted.
sources.supports: That the partnership was legible to contemporaries as a couple, and that the surviving evidence is the two men's own diaries and letters.
sources.provenance: https://1890s.ca/shannon_bio/ fetched (curl) and read in full 2026-08-03; quote sliced from the downloaded HTML, then whitespace artifacts introduced by stripping inline markup normalized to the printed reading. Paragraph number counts body paragraphs from the first, including the two block quotations.

sources.quote: MY DEAR BOY, Shannon met with a bad accident a week ago and remained unconscious for four days and nights in the hands of three male nurses and two doctors. This morning, at noon, Sir Farquhar Buzzard declared him out of danger, though Shannon is still only semi-conscious and recognizes no one. He slipped on the stairs hanging a picture, struck his temple, and fell head foremost. He is in my studio. … I did not undress or go to bed for four days and nights, and lived in a strange blending of the Past, Present, and Future.
sources.context: Ricketts to Cecil Lewis, Townshend House, "Wednesday night, 1 a.m.", January 1929 - the week after Shannon slipped from a ladder hanging a picture and struck his temple. Lewis is the editor of this volume. The running head reads "1929] Byron : Shannon's accident". Shannon never fully recovered; Ricketts died in 1931. The elision drops one sentence about the medical prognosis.
sources.supports: Ricketts's own words about Shannon and their household, at first hand rather than through a historian's quotation.

sources.quote: Then, a little more than a fortnight ago, Shannon met with a serious accident.... Please do not write to express sympathy; this is unnecessary and painful to both, and well-meaning friends have added to the sadness of the situation. … Should all go well, and should we meet again, do not mention any of these facts to Shannon; he will probably never be told how dangerous his case has been. For the moment, my dear friend, don't ask me to write more. I am being well cared for, but have gone through a great deal during these tragic days.
sources.context: Ricketts to R. N. R. Holst, Townshend House, 29 January 1929 - the Dutch artist Richard Roland Holst. sources.quote: There are quite a few websites posting information on Charles Ricketts and Charles Shannon as a gay couple, which, historically and factually, poses a few problems of interpretation. … Shannon may have been gay in his early years, but eventually turned out to be a heterosexual, and his lithographs testify of that. … Presumption, projection, and suggestion may blossom as there is a lack of evidence.
sources.context: The dissent, from the co-editor of the forthcoming Brill Collected Letters and the leading Ricketts scholar. Recorded because it is the strongest published objection to reading the pair as a couple. Weigh it accordingly: the post cites no sources, and offers Shannon's lithographs as evidence of his sexuality.
sources.supports: A named scholarly objection to the couple reading - kept so the dissent is visible in the record rather than only the affirming sources.
sources.provenance: https://charlesricketts.blogspot.com/2017/10/325-gay-pride.html retrieved 2026-08-04 with a verbatim-quotation request; the three sentences are separated in the post and the ellipses mark that separation.

null_findings.finding: The "forty years of perfect companionship" line is NOT in Ricketts's Self-Portrait (1939). Searched across two independent digitisations: the repo per-leaf OCR of the NYPL copy (486 leaves) and HathiTrust uc1.$b73973, the University of California copy (488 scans), whose search-only index returns no results for "perfect companionship". A control phrase from the same region of the book, "Farquhar Buzzard", returns scan #449 = printed p. 409, so the index works and the negative is real. The line is from an unpublished letter to John Gray of late 1929, which Cook 2014 p. 52 cites to Delaney p. 389; it is now recorded from Delaney, read at the page. Do not hunt it in Self-Portrait again.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Against the README bar - that the desire be legible as desire to a reader who does not already hold the coding hypothesis - this project reads this as clearing it, on the strength of the four-sentence run itself: a named young man, a physical description ('He has fair hair, and is always in dark blue'), the fact that Wilde has written ahead to arrange the meeting ('I have written to him'), and then, immediately, an explicit statement of longing set against virginity - 'After the chill virginity of Swiss Alps and snow, I long for the red flowers of life that stain the feet of summer in Italy.' A reader without the hypothesis reads an older man looking forward to a young man he has written to. What such a reader would not independently supply is the sexual character, and that is not proposed here. Whose reading: the agent's, as transcriber; no scholarly source was consulted, and the editors' index classing 'Rolla, Edoardo (boy)' (triage mirror, unverified in the source) is an editorial classing, not a reading of desire. Outcome is genuinely unknown rather than unreciprocated: nothing in the pages read says whether the meeting happened.
relationships.date_label: Anticipated meeting at Genoa, first week of April 1899. The letter is dated '[early April 1899]' by the editors; the two Ross postcards on the same printed page are postmarked 7 April 1899 from Santa Margherita.
relationships.summary: Leaving Mellor's villa at Gland at the start of April 1899, Wilde wrote to Robert Ross that he hoped to find a young seaman named Edoardo Rolla waiting for him at Genoa, having written ahead to him, and set the hope beside a statement of longing for Italy after the Swiss months. It is an approach on the page and nothing more: no letter read records whether the two met, and Rolla appears nowhere else in the correspondence consulted.

sources.quote: I hope to find at Genoa, waiting for me, a young lad, by name Edoardo Rolla, one of the sea-farers. He has fair hair, and is always in dark blue. I have written to him. After the chill virginity of Swiss Alps and snow, I long for the red flowers of life that stain the feet of summer in Italy. Ever yours O. W.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [early April 1899], Gland - the final paragraph of the letter announcing his departure for Genoa, where he had taken a room at the Albergo di Firenze on the quay.
sources.supports: The approach itself: a named young man written to in advance, described, and awaited, with Wilde's longing stated in the same breath; no outcome recorded
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1186, printed folio 1140 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The longest documented relationship of Ross's life - roughly a decade, 1903 to autumn 1913 - and the fullest treatment of it is Fryer's, in his own narrating voice. No words of either participant about the other have been read for this record: what survives here is a biographer's account plus, at the 1914 trial, hostile witnesses reporting what they saw and heard. Hence second-hand. Fryer states the relationship plainly and repeatedly rather than hedging it, so the class reflects who is talking, not any doubt that it happened. Margery Ross, Friend of Friends (1952), is Fryer's main source for Ross's own voice and is the place to look for first-hand material.
relationships.date_label: early 1903 - autumn 1913
relationships.summary: Ross met Smith early in 1903, when Smith was an eighteen-year-old clerk. Smith became his secretary - a post that doubled as cover - and moved into 15 Vicarage Gardens in 1906 despite his family's objections. The relationship lasted about a decade, ending in the autumn of 1913, months before Douglas named Smith in the 1914 plea of justification.

sources.quote: And early in 1903, he met a young man with whom he entered into a relationship quite unlike his other brief encounters with boys.   Frederick (Freddie) Smith was an attractive, unpretentious, eighteen-year-old clerk; not someone of Robbie's class or intellectual capacity, but nonetheless keen to learn and improve himself.
sources.context: Fryer opening the Freddie Smith thread. He continues on the same page: 'The fact that Robbie was almost twice his age does not seem to have particularly bothered either of them'. Ages stated exactly as Fryer states them (README register rule).
sources.supports: Start of the relationship, the ages, and Fryer's framing of it as unlike Ross's other encounters.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 199 of Fryer_2000_Robbie-Ross, printed folio 177 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Offset is +22 in this half of the scan.

sources.quote: Astonishingly, Robbie reacted to this latest example of Edwardian England's homophobia by defiantly inviting his young secretary-companion Freddie Smith to move in with him in a charming house, on which he had taken a short lease, at 15 Vicarage Gardens, Kensington, just a few minutes walk from his previous rooms in Hornton Street.
sources.context: 1906, in the paragraph immediately after Christopher Millard's arrest and three-month sentence for gross indecency. The next sentences record the family's horror and their deputing of Ross's nephew Edward Jones to remonstrate.
sources.supports: Documented cohabitation, and the pivot out of the Adey household into a household with Smith.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 214, printed folio 192 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Though he never flaunted his homosexuality in public, Robbie saw no reason to be ashamed of his relationship with Freddie, who had not yet turned twenty.   Moreover, he was becoming increasingly proud of his young protege, who had developed into a talented amateur actor.   He used his second name Stanley on stage.   Shamelessly, Robbie took advantage of his journalistic outlets to promote his lover's acting career
sources.context: c. 1906. Ross's own Academy review of Smith's performance is block-quoted on the same page ('rendered with marvellous skill by Mr F. Stanley Smith').
sources.supports: Fryer's flat use of 'his lover' for Smith; the age; and Ross's public unashamedness about the relationship.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 215, printed folio 193 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. The quotation stops at a clause boundary without elision marks because the remainder of the sentence names the play reviewed; no words are dropped from within the quoted span.

sources.quote: On the home front, he had decided to terminate his relationship with Freddie Smith, who had failed to give him the sort of loving support he had needed during his recent troubles.   Although he knew Freddie would feign enthusiasm at his return, he was conscious that the passion had gone out of their union, and that more disappointment and heartache would lie ahead if he did not bring things to an end.
sources.context: Autumn 1913, on Ross's journey home from Russia, reaching London on 5 October, amid the threat of action by Douglas and Crosland.
sources.supports: End of the relationship, and its decade-long span (early 1903 to autumn 1913).
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 252, printed folio 230 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Thirteen other witnesses were produced in Bosie's defence, including a young woman who had taken part in amateur dramatics with Freddie Smith.   She testified that she had seen Robbie hug Freddie and call him 'my darling'.   A priest, whom Freddie had served as an acolyte, spoke of his revulsion when he had seen Robbie's lover with make-up on his face.
sources.context: Ross's prosecution of Douglas for criminal libel, Old Bailey, opened 19 November 1914. Douglas's plea of justification (p. 237) cited 'four cases of alleged gross indecency: with Biscoe Wortham's Bruges pupil, Dansey, two decades before, Freddie Smith, Charlie Garratt and a boy called William Edwards.' H. G. Wells testified for the prosecution that he had met Smith several times at Ross's home 'and never noticed anything of the sort'.
sources.supports: The third-party attestation of the Ross-Smith relationship that survives is sworn testimony gathered by a hostile ex-friend for a prosecution - the evidentiary shape the revised taxonomy exists to record.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 260, printed folio 238 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03; the plea-of-justification sentence quoted in the context line was verified at repo PDF page 259, printed folio 237.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Proposed 'consensus', not 'documented-sexual'. The primary evidence read for this file - Wilde's letters to Ross 1888-1900 and Ross's December 1900 letters - documents a lifelong bond of the first intimacy (affectionate registers rising to 'Yours, with much love' by 1889, shared secrets, daily attendance in the final illness, the deathbed, the executorship) but contains no first-person statement of sexual relations. The sexual reading, standard across major biographers, rests on later Ross statements reported in secondary literature not yet read in the source for this project (Ellmann/McKenna verification is a standing next step). Dating tension to preserve: the biographical tradition makes Ross Wilde's first male lover from c. 1886, the year they met, but Ross himself, to Adela Schuster (14 Dec. 1900), wrote that he 'only became intimate with him when he was writing Lady Windermere' - i.e. c. 1891 - with 'long intervals when I never saw him' and no regular correspondence 'until after the downfall'. Start is the documented 1886 meeting; the onset of any sexual phase is deliberately not sharpened.
relationships.date_label: Met 1886 (Ross: 'I only met him in '86'); Ross dated the intimacy to the Lady Windermere period, c. 1891; regular correspondence only after the downfall; to Wilde's death, 30 Nov. 1900, with Ross at the bedside; literary executor thereafter.
relationships.summary: Ross met Wilde in 1886 and remained, in the editors' words, 'his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate'. The surviving correspondence opens in October 1888 ('My dear Bobbie … I shall miss you in town') and by 1889 runs to 'Yours, with much love'; Ross himself dated their intimacy to the period when Wilde was writing Lady Windermere (c. 1891). After 1895 Ross became the relationship's practical center - regular correspondent, supervisor of the De Profundis typescript at his Hornton Street lodgings, daily attendant of the final illness who fetched the priest for Wilde's deathbed reception into the Catholic Church - and he was holding Wilde's hand at the death on 30 November 1900. He buried Wilde at Bagneux in a concession hired in his own name, moved the remains to Père Lachaise in 1909, and administered the literary estate.

sources.quote: No other friend have I now in this beautiful world. I want no other. … My poem should have run, 'When I came out of prison you met me with garments, with spices, with wise counsel. You met me with love.' Not others did it, but you.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, [28 May 1897], Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer - his first days out of prison, alone for the first time. Editors' n. 2 gives the lines in their verse form and records that they were intended as a second dedication to The Ballad of Reading Gaol and removed at proof stage.
sources.supports: Wilde naming what Ross was to him, in his own words: the one friend left to him, and the one who met him at his release with love rather than counsel - the most explicit first-hand characterization of the bond in the correspondence read
sources.provenance: Repo PDF pages 908-909, printed folios 858 and 859 confirmed on the rendered pages, read as page images 2026-08-03. The quoted run spans the page-turn; the elision drops the passage on Wilde fearing he harms Ross, the naming of him as St Robert of Phillimore, and the sentence introducing the misquoted lines. 'you' is italicised in the printed text of the poem lines.

sources.quote: Robert Baldwin Ross (1869–1918) was a Canadian. … He first met Wilde in 1886 and remained his most faithful friend until Wilde's death when he became the literary executor to the estate.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, biographical footnote on Ross, hung on Wilde's first surviving letter to him (c. 13 October 1888); the note asserts friendship and executorship only, no sexual claim
sources.supports: Frame of the bond: met 1886; 'most faithful friend' to Wilde's death; literary executor
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 382, printed folio 360 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03 (ROSS_dossier.md Passage 2). Genealogical detail between the two quoted sentences elided; paraphrase in dossier.

sources.quote: And oh! Bobbie, let us have an evening together. What ages since we had a talk! Yours, with much love OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Ross, [Late July 1889], from Kreuznach; close of the letter, valediction and signature as printed
sources.supports: Warmest register of the early correspondence: 'Yours, with much love' (1889)
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 431, printed folio 409 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03 (ROSS_dossier.md Passage 6; this is the contiguous close of the letter, transcribed without elision).

sources.context: Ross to Adela Schuster, 14 December 1900, printed in the Epilogue; 'Lady Windermere' italicized in the original; Ross declining the suggestion that he become Wilde's Boswell

sources.quote: I went to the bedside and held his hand, his pulse began to flutter. He heaved a deep sigh, the only natural one I had heard since I arrived, the limbs seemed to stretch involuntarily, the breathing came fainter; he passed at 10 minutes to 2 p.m. exactly.
sources.context: Ross to More Adey, 14 December 1900, narrating Wilde's death at the Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris, on 30 November 1900; Ross and Reggie Turner were the two friends present
sources.supports: Ross at the bedside holding Wilde's hand at the moment of death - the terminal point of the lifelong bond
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1265, printed folio 1220 confirmed on rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03 (ROSS_dossier.md Passage 12; this sentence-pair is contiguous in the transcription, no internal elision).
