sources.quote: Little did Eliza Ross or Constance Wilde suspect, when they finalized this arrangement, that some time the previous year, the thirty-two-year-old Oscar and the seventeen-year-old Robbie had become lovers.
sources.context: Fryer introducing Ross's 1887 residence as the Wildes' lodger at 16 Tite Street, Chelsea. The biographer's own assertion, not a participant's words. Ages stated exactly as Fryer states them (README register rule).
sources.supports: Ross's dedicated biographer dates the start of a sexual relationship to 1886 - the traditional dating, against which Ross's own 1900 letter to Adela Schuster stands.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 32 of Fryer_2000_Robbie-Ross (docs/research/queer-history/victorian/ross/sources/), printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. NOTE the offset is not constant in this scan (+14 here, +22 after the plate section) - see the pagination box in dossiers/ROSS-FRYER_dossier.md.

sources.quote: Whatever the precise circumstances of the contact being forged, it would appear that young Robbie seduced Oscar some time in 1886, and that this was Oscar's first experience of a homosexual act.   Oscar told his friend, the journalist and wit Reggie Turner, that this was the case.   Robbie himself later confirmed it to one of Wilde's earliest biographers, Arthur Ransome.
sources.context: Same page, after Fryer dismisses Frank Harris's public-lavatory story of the first meeting. Fryer gives no note for these sentences; neither Wilde's remark to Turner nor Ross's confirmation to Ransome is quoted or sourced on the page.
sources.supports: A reported chain of PARTICIPANT testimony for the 1886 dating - Wilde told Turner, Ross told Ransome - which is the nearest thing Fryer offers to first-person evidence. It remains Fryer's report of an unsourced oral confirmation, not the participant's surviving words: a lead toward self-reported evidence rather than an instance of it.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 32, printed folio 18 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Contiguous sentences; the preceding block on the same page is quoted separately, with no elision joining them.

sources.quote: It should not be assumed, however, that Oscar and Robbie conducted a passionate, clandestine affair on the premises.   On the contrary, it is unlikely that they did, and not only for reasons of propriety.   Despite the initial seduction, and the huge bond of affection between them, neither was physically each other's 'type'.
sources.context: Fryer on the months of 1887 when Ross lodged at Tite Street. He continues that Ross 'was far more interested sexually in youths of his own age than in the rather portly, flabby, albeit fascinating Oscar Wilde.'
sources.supports: Fryer separates a single initiating episode in 1886 from a sustained affair, and denies the latter for 1887 - supplying the middle term under which the 1886 tradition and Ross's own 'only became intimate... Lady Windermere' (1900) can both be true. Fryer never cites the Schuster letter, so the reconciliation is available from him but not stated by him.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 35, printed folio 21 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: In fact, Robbie was already, at the age of nineteen, much more than a disciple and sometime lover for Oscar.   The two could talk frankly, despite the difference in their ages, and bounce ideas off each other.
sources.context: Fryer at the turn of 1888-89, Ross's first year at King's College, Cambridge. Age stated exactly as Fryer states it.
sources.supports: Fryer's summary formula for the bond - 'disciple and sometime lover'. 'Sometime' is his word, and his second signal that he does not read the relationship as a continuous affair.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 47, printed folio 33 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Robbie seems to have felt no jealousy towards John Gray.   Indeed, he was remarkably generous and understanding when it came to Oscar's other lovers.   Of course, he himself was enjoying various encounters with youths, though none at this stage held any claim to his affections, let alone to the sort of love he felt for Oscar.
sources.context: c. 1889-90, immediately before the family council that sent Ross to Edinburgh away from 'myriad temptations, including Oscar Wilde'. Fryer's own characterisation of Ross's feeling; no participant statement is quoted.
sources.supports: The asymmetry Fryer builds the life on: Ross in love with Wilde and unpossessive about Gray and Wilde's other lovers, while sexually occupied elsewhere. Bears on the ross--wilde bond and on why no jealousy edge to gray or douglas is warranted.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 56, printed folio 42 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: The sexual allegation exists only in Queensberry's plea (10 St James's Place, October 1893 - April 1894). Scarfe never testified and no indictment count concerned him. What the trial record documents on oath: Taylor introduced Scarfe to Wilde at St James's Place, Scarfe called there five or six times (the waiter Price), dined alone with Wilde, received a £4 cigarette case, and last dined with Wilde at the Avondale Hotel in February 1895; Wilde swore he 'never embraced, kissed or caressed him.' Plea-only → 'alleged' with disputed block.
relationships.date_label: late 1893 – February 1895 (acquaintance); Oct 1893 – Apr 1894 (plea allegation)
relationships.summary: Ernest Scarfe, a young valet-turned-clerk who had been to the Australian gold-diggings — meeting Lord Douglas of Hawick on the voyage out in 1893 — knew Taylor from the Knightsbridge Skating Rink and was introduced by him to Wilde at 10 St James's Place. He visited repeatedly, dined alone with Wilde, and received the customary cigarette case; the acquaintance ran to a dinner at the Avondale in February 1895. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at St James's Place; Scarfe was never called and the allegation never charged.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Wilde states the feeling himself and in plain words - 'fell in love with a Sea-God' - which puts this well over the README bar without any coding hypothesis: a reader is told, in the writer's own sentence, that he fell in love. What the page does not give is any second party to it. Nothing is recorded of the young man's response, of a meeting beyond the Naples stop, or of anything that followed; the whole notice is one clause inside a travel report. That is the textbook desire-expressed shape - a declaration, not a relationship - so direction 'wilde', outcome 'unknown'. romantic-nonsexual was weighed against didaco--wilde, which the corpus classes that way on a comparable declaration of love: the difference is that the Didaco entry also records mutual conduct ('We spent three days together'), and here there is none - the three days are the length of the stop at Naples, not of anything between them. documented-sexual is unavailable: no first-person statement of sexual relations appears. Standing caveat for this tier: the record is one-sided by nature. These men left no papers; everything known is what Wilde wrote to a friend. An unrecorded outcome is not evidence of no outcome, and the young man's own account of the encounter does not exist.
relationships.date_label: During a three-day stop at Naples on the Italian journey Wilde made with Harold Mellor in April 1900, before they reached Rome on Holy Thursday. The reporting letter is dated 16 April 1900 by the editors' heading - located in the OCR mirror, not read in the source; the editors' footnote on the page read gives Easter Day 1900 as 15 April, and Wilde dates his Vatican appearance 'yesterday'.
relationships.summary: Travelling up through Italy with Harold Mellor in April 1900, Wilde stopped three days at Naples and wrote to Robert Ross that he had fallen in love with a Sea-God, joking that the young man was for some extraordinary reason at the Regia Marina School instead of being with Triton. In the same breath he notes that most of his Naples friends are in prison. Nothing further about the young man appears in the pages read: no name, no age, no outcome.

sources.quote: At Naples we stopped three days. Most of my friends are, as you know, in prison, but I met some of nice memory, and fell in love with a Sea-God, who for some extraordinary reason is at the Regia Marina School, instead of being with Triton.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 16 April [1900], from Rome - a travel narrative running from Palermo through Naples to the Easter pilgrimage at the Vatican. 'H. M.' in the next paragraph is Harold Mellor, his travelling companion.
sources.supports: The whole of the record: Wilde's own statement that he fell in love, the young man's institution, and the absence of any recorded outcome

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Shelley's sworn testimony describes Wilde kissing and embracing him and a shared bed on two consecutive nights at the Albemarle Hotel (Feb 1892), but he repeatedly denied that completed acts occurred ('attempts at improprieties took place on two occasions'; Wilde 'never practised any actual improprieties upon' him because he 'would never allow' it). Wilde denied everything on oath. Mr Justice Wills withdrew the Shelley count for want of corroboration, treating Shelley as an accomplice on his own evidence, and the jury formally returned not guilty on it. Sexual relations are asserted by the plea and the Crown but contested by the witness's own account and the verdict — 'alleged' fits; a human reviewer may weigh the kisses/shared-bed testimony differently.

relationships.summary: Edward Shelley, a clerk at Wilde's publishers the Bodley Head, dined with Wilde at the Albemarle Hotel in February 1892; his testimony describes being kissed and embraced, objecting, and nonetheless staying the night in Wilde's bed, with 'a repetition of the previous night's performance' the next day. He received inscribed books and letters, quarrelled with Wilde at the Savoy in March 1893, and broke off the acquaintance. The count concerning him was withdrawn from the jury for lack of corroboration at the final trial.

I had been taking a lot of wine. I felt insulted, degraded, and objected vigorously. Mr. Wilde said he was sorry and that he had drunk too much wine. I stayed the night and shared his bed. Mr. Wilde saw me next day and again kissed me and there was a repetition of the previous night's performance.

I was excited, but not drunk. I resented the prisoner's acts at the time.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Wood's sworn testimony: he lived at Taylor's Little College Street rooms for about three weeks in January 1893, sleeping 'in the same room with Taylor. There was only one bed there,' and in re-examination he dated his first acts of indecency 'with any man' to going to College Street. The landlady corroborates the three-week stay. But no witness states an act with Taylor himself; no charge of indecency between them was ever put to a jury (Taylor's Wood counts were for procuring, and ended in a directed not-guilty); and Taylor dated their meeting differently (May 1892, at Atkins's rooms). Strong implication, no attestation → 'alleged'.
relationships.date_label: January 1893 (three weeks' cohabitation; acquaintance possibly from May 1892 per Taylor)
relationships.summary: Alfred Wood, an out-of-work clerk, lived at Taylor's one-bed rooms at 13 Little College Street for about three weeks in January 1893, sharing the room and — on the arithmetic of his own testimony that the rooms held 'only one bed' — the bed. He dated his first acts of indecency to going to College Street without naming a partner. Taylor said they had met earlier, in May 1892 at Atkins's rooms. The procuring-Wood counts against Taylor ended in a directed not-guilty; no count alleged acts between the two men.

disputed.disputed_by: no direct attestation by any witness; no charge concerning acts between Taylor and Wood; the counts charging Taylor with procuring Wood for Wilde ended in a directed verdict of Not Guilty (Hyde pp. 292-293)

relationships.date_label: A single evening or afternoon, Paris, late March 1900
relationships.summary: Wilde was seen in a boy's company outside a cafe behind the Madeleine by Aleck Ross, and wrote about it to Aleck's brother Robbie the same week. The encounter is known only from Wilde's own sentence, and his framing of it - 'half rough, all Hylas' - is the whole of the evidence for reading it as more than company.
relationships.certainty_reasoning: Self-reported: the only witness who writes anything down is Wilde, and he writes it in his own letter. He is not confessing to anything - the comedy of the passage is being caught, not what he was caught at - so the erotic reading rests on his own choice of words rather than on any statement of what happened. 'Hylas' is the youth Herakles loved; 'half rough' places the boy socially, a rough being a working-class young man. No act is described and none is claimed here. The class note is the point of his inclusion: he is one of the men who reached the record only because someone respectable saw them together.

sources.quote: Only an hour after I, with 'waving hands' like Tennyson's Vivien, had evolved a new evangel of morals, dear Aleck passed before the little cafe behind the Madeleine, and saw me with a beautiful boy in grey velvet - half rough, all Hylas. Alas, the eye he turned on me was not the sightless one. His smile was terrible. It was like one of Besant's novels. I really felt it very much. At luncheon I had been singularly ethical. I am always ethical at the Cafe de la Paix.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, Thursday [Late March 1900], Grand Cafe, 14 boulevard des Capucines, Paris. 'Aleck' is Ross's brother; the editors' note explains the joke - he had lost the sight of one eye in early youth, so the eye he turned on Wilde was the seeing one.
sources.supports: The encounter, in Wilde's own words, and his framing of the boy.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1223, printed folio 1177 read on the rendered page 2026-08-04. 'cafe' is italicised in the printed text; accents normalised here.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Parallel precedent is the Wilde-Ives edge (documented kiss, no sexual claim). (a) The kiss: 'The kiss of Walt Whitman is still on my lips' is transcribed from Richard Ellmann's 'Oscar Meets Walt' (NYRB, 3 Dec. 1987), read at the article page so far; Ellmann's prose attributes it as what Wilde 'would later tell George Ives' and places it at the parting of the second (early-May 1882) visit. The deeper traditional chain - Ives's diary, commonly printed in the source in McKenna 2003 and in Ellmann's 1988 biography - was NOT verified so far (both lending-only); the article's footnote text was unreachable. (b) The romantic reading is the editor's directed interpretation of a brief encounter: two documented afternoon visits in 1882, Wilde's 'There is no one in this wide great world of America whom I love and honour so much', and the reported parting kiss; no source read asserts sexual relations. (c) Whitman's side attests warm mutuality, not romance: his next-day Press account ('thee and thou' terms, the hand on his knee, 'a great big, splendid boy'), and his 1888 verdict handing Traubel the letter he had kept six years - 'both of us friends according each other a mutual respect.'
relationships.date_label: Two Camden visits, 1882: 18 Jan. (at Whitman's written invitation, taken by Stoddart) and 'early in May' (Ellmann; Stoddart absent) - the reported parting kiss attaches to the second; Wilde's letter between them postmarked 1 Mar. 1882.
relationships.summary: On his American lecture tour Wilde twice spent an afternoon with Whitman in Camden - 18 January 1882 (elderberry wine downstairs, then milk punch and two hours' talk in the third-floor 'den') and again in early May. Whitman told the Philadelphia Press next day that they were on 'thee and thou' terms, that Wilde laid his hand on his knee, and that he 'seemed to me like a great big, splendid boy'; Wilde wrote him 'Before I leave America I must see you again. There is no one in this wide great world of America whom I love and honour so much', and later told George Ives that 'The kiss of Walt Whitman is still on my lips' (per Ellmann). Whitman kept the letter, and in 1888 gave it to Traubel with the verdict: 'both of us friends according each other a mutual respect.'

sources.quote: My dear dear Walt, Swinburne has just written to me to say as follows … There! You see how you remain in our hearts, and how simply and grandly Swinburne speaks of you, knowing you to be simple and grand yourself. … Before I leave America I must see you again. There is no one in this wide great world of America whom I love and honour so much. With warm affection, and honourable admiration
sources.context: Wilde to Walt Whitman, [Postmark 1 March 1882], [Postmark Chicago]; the letter relays Swinburne's admiration of Whitman and closes with Wilde's own declaration
sources.supports: Wilde's side after the January Camden visit: love-and-honour declaration and stated intent to visit again before leaving America

sources.quote: "Wilde and I drank a bottle of wine down stairs," he continued, "and when we came up here, where we could be on 'thee and thou' terms, one of the first things I said was that I should call him 'Oscar;' 'I like that so much,' he answered, laying his hand on my knee. He seemed to me like a great big, splendid boy," said Whitman, stroking his silvery beard. "He is so frank and outspoken, and manly. I don't see why such mocking things are written of him."
sources.context: Whitman interviewed at home by the Philadelphia Press the evening of the first visit; earlier in the piece: 'we had a jolly good time … I think him genuine, honest and manly'

sources.quote: W. gave me the Wilde letter. I thought he might say more about it. He said little: only this: "It seems all straight and honest to me. I have been told a thousand times what Wilde is but I do not see why Wilde is not what he is and I am not what I am with both of us friends according each other a mutual respect. There is no parade in this note: it wears the simplest clothes—has no sunflower in its button hole—has in fact a cast of virgin simplicity, sincerity. Read it for yourself: see if the letter does not bear me out." He said nothing while I read.
sources.context: Traubel's entry for Sunday 9 September 1888: Whitman hands over Wilde's 1882 letter, kept six years; the envelope endorsed in his blue pencil 'from Oscar Wilde early in '82' (p. 288)
sources.supports: Whitman's side, six years on: he preserved the letter and framed the bond as 'both of us friends according each other a mutual respect'

sources.quote: He promised to see Whitman again, and did so early in May. This time Stoddart was not present, and the two could talk more freely. Their conversation has not survived, but their parting has. Wilde would later tell George Ives, a proselytizer for sexual deviation in the Nineties, that Whitman had made no effort to conceal his homosexuality from him, as he would do with John Addington Symonds. "The kiss of Walt Whitman," Wilde said, "is still on my lips."
sources.context: Ellmann on the second Camden visit and its parting; the passage carries his footnote marker 8, whose text is not retrievable on the article page
sources.supports: The second visit ('early in May' 1882) and the reported parting kiss, with the attribution chain as Ellmann prints it: Wilde said it later to George Ives. Deeper chain (Ives diary; in the source prints in McKenna 2003 / Ellmann 1988 bio) unverified so far - see dossier pointer.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Proposed on the primary record and the editors' apparatus, read in the source. THE DECIDING FACT IS THAT THEY NEVER MET. The editors state it flatly in the main-particulars footnote: Wilkinson invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray 'so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met' (p. 1109 n. 1). Nothing read so far contradicts it; the correspondence is epistolary from first letter to last, and the surviving record is one-sided - Wilde's letters to Wilkinson are printed here, Wilkinson's to Wilde are not. AGE, STATED AS THE RECORD STATES IT: the editors give his dates as 1881-1966 and say he 'was at this time a Radley schoolboy' (p. 1109 n. 1); Wilde, describing the correspondence to Reginald Turner on 3 January 1899, calls him 'a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen' (p. 1118). Wilde was forty-four. DIRECTION is Wilde's, and rests on documented acts rather than on tone: Wilde asks for a photograph in his first letter (p. 1109), asks again when a promised enclosure proved missing from the envelope (p. 1113), comments on the photographs when they arrive (p. 1122), reports to Turner that the boy sends them constantly (p. 1118), and asks Robert Ross to go to Radley and see him (p. 1127). The salutation and signature move over four months from 'Dear Mr Wilkinson / Sincerely yours' to 'My dear Boy / Affectionately yours' - the same 'My dear Boy' Wilde used to Douglas. OUTCOME is unknown, and cannot be otherwise: no meeting took place, no Wilkinson letter survives in this edition, and the boy's own account came fifty-four years later in Seven Friends (1953), unread here. WEIGH THIS AGAINST THE EDGE: the initiative in the whole affair was Wilkinson's, not Wilde's - he manufactured a theatrical society and, per the editors, at least one further false claim to attract Wilde's attention (p. 1127 n. 2), so the approach that started it ran the other way. The ANNOTATIONS-TRIAGE pass judged him 'context-engagement-worthy' rather than edge-worthy precisely because a correspondence between people who never met fails the usual bar. desire-expressed edges are hidden by default on the map and are a lead pool, not the documented web; if Lovelle reads this as a famous author indulging a starstruck schoolboy correspondent, the correct disposition is no edge and a context engagement on wilde. That call is his.
relationships.date_label: First surviving Wilde letter [postmark 14 December 1898] (p. 1109) to the letter of [postmark 15 July 1900] (p. 1192), four months before Wilde's death. The end date was previously pinned at March 1899, the last letter then read; the General Index leads were followed on 2026-08-04 and the correspondence runs a year and a third longer than the record showed. Wilkinson is also among the senders of funeral wreaths in Ross's post-mortem account (p. 1222).
relationships.summary: In the winter of 1898 a seventeen-year-old Radley schoolboy named Louis Wilkinson wrote to Wilde in exile, having invented an Ipswich Dramatic Society and its wish to stage The Picture of Dorian Gray in order to have a reason to write. Wilde, who was forty-four, answered, granted the imaginary society four performances, asked who was to play Dorian - he should be beautiful - and closed by asking for the boy's photograph. Over the next four months Wilde asked for the photograph twice more, discussed the ones that arrived, praised and criticised the verse Wilkinson sent him, recommended his own 'The Portrait of Mr W. H.' when the boy said he loved Shakespeare's sonnets, told Reggie Turner and Robert Ross about him, and asked Ross to go down to Radley and look at him. The salutation moved from 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' to 'My dear Boy' and the signature from 'Sincerely yours' to 'Affectionately yours'. They never met. Wilkinson went up to Oxford, became the novelist Louis Marlow, sent a wreath to Wilde's funeral in 1900, and in 1953 printed the letters in Seven Friends, where he confessed that the dramatic society had never existed.

sources.quote: Louis Umfreville Wilkinson (1881–1966) was at this time a Radley schoolboy. … In his Seven Friends (1953) he quotes many of Wilde's letters to him, and confessed that he invented an 'Ipswich Dramatic Society' and its wish to dramatise The Picture of Dorian Gray, so as to get into correspondence with Wilde, whom he never met.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote (n. 1) on Wilkinson's first appearance, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 14 December 1898]. The note begins at the foot of printed 1109 and concludes at the foot of 1110. The elision drops one sentence stating that he published many novels and other books under the name Louis Marlow; a closing sentence not quoted records that his first letter to Wilde and some of the subsequent ones are in the Hyde Collection. Seven Friends italic in the original.
sources.supports: THE CLASS-DECIDING FACT - 'whom he never met' - together with his dates, his being a Radley schoolboy at the time, the pen-name, the 1953 memoir, and the fabricated Ipswich Dramatic Society that opened the correspondence

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Turner, [postmark 3 January 1899], Hotel des Bains, Napoule; opening sentence of the paragraph in which Wilde tells Turner about the correspondence. Heading as printed: 'To Reginald Turner / MS Hyde'. The three sentences that follow, not transcribed here, report that the boy sends his photograph constantly and praise it, report that he reads nothing but Wilde's books and wishes to follow in Wilde's footsteps, and record Wilde's reply that they lead to terrible places. The letter is signed 'Ever affectionately yours OSCAR'.
sources.supports: Wilkinson's age at the time of the correspondence, in Wilde's own contemporaneous words and exactly as the record states it - seventeen; and the fact that Wilde described the correspondence to a third party as constant
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Single sentence, complete.

sources.quote: Wilkinson had invented this, like the dramatisation of Dorian Gray, to attract Wilde's attention.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 2) at printed 1127, keyed to Wilde to Robert Ross, Saturday [25 February 1899], in which Wilde urges Ross, if he is down at Oxford, to go to Radley and see Wilkinson, reporting the boy's claims that he had known FitzGerald and had been at the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan - the latter being the claim this note corrects. Dorian Gray italic in the original.
sources.supports: That the fabrications continued past the opening gambit, and that the initiative in the acquaintance was Wilkinson's; also that Wilde was recommending him to Ross in person
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1173, printed folio 1127 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Whole footnote.

sources.quote: It was not Louis Wilkinson but his father who had known FitzGerald. They were neighbours in Suffolk.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note (n. 1) at printed 1133, keyed to Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899]. The elided opening of the note corrects Wilde's attribution of the Omar Khayyam manuscript to a kinsman, Sir Ralph Ouseley, naming Sir William Ouseley (1767-1842) instead.
sources.supports: A correction to the 1127 n. 2 picture of wholesale invention - the FitzGerald connection was real but paternal, so not every claim Wilkinson made was manufactured
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1179, printed folio 1133 confirmed on the rendered page, read as page image 2026-08-03. Final two sentences of the footnote, quoted complete; the preceding sentences concern the manuscript's provenance.

sources.quote: My dear Boy
sources.context: Salutation of Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [postmark 20 March 1899], Gland, Switzerland; heading as printed 'To Louis Wilkinson / MS Wilkinson', signed 'Affectionately yours OSCAR'. Recorded as the endpoint of a documented four-month register shift, each element read in the source so far or the last: [postmark 14 December 1898] p. 1109 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; 28 December [1898] p. 1113 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Sincerely yours'; [postmark 3 February 1899] pp. 1122-23 opens 'Dear Mr Wilkinson' and signs 'Your friend'; this letter opens 'My dear Boy' and signs 'Affectionately yours'. 'My dear Boy' is the salutation Wilde also used to Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.supports: The escalation of address across the correspondence, as a matter of documented salutation and signature rather than of interpretation

sources.quote: I am in constant correspondence now with a Radley schoolboy, aged seventeen. His photograph, which he has sent me, and sends me constantly, is most beautiful. He seems to read nothing but my books, and says his one desire is to 'follow in my footsteps'! But I have told him that they lead to terrible places. … My Radley boy is called Louis Wilkinson – a horrid name – but his photograph is most interesting, and his poetry passionate and incoherent. He seems a most astonishing boy. He has dramatised Dorian Gray!
sources.context: Two passages printed on the same page, from different letters: the first is Wilde to Reginald Turner (postmark 3 January 1899), the second Wilde to Robert Ross (Thursday [? 12 January 1899]). Wilkinson is named only in the second.
sources.supports: The documented acts on which direction rests - three photograph requests, the comments on the photographs when they came, and the reports to Turner and Ross; recorded as description because the addressee was seventeen
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1164, printed folio 1118 read off the rendered page. The ellipsis spans the end of the Turner letter and the opening of the Ross letter, both on this folio - it is not an elision inside a single letter., read as a page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote:
Dear Boy, Come and see me next week. I can get you a room in my hotel.
I am not going to write to you any more: I want to see you. I have waited long enough. [Signature cut away.]
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, [Postmark 15 July 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris
sources.supports: The last surviving letter of the run, and the most direct: an invitation to Paris with a room offered in his own hotel, and the correspondence itself set aside in favour of meeting.

sources.quote: I fear you would not like my hotel. I live there because I have no money ever. It is an absurd place: it is not a background: the only thing really nice in the whole hotel is your own photograph: but one cannot, or one should not, play Narcissus to a photograph: even water is horribly treacherous: the eyes of one who loves one are the only mirror.
sources.context: Wilde to Louis Wilkinson, postmark 4 January 1900, from the Hôtel d'Alsace. The photograph is the one Wilkinson had sent him, which Wilde had already reported to Ross (printed 1118). The letter opens 'My dear Boy'. Wilde is dead within the year.
sources.supports: Wilde's own words placing Wilkinson's photograph at the centre of his room and his attention - the desire, expressed obliquely and unmistakably.

relationships.certainty_reasoning: Alfred Wood's sworn testimony (April 1895) describes an act of 'the grossest indecency' at 16 Tite Street after Lord Alfred Douglas introduced him to Wilde by telegram in January 1893, and the jury at the final trial convicted Wilde on count 13 (gross indecency with Wood at Tite Street). Wilde denied the relations on oath at the libel trial ('It is perfectly untrue'). Wood was an admitted blackmailer (he took £175 from the Allen extortion), recorded in the dossier for credibility assessment; the conviction plus first-person testimony anchors the class.
relationships.date_label: January – spring 1893 (Wood left for America with Wilde's £35)
relationships.summary: Douglas telegraphed Wilde from Salisbury to look after Alfred Wood, an out-of-work clerk then living at Taylor's; Wilde met him at the Café Royal, dined him in a private room at the Florence, and took him home to 16 Tite Street, where Wood's testimony describes an act of gross indecency. Wood had found letters from Wilde to Douglas in a suit Douglas gave him; in spring 1893 Wilde gave him £30 plus £5 and Wood left for America. Wilde was convicted on the Tite Street count at the final trial.

sources.quote: When did you first know Wilde?—About a month after I made the acquaintance of Taylor. How did you come to know Wilde?—I was introduced to him by a gentleman at the Café Royal. Who was the gentleman?—Must I give the name? Yes.—Lord Alfred Douglas. What took place when you were introduced to Wilde?—I was introduced by telegram. By Mr. Justice Charles—You would have led anyone to believe that you were personally introduced?—In consequence of the telegram I went to the Café Royal at nine o'clock one evening. Mr. Wilde was sitting down. He spoke to me first. He asked "Are you Alfred Wood?" I said, "Yes." Then he offered me something to drink and I had something; and then he invited me to go round to the Florence in Rupert Street to dinner. I went with him and we dined in a private room. Examination continued—What kind of meal was it?—Very nice, one of the best to be got. What wine did you have?—Champagne. After dinner I went with Mr. Wilde to 16 Tite Street. There was nobody in the house to my knowledge. Mr. Wilde let himself in with a latchkey.
sources.context: Alfred Wood's examination-in-chief by Mr. Avory, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895, with an interjection from the bench by Mr. Justice Charles. Wood had just testified that in January 1893 he was out of work and went to live at Taylor's Little College Street rooms for about three weeks. The page ends on 'latchkey'; what follows on p. 202 is the act evidence quoted below.
sources.supports: How the two men met, in the participant's own sworn words: Douglas's telegram introduction, Wilde waiting at the Café Royal and opening with 'Are you Alfred Wood?', the drink, the private room at the Florence, and the walk back to 16 Tite Street. The plainest first-hand characterization of the connection, chosen in preference to the act evidence that follows it.
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 241 (printed p. 201, folio in the source foot), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03. No elisions.

sources.quote: How did you come to know Wilde?—I was introduced to him by a gentleman at the Café Royal. Who was the gentleman?—Must I give the name? Yes.—Lord Alfred Douglas. … After dinner I went with Mr. Wilde to 16 Tite Street. There was nobody in the house to my knowledge. Mr. Wilde let himself in with a latchkey. We went up to a bedroom where we had hock and selzer. Here an act of the grossest indecency occurred. Mr. Wilde used his influence to induce me to consent. He made me nearly drunk. … Afterwards I lay on a sofa with him. It was a long time, however, before I would allow him to actually do the act of indecency.
sources.context: Alfred Wood's examination-in-chief, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895 (the second ellipsis is printed in Hyde's text)
sources.supports: sworn first-person testimony of gross indecency at 16 Tite Street, January 1893, after Douglas's telegram introduction — the class-deciding quote
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaves 241 and 242 (printed pp. 201 and 202, folios in the source foot), both read as IIIF page images 2026-08-03. Supersedes the earlier note that the p. 201 opening was OCR-derived - both pages have now been read at the image. The ellipsis after 'He made me nearly drunk.' is printed in Hyde's text; the first is an elision by us.

sources.quote: Did you ever meet Wilde again?—He once came to my room in Langham Street. Did you know he was coming?—Yes. How did you know?—He came by appointment. He took me out to buy me a present. He bought me half-a-dozen shirts, some collars, and handkerchiefs, and a silver watch and chain. Before he took me out we had some tea. Has he given you money on any other occasion?—Yes; he has given me two or three pounds when he has met me. Up to what time did your acquaintanceship with Wilde go on?—Up to the end of March. How did it cease?—I told Taylor that I would like to get away from a certain class of people, and I think I mentioned it to Mr. Wilde, who gave me £30. I saw him at Taylor's rooms.
sources.context: Alfred Wood's examination-in-chief, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895, immediately preceding the evidence about the letters. Earlier on the same page Wood put the money given on the first night at 'About £3 I think it was', given at the Florence before Tite Street was mentioned.
sources.supports: What was given, how often, and how the acquaintance ended - in the participant's own words: the Langham Street visit by appointment, presents of half-a-dozen shirts, collars, handkerchiefs and a silver watch and chain, two or three pounds on other meetings, and the £30 in March 1893 on Wood's asking to get away
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 242 (printed p. 202, folio in the source foot), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03. No elisions.

sources.quote: He said, "You have some letters I should like to get back," and he gave me £30. In what form?—Two £10 notes and two £5 notes. … Did the letters belong to you?—No. They were letters I found in some clothes Lord Alfred Douglas had given me. They were letters from Mr. Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.context: Alfred Wood's examination-in-chief on the letters and the passage money, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
sources.supports: the stolen-letters affair that ended the acquaintance: £30 (plus £5 next day, p. 203) and Wood's departure for America
sources.provenance: IA in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, leaf 242 (printed p. 202), read as IIIF page image 2026-08-03

sources.quote: How long had you known Wood?—I think I met him at the end of January, 1893. I met him at the Café Royal where he was sent to find me by Lord Alfred Douglas who telegraphed from Salisbury. Lord Alfred asked me to do what I could for Wood, who was seeking a post as a clerk. … I suggest that you first had immoral relations with him and then gave him money?—It is perfectly untrue.
sources.context: Wilde's cross-examination by Carson, Regina (Wilde) v. Queensberry, April 1895
sources.supports: Wilde's on-oath denial of the relations, and his account of the Douglas introduction

works._voice_note: Quotes carry a per-quote `voice`: 'period' when the text is ENTIRELY in the words of someone alive in the world this map describes (a letter, a diary, sworn testimony, a contemporary memoir or interview), 'modern' when a historian, biographer or editor is writing about them. It is deliberately per-quote, not per-work: Holland & Hart-Davis's footnotes are modern prose inside a primary volume, while a Douglas or Langtry letter printed inside one of those same footnotes is still a period voice. Mixed text - a biographer's sentence with a period phrase quoted inside it - counts as modern, because it is not entirely the period voice. The panel sets period quotes between large quotation marks; modern ones keep a plain rule.
works._evidence_date_note: A source's `evidence_date` is the date of the THING BEING EVIDENCED - when the letter was written, the testimony sworn, the meeting held - never the publication year of the book it is quoted from. A 1985 biography describing an 1908 holiday carries 1908. The panel orders a connection's sources by this field, so a publication year files modern commentary among the contemporary record. Where a card evidences no dated event at all - historiography, a statement about how a claim is treated in scholarship - leave it null; undated cards sort to the end.

This volume nonetheless mentions Robinson on 64 pages and Anstruther-Thomson on 84, so it may well carry Lee looking back on it - but a contemporaneous account of the ending is not in this volume.

vivien-foster-1982.author: Renée Vivien
vivien-foster-1982.title: A Woman Appeared to Me
vivien-foster-1982.short_cite: Vivien, A Woman Appeared to Me, trans. Foster (1982)
vivien-foster-1982.note:
116 pp, text-layered but the layer is BADLY CORRUPT - it renders 'like' as 'Hke', 'little' as 'Httle', 'delicate' as 'dehcate'. Use it to find; transcribe only from the rendered page.
THIS IS THE FIRST-EDITION TEXT. Its copyright page states 'French text printed by Alphonse Lemerre, Paris, 1904', and Dagmar is present throughout (39 occurrences) - so it translates the 1904 original, not the 1905 rewrite. Translation © 1976, this printing 1982. It unblocks what had been blocked since 2026-08-03: the 1904 French is still unobtained, but its content is now readable. Quotations from it are Foster's English, not Vivien's French - flag that in provenance and do not treat the wording as Vivien's own.
Gayle Rubin's introduction is a substantial piece of scholarship in its own right and identifies the roman-a-clef cast independently of Parker.

vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.author: Renée Vivien
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.title: Une femme m'apparut…
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.short_cite: Vivien, Une femme m'apparut… (1905 nouvelle édition)
vivien-une-femme-1905-repo.note:
208 pp, text-layered and the layer is good (French accents intact). It IS the French - but it is the 1905 rewrite, NOT the 1904 first edition, and the book says so itself: the title page at PDF p. 19, read as a page image 2026-08-04, reads 'Une Femme m'apparut. / NOUVELLE ÉDITION / PARIS / ALPHONSE LEMERRE, ÉDITEUR / 23-31, PASSAGE CHOISEUL / M DCCCCV'. A HardPress reprint of a Boston Public Library copy digitised by the Internet Archive; the '1877' in the filename is Vivien's birth year, not an edition date.
The cast confirms it independently: Lorély (165 occurrences), Ione, Nedda, Doriane, Undine, San Giovanni - and no Dagmar in any spelling. Lorély is the 1905's replacement for the 1904's Vally, so her presence is positive evidence for the rewrite rather than mere absence of Dagmar. NOTE FOR SEARCHING: 'Lorély' carries an acute accent and an unaccented grep for 'Lorely' returns nothing - that briefly made this copy look like it had no leading lady at all.
For Dagmar use vivien-foster-1982, whose copyright page states it translates the Lemerre 1904.
OPEN DISCREPANCY, 2026-08-04. This scanned 1905 runs to printed p. 168 and contains no Dagmar chapters - an accent- and OCR-tolerant search of all 208 pages finds no 'dagmar', 'poetesse', 'saxe' or 'ressentais', while distinctive phrases elsewhere in the book are found normally, so it is not a search failure. But the French Wikisource text explicitly labelled 1905 (fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Une_femme_m'apparut/1905, in the Anna's Archive EPUB in this folder) has Lorély 207 times AND Dagmar 32 times, in chapters XXXV-XXXVIII. Both cannot be right. Either this printed copy is shorter than the text Wikisource transcribed, or Wikisource's 1905 is conflated. Until that is resolved, do not repeat the flat claim that Dagmar appears only in the 1904 - what IS established is that she is absent from this printed 1905 copy and present in the 1904.

bucke-calamus-1897.author: Walt Whitman
bucke-calamus-1897.title: Calamus: A Series of Letters Written During the Years 1868-1880 by Walt Whitman to a Young Friend (Peter Doyle)
bucke-calamus-1897.note: PUBLIC DOMAIN and fully open on archive.org - no borrowing account needed. Three copies are on IA; this is the one used. Two things in one volume: Bucke's introduction, which contains a long verbatim INTERVIEW WITH PETER DOYLE (printed c. 21-34, its own running head), and Whitman's letters to Doyle 1868-1880. So the volume carries BOTH participants' voices, which is why the edge is self-reported. PAGINATION: scan number = printed folio + 13, verified by reading the folio on three rendered page images (n30 = printed 17, n36 = printed 23, n48 = printed 35). Confirm on each page read - this project has been bitten by non-constant offsets in four other volumes. Page images download directly at https://archive.org/download/calamusseriesofl00whitrich/page/nN.jpg and the OCR is at .../calamusseriesofl00whitrich_djvu.txt - text locates, image verifies. NOTE Bucke's title says 'a young friend'; the 1897 volume is discreet by design, and the discretion is itself evidence of what was being handled.
